AI.motivation: LLM agent programs combine conventional code with framework-induced semantics (e.g., agent constructors, tool decorators, agent handoff declarations), creating a new class of agent dependencies that existing static analysis and dependency tracking tools cannot recover.
AI.method: AgentFlow constructs Agent Dependency Graphs (ADGs), a framework-agnostic graph with typed nodes (agents, prompts, models, capabilities, memory states, control policies) and typed edges (component-dependency, control-flow, data-flow). Built on ADGs, it supports analyses like Agent BOM generation and prompt-to-tool taint-style risk detection. Implemented for five agent frameworks and evaluated on AgentZoo (5,399 programs).
AI.result: AgentFlow recovers richer agent entities and dependencies than existing AST-based tools, generates more dependency-aware Agent BOMs, and uncovers 238 taint-style prompt-to-tool risks in real-world agent programs.
AI.conclusion: ADG provides a practical foundation for understanding, governing, and securing emerging agent software.

title: The Agentic Garden of Forking Paths
summary: Empirical research rarely admits a unique analysis. Different analytical choices can lead to different conclusions from the same data, yet these hidden forking paths are difficult to observe. We show that AI agents capture much of the analytical variation among human researchers while making these paths explicit. Across four high-stakes domains, assigning different personas is sufficient for AI agents to report divergent, often opposing, conclusions from the same data and question, with findings systematically aligned with those beliefs. In a study in which 42 human research teams analyzed the same immigration dataset, AI agents reproduced 72% of the human ideological gap in reported effect estimates. Despite reaching opposing conclusions, it is difficult to identify clear issues in each analysis based on the final AI reports: 86% passed independent AI review and 78% passed majority human expert review. These findings suggest that the central challenge is often not flawed analyses, but selective exploration and reporting from a large space of methodologically defensible analyses. AI agents may amplify this longstanding problem by making such exploration inexpensive and scalable. To address this, we introduce the m-value (multiverse value), the probability that an analysis path would produce a claim at least as extreme as the reported one. We further introduce Agentic Bootstrap, which estimates the m-value by using AI agents to sample plausible analysis paths. Applied to the human immigration study, 13.5% of reported human analyses fell in the most extreme 5% of the analysis space (m<0.05). Scientific evidence should therefore be evaluated not only by a single reported analysis but also by its position within the distribution of analyses that could reasonably have been reported. Agentic Bootstrap makes this distribution observable and turns it into a criterion for scientific credibility.

AI.tldr: AI agents reproduce the analytical variation of human researchers, capturing 72% of ideological gaps in data analysis. The authors propose the m-value (multiverse value) and Agentic Bootstrap to estimate how extreme a reported analysis is within the space of plausible analyses.
AI.motivation: Empirical research lacks unique analyses; different analytical choices lead to divergent conclusions from the same data, but these forking paths are hidden. The authors aim to make these paths explicit and measurable.
AI.method: AI agents with assigned personas analyze same datasets across four domains. Agentic Bootstrap uses AI agents to sample plausible analysis paths and estimate the m-value—the probability that an analysis path produces a claim at least as extreme as the reported one.
AI.result: AI agents reproduced 72% of the human ideological gap in effect estimates from the same immigration dataset. 86% of AI analyses passed independent AI review; 78% passed majority human expert review. 13.5% of human analyses fell in the most extreme 5% of the analysis space (m<0.05).
AI.conclusion: Scientific evidence should be evaluated not just by a single reported analysis but by its position within the distribution of defensible analyses. Agentic Bootstrap makes this distribution observable and serves as a criterion for scientific credibility.

title: How Should Transformers Encode Numeric Values in Electronic Health Records?
comment: 16 pages, 15 figures, 3 tables, accepted to ICML 2026, to be published in Proceedings of Machine Learning Research
summary: How do we encode numeric values in transformer-based sequence processing, particularly in electronic health record (EHR) data? We systematically compare discrete, continuous, and hybrid value encoding strategies using synthetic arithmetic tasks embedded within real-world EHR data, as well as real-world clinical prediction tasks. Our study reveals trade-offs between numeric precision, optimisation stability, and architectural flexibility. We find that approaches that explicitly model value-concept interactions perform best on precision-sensitive arithmetic tasks when architectural constraints permit. Hybrid token-based approaches that retain numeric values but apply binning prior to projection provide a more robust and broadly applicable alternative, with the optimal number of bins following a simple empirically derived power-law in dataset size. Across tasks, models consistently exhibit reliable "good enough" numeric computation rather than exact arithmetic, while clinical gains from incorporating laboratory values are task-dependent. This suggests that robustness and deployability often outweigh maximal numeric precision in practice, motivating hybrid token-based approaches as a practical default.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically compares discrete, continuous, and hybrid numeric encoding strategies for transformer models in EHR data, finding that hybrid token-based approaches with binning offer the best practical trade-off between precision and robustness, with optimal bin count following a power-law in dataset size.
AI.motivation: To determine how to best encode numeric values in transformer-based sequence processing for EHR data, given the lack of systematic comparison between discrete, continuous, and hybrid encoding strategies in realistic clinical settings.
AI.method: Systematically compared discrete, continuous, and hybrid value encoding strategies using synthetic arithmetic tasks embedded within real-world EHR data, combined with real-world clinical prediction tasks, and derived an empirical power-law for optimal bin count.
AI.result: Value-concept interaction modeling excels on precision-sensitive tasks under appropriate architectural constraints; hybrid token-based binning is more broadly robust; optimal bin count follows a power-law in dataset size; models exhibit "good enough" computation rather than exact arithmetic; clinical gains from lab values are task-dependent.
AI.conclusion: Robustness and deployability often outweigh maximal numeric precision in practice, motivating hybrid token-based approaches as a practical default for numeric encoding in EHR transformer models.

title: How Much Future Helps? A Controlled Study of Future-Privileged Supervision for Causal Egocentric Gaze Estimation
comment: Accepted to the 7th International Workshop on Eye and Gaze in Computer Vision (GAZE 2026), CVPR 2026. Best Paper Award
summary: Egocentric gaze estimation is commonly studied using models that process the full video with access to future frames, while real-world applications require strictly causal, online prediction. This discrepancy raises key questions: Does future context inherently provide valuable signals for gaze estimation? If so, how much future look-ahead optimally supervises a causal model during training? To investigate, we propose a controlled framework featuring a future-aware branch that accesses a tunable look-ahead horizon during training but is discarded at inference. This design isolates the impact of future context while keeping the inference architecture fixed and strictly causal. Across EGTEA Gaze+ and Ego4D, we find that future-privileged supervision consistently improves causal gaze prediction, confirming its utility. However, performance gains do not increase monotonically with longer look-ahead, but rather peak within a bounded temporal regime. Specifically, optimal performance corresponds to roughly 1.7--3.3 seconds of future context ($H{\in}[5, 10]$) on EGTEA Gaze+ and 2.7 seconds ($H{=}10$) on Ego4D. Our results demonstrate that lightweight causal models can effectively absorb future-aware signals, providing practical guidance for real-time egocentric gaze modeling.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates whether future context benefits egocentric gaze estimation in causal models, finding it does help but with optimal performance at a limited look-ahead horizon (1.7-3.3 seconds), not monotonically increasing with longer future access.
AI.motivation: There is a gap between egocentric gaze estimation research (non-causal models with future frames) and real-world applications (strictly causal, online prediction). The authors aim to determine if future context is inherently useful for gaze estimation and what look-ahead horizon optimally supervises a causal model.
AI.method: A controlled framework with a future-aware branch (accessing tunable look-ahead during training, discarded at inference) is proposed, keeping the inference architecture strictly causal and fixed. Experiments are conducted on EGTEA Gaze+ and Ego4D datasets with varying look-ahead horizons H.
AI.result: Future-privileged supervision consistently improves causal gaze prediction. Performance gains peak within a bounded temporal regime rather than increasing monotonically: optimal at H∈[5,10] (≈1.7-3.3s) on EGTEA Gaze+ and H=10 (≈2.7s) on Ego4D.
AI.conclusion: Lightweight causal models can effectively absorb future-aware signals from training, providing practical guidance for real-time egocentric gaze modeling.

title: When Agents Do Not Stop: Uncovering Infinite Agentic Loops in LLM Agents
summary: LLM agents increasingly rely on iterative execution to solve tasks through planning, tool use, state updates, and agent collaboration. While this design enables flexible automation, it also creates a new class of failures: an agent may repeatedly execute model calls, tools, workflow transitions, or agent handoffs when the feedback path is not effectively bounded. We call this problem Infinite Agentic Loops (IALs). IALs are not ordinary programming loops; they arise from the interaction between agent logic, framework semantics, runtime observations, and termination mechanisms. Such failures can amplify a single request into long running model and tool execution, causing cost exhaustion, model denial of service, context growth, and repeated external side effects. We propose IAL-Scan, a static analysis tool for detecting IAL failures in real-world LLM agent projects. IAL-Scan abstracts heterogeneous agent code into a framework independent Agent IR, builds an Agentic Loop Dependence Graph (ALDG) to recover explicit and framework induced feedback paths, and checks whether these paths can repeatedly reach costly or state growing operations without an effective bound. We evaluate IAL-Scan on 6,549 LLM agent repositories. It reports 74 potential findings, among which manual review confirms 68 IAL failures across 47 projects, achieving 91.9% precision.

AI.tldr: IAL-Scan is a static analysis tool that detects Infinite Agentic Loops (IALs) in LLM agent projects by analyzing feedback paths that cause unbounded iterative execution, achieving 91.9% precision across 47 projects from 6,549 repositories.
AI.motivation: LLM agents performing iterative execution via planning, tool use, and handoffs can suffer from unbounded feedback loops (IALs) that cause cost exhaustion, model denial of service, context growth, and repeated side effects. Existing tools do not address this failure class.
AI.method: IAL-Scan abstracts agent code into a framework-independent Agent IR, constructs an Agentic Loop Dependence Graph (ALDG) to recover explicit and framework-induced feedback paths, and checks whether these paths can repeatedly reach costly or state-growing operations without an effective bound.
AI.result: Evaluated on 6,549 LLM agent repositories; reported 74 potential findings, manual review confirmed 68 IAL failures across 47 projects, achieving 91.9% precision.
AI.conclusion: IALs are a distinct class of failures in LLM agent systems arising from unbounded feedback paths. IAL-Scan effectively detects them via static analysis, demonstrating high precision on real-world projects.

title: Janus: a Playground for User-Involved Agentic Permission Management
comment: Code and data released on GitHub: https://github.com/GraceBrigham/Janus
summary: AI agents that autonomously execute tool calls on a user's behalf raise pressing questions about permission management: what role could users play, and what role should they play? Despite many proposed approaches, the user's role in agentic permission management remains under explored. We introduce Janus, a playground system for implementing and evaluating user-involved agentic permission management designs. Janus consists of two components: Janus-Core, a modular agentic system supporting a diverse spectrum of permission management designs, and Janus-Harness, an automated evaluation framework. Grounded in a conceptual model that identifies key design axes for user involvement, we implement six permission assistants spanning the design space and evaluate them across three scenarios and three synthetic responders. We demonstrate that user input is critical and can significantly strengthen privacy and security, that AI augmentation of user decisions can help reduce cognitive load, and that realistic user behavior including permission fatigue must be accounted for in system design. No single design performs optimally across all contexts, motivating a more principled and context-sensitive approach to deploying permission assistants in agentic systems. Janus is publicly available to support future investigation into this dimension of agentic system design.

AI.tldr: Janus is a playground system for designing and evaluating user-involved permission management in AI agent systems, demonstrating that user input significantly strengthens security but no single design works optimally across all contexts.
AI.motivation: The user's role in agentic permission management (when AI agents autonomously execute tool calls on behalf of users) remains under-explored despite many proposed approaches, raising pressing questions about what role users could and should play.
AI.method: Janus consists of two components: Janus-Core (a modular agentic system supporting diverse permission management designs) and Janus-Harness (an automated evaluation framework). Grounded in a conceptual model identifying key design axes for user involvement, the authors implemented six permission assistants spanning the design space and evaluated them across three scenarios and three synthetic responders.
AI.result: User input is critical and can significantly strengthen privacy and security; AI augmentation of user decisions can help reduce cognitive load; realistic user behavior including permission fatigue must be accounted for; no single design performs optimally across all contexts.
AI.conclusion: A more principled and context-sensitive approach to deploying permission assistants in agentic systems is needed. Janus is publicly available to support future investigation into this dimension of agentic system design.

title: NeuroBridge: Bridging Multi-Task MRI Knowledge for Neurodegenerative Disease Diagnosis
summary: INTRODUCTION: Accurate MRI-based identification of Alzheimer's disease (AD), mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and related dementias remains challenging because disease-related structural changes are often subtle and heterogeneous. We developed NeuroBridge, a clinically guided multi-task MRI framework for neurodegenerative disease diagnosis. METHODS: NeuroBridge integrates large-scale self-supervised MRI pretraining with hippocampal segmentation, hippocampal atrophy classification, and reconstruction objectives, followed by gated fusion fine-tuning. Performance was evaluated across ADNI and OASIS cohorts, including cross-cohort transfer, probability-based analysis, and opportunistic screening. RESULTS: NeuroBridge achieved the highest performance across evaluated classification tasks, reaching 88.17% accuracy for AD versus cognitively normal controls in ADNI and 82.78% in OASIS. The largest gains occurred in MCI-related and mixed-diagnosis settings. The framework demonstrated strong cross-cohort generalization, systematic associations between predicted-class probability and accuracy, and the feasibility of probability-based opportunistic screening. DISCUSSION: Clinically guided multi-task representation learning improves neurodegenerative MRI diagnosis beyond conventional single-task approaches. NeuroBridge provides a robust and scalable framework for dementia assessment and MRI-based opportunistic screening.

AI.tldr: NeuroBridge is a clinically guided multi-task MRI framework that integrates self-supervised pretraining with hippocampal segmentation, atrophy classification, and reconstruction, achieving state-of-the-art performance (88.17% AD vs. CN accuracy on ADNI, 82.78% on OASIS) and demonstrating strong cross-cohort generalization and feasibility for opportunistic screening.
AI.motivation: Accurate MRI-based identification of Alzheimer's disease (AD), mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and related dementias is challenging due to subtle and heterogeneous disease-related structural changes.
AI.method: NeuroBridge integrates large-scale self-supervised MRI pretraining with hippocampal segmentation, hippocampal atrophy classification, and reconstruction objectives, followed by gated fusion fine-tuning. Evaluation was conducted on ADNI and OASIS cohorts with cross-cohort transfer, probability-based analysis, and opportunistic screening.
AI.result: Achieved 88.17% accuracy for AD vs. cognitively normal controls in ADNI and 82.78% in OASIS, with largest gains in MCI-related and mixed-diagnosis settings. Demonstrated strong cross-cohort generalization and systematic associations between predicted-class probability and accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Clinically guided multi-task representation learning improves neurodegenerative MRI diagnosis beyond conventional single-task approaches, providing a robust and scalable framework for dementia assessment and MRI-based opportunistic screening.

title: A Cost-Aware, Paired Protocol for Auditing Dynamic Tool Synthesis in Agentic Video Question Answering
summary: Agentic Video Question Answering (VideoQA) systems invoke tools during inference, but their tool libraries are fixed, so recurring procedures are rebuilt from primitives on every question. Synthesizing composite tools could remove this overhead, but whether such expansion helps is hard to assess: final-answer accuracy, the standard metric, ignores inference effort, so it cannot reveal how a system shifts cost. We propose a cost-aware, paired protocol for auditing tool-augmented video agents. The protocol pairs two complete systems on the same input for each question and reports their net difference across accuracy and cost jointly. For each question, it sorts the paired outcome into one of six groups defined by joint correctness and by the change in visible tool calls, separating accuracy-preserving efficiency gains from harmful regressions. Significance is reported with McNemar's test and paired bootstrap confidence intervals. We instantiate the protocol on Dynamic-SAGE, an agentic VideoQA framework that synthesizes, validates, and persistently registers executable composite tools for reuse on unseen questions, and evaluate it against the SAGE baseline on SAGE-Bench. The audit reveals a multi-axis profile that a scalar accuracy comparison would miss: Dynamic-SAGE improves accuracy by 7.5 points (p < 0.001) and reduces reasoning turns and visible tool calls by roughly 28%, while shifting rather than reducing inference cost, as token usage rises 34% and cost 26%. Gains are largest on visual and open-ended questions and neutral on verbal and multimodal ones, and residual failures concentrate on hard, open-ended questions where the pipeline does the most work. By measuring accuracy and cost jointly, the protocol shows where the pipeline-level difference is reliable and where it is not. The code is available at https://github.com/KurbanIntelligenceLab/Dynamic-SAGE.

AI.tldr: Dynamic-SAGE is an agentic VideoQA framework that synthesizes reusable composite tools dynamically, evaluated via a cost-aware paired audit protocol that jointly measures accuracy and inference cost. It improves accuracy by 7.5 points while reducing reasoning turns ~28%, but increases token usage 34% and cost 26%.
AI.motivation: Standard VideoQA systems rely on fixed tool libraries, forcing recurring procedures to be rebuilt from scratch per question. Moreover, accuracy alone cannot capture inference cost shifts, making it hard to assess whether dynamic tool expansion is beneficial.
AI.method: Proposes a cost-aware paired audit protocol that reports joint accuracy-cost differences via six outcome groups, McNemar's test, and paired bootstrap CI. Instantiates Dynamic-SAGE, which synthesizes, validates, and persistently registers executable composite tools for reuse on unseen questions.
AI.result: Dynamic-SAGE improves accuracy by 7.5 points (p<0.001), reduces reasoning turns and visible tool calls ~28%, but increases token usage 34% and cost 26%. Largest gains on visual and open-ended questions; neutral on verbal/multimodal ones.
AI.conclusion: The joint protocol reveals multi-axis trade-offs hidden by scalar accuracy comparisons, showing where pipeline-level differences are reliable and where they are not.

title: Refploit: Facilitating Exploit Construction via Code-Agent Trajectory Repair
summary: Vulnerability exploits play a crucial role in assessing the downstream impact of Java library vulnerabilities. While some vulnerabilities are accompanied by disclosed exploit references, automatically reproducing such references into runnable exploits remains challenging because they are often incomplete, unstructured, or only describe partial reproduction steps. Recent code agents provide a promising way to automate this process, but our study shows that their generated exploits often appear successful without triggering the actual vulnerable logic, such as replacing vulnerable APIs with self-implemented functions. To address this, we propose Refploit, an LLM-based trajectory recovery framework for facilitating vulnerability reproduction from public exploit references. The key insight is that a failed agent trajectory is not entirely useless. It may have already completed some reproduction subtasks while also revealing misleading directions that should be avoided. Refploit first validates an agent-generated exploit through differential execution. When the exploit is ineffective, Refploit analyzes its reproduction progress, locates the trajectory segments associated with the reproduction progress, and derives constraints to guide focused recovery. We evaluate Refploit on three open-source Java vulnerability datasets, covering 172 exploit references for 143 vulnerabilities. Under DeepSeek-V4-Flash, Refploit successfully reproduces 138 exploits, achieving a reproduction rate of 80.2%. It achieves a 64.3% relative improvement over the initially generated trajectories and outperforms both the SOTA exploit-generation method PoCGen and advanced code agents such as Codex with GPT-5.4. We further adapt Refploit to another code agent and observe consistent improvements, demonstrating its generality.

AI.tldr: Refploit is an LLM-based framework that recovers valid exploits from failed agent trajectories by analyzing reproduction progress, locating relevant segments, and deriving constraints, achieving 80.2% reproduction rate on 172 exploit references across 143 Java vulnerabilities.
AI.motivation: Automatically reproducing runnable exploits from public exploit references is challenging because references are often incomplete, unstructured, or partial. Existing code agents often produce exploits that appear successful but fail to trigger actual vulnerable logic (e.g., replacing vulnerable APIs with self-implemented functions).
AI.method: Refploit first validates agent-generated exploits via differential execution. When ineffective, it analyzes reproduction progress, locates trajectory segments associated with that progress, derives constraints from those segments, and guides focused recovery of the exploit.
AI.result: On 172 exploit references for 143 Java vulnerabilities with DeepSeek-V4-Flash, Refploit reproduced 138 exploits (80.2% reproduction rate), achieving 64.3% relative improvement over initial trajectories, outperforming PoCGen and Codex with GPT-5.4. Consistent improvements were observed when adapted to another code agent.
AI.conclusion: Failed agent trajectories are not useless—they contain partially completed subtasks and reveal misleading directions. Leveraging these signals via trajectory recovery significantly improves automated vulnerability reproduction, and the approach generalizes across different code agents.

title: Revisiting Chain-of-Thought Reasoning under Limited Supervision: Semi-supervised Chain-of-Thought Learning
summary: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning has emerged as an effective approach for activating latent reasoning capabilities in large language models. However, most existing CoT methods use reasoning chains mainly as inference-time prompts, while the generated reasoning traces are rarely reused as semi-supervised learning signals. In this report, we define \textbf{Semi-supervised Chain-of-Thought Learning} and propose \textbf{Semi-CoT}, a simple framework that uses unlabeled questions to construct pseudo reasoning supervision. Semi-CoT samples multiple pseudo-CoTs for each unlabeled question, estimates answer-level semantic entropy, and selects low-entropy reasoning chains as reliable pseudo-CoT demonstrations. This extends the self-training view of CoT from inference-time refinement to semi-supervised pseudo-supervision. Pilot experiments on AQuA, SVAMP, GSM8K, and MultiArith show that the entropy gate selects high-precision pseudo-CoTs, with pseudo-answer precision ranging from $91.36\%$ to $100\%$. Semi-CoT also gives small gains on SVAMP and GSM8K, while AQuA shows negative transfer and MultiArith reaches a ceiling. These results suggest that unlabeled questions can provide reliable pseudo reasoning signals, but their effective use still requires stronger demonstration selection or student training.

AI.tldr: Semi-CoT proposes using unlabeled questions with answer-level semantic entropy filtering to generate pseudo chain-of-thought reasoning chains for semi-supervised learning, showing high precision but mixed task improvements.
AI.motivation: Most existing CoT methods use reasoning chains only as inference-time prompts; the generated reasoning traces are rarely reused as semi-supervised learning signals.
AI.method: Semi-CoT samples multiple pseudo-CoTs for each unlabeled question, estimates answer-level semantic entropy, and selects low-entropy reasoning chains as reliable pseudo-CoT demonstrations for semi-supervised learning.
AI.result: Entropy gate selects high-precision pseudo-CoTs (91.36%-100% precision); small gains on SVAMP and GSM8K, negative transfer on AQuA, ceiling effect on MultiArith.
AI.conclusion: Unlabeled questions can provide reliable pseudo reasoning signals, but effective use still requires stronger demonstration selection or student training.

title: Spin-Weighted Spherical Harmonics Enable Complete and Scalable $\mathrm{E}(3)$-Equivariant Networks
summary: $\mathrm{E}(3)$-equivariant networks are promising for 3D atomistic system modeling, yet their scalability is limited by the $O(L^6)$ complexity of the Clebsch-Gordan Tensor Product (CGTP). The recently proposed Gaunt Tensor Product (GTP) reduces the complexity but is unable to capture the antisymmetric paths, resulting in incomplete expressivity. In this work, we present SpinGTP, an approach to overcome the GTP incompleteness by generalizing from scalar functions to Spin-Weighted Spherical Harmonics (SWSH). By relying on the algebraic properties of SWSH, SpinGTP recovers the missing antisymmetric interactions while maintaining the asymptotic efficiency of GTP. It also allows for a more expressive equivariant basis that naturally accounts for the parity-odd components of tensor products. We evaluate SpinGTP across diverse benchmarks, including Tetris, 3BPA, SPICE-MACE-OFF, and OC20. Our results show that SpinGTP achieves accuracies comparable to full CGTP. Notably, by explicitly capturing antisymmetric paths, SpinGTP exhibits superior performance in tasks involving chiral materials and non-centrosymmetric geometries. This work provides a complete, scalable, and mathematically rigorous path toward high-order equivariance in large-scale 3D atomistic system simulations.

AI.tldr: SpinGTP extends the Gaunt Tensor Product to Spin-Weighted Spherical Harmonics, recovering missing antisymmetric interactions in E(3)-equivariant networks, achieving full expressivity comparable to CGTP but with O(L^6) complexity reduced to GTP-level efficiency. It shows superior performance on chiral and non-centrosymmetric tasks.
AI.motivation: E(3)-equivariant networks are limited by the O(L^6) complexity of CGTP. The recently proposed GTP reduces complexity but loses antisymmetric interaction paths, resulting in incomplete expressivity. The goal is to achieve both efficiency and full expressivity.
AI.method: SpinGTP generalizes GTP from scalar functions to Spin-Weighted Spherical Harmonics (SWSH), using their algebraic properties to recover antisymmetric interactions while maintaining GTP's asymptotic efficiency and introducing a more expressive equivariant basis that naturally handles parity-odd tensor product components.
AI.result: Evaluated on Tetris, 3BPA, SPICE-MACE-OFF, and OC20 benchmarks. SpinGTP achieves accuracies comparable to full CGTP, with superior performance specifically on chiral materials and non-centrosymmetric geometry tasks due to explicit capture of antisymmetric paths.
AI.conclusion: SpinGTP provides a complete, scalable, and mathematically rigorous approach to high-order equivariance in large-scale 3D atomistic simulations, bridging the gap between CGTP's expressivity and GTP's efficiency.

title: Anti-Prompt: Image Protection against Text-Guided Image-to-Video Generation
summary: Recent advances in Image-to-Video generation allow a single image to be animated into a convincing video under text guidance, raising serious copyright and privacy risks. We propose Anti-Prompt, an image protection approach that injects imperceptible perturbations into an image, inducing visible inconsistencies and structural failures in text-guided I2V generation. Our method is motivated by a simple empirical observation. When text guidance is removed from modern I2V models, generation quality degrades markedly, not only in motion realism but also in subject preservation, structural coherence, and temporal consistency. Building on this insight, Anti-Prompt exploits the model reliance on textual guidance by attenuating text-conditioned interactions during denoising while strengthening visual-only pathways. To further systematically evaluate protection effectiveness, we introduce a Video-LLM-assisted evaluation protocol that provides interpretable, frame-grounded analyses of generation artifacts and inconsistencies. Experiments on two representative I2V architectures demonstrate that our method achieves strong protection performance while improving efficiency and cross-model transferability.

AI.tldr: Anti-Prompt is an image protection method that adds imperceptible perturbations to images, causing visible failures in text-guided Image-to-Video generation by weakening text-conditioned interactions and strengthening visual-only pathways during denoising.
AI.motivation: To protect images from unauthorized animation by text-guided Image-to-Video (I2V) generation models, which pose copyright and privacy risks by animating a single image into convincing videos under text guidance.
AI.method: Injecting imperceptible perturbations into images that exploit I2V models' reliance on textual guidance. It attenuates text-conditioned interactions during denoising while strengthening visual-only pathways, based on the observation that removing text guidance degrades generation quality severely.
AI.result: Achieves strong protection performance across two representative I2V architectures with improved efficiency and cross-model transferability.
AI.conclusion: Anti-Prompt effectively induces visible inconsistencies and structural failures in text-guided I2V generation, offering a practical defense against unauthorized image animation. The Video-LLM-assisted evaluation protocol provides interpretable artifact analysis.

title: KRCA: An Efficient Root Cause Analysis System in Hyper-Scale Microservice Systems via Agentic AI
summary: Hyper-scale microservice systems have become the standard infrastructure for large-scale Internet companies. These systems consist of numerous loosely coupled microservices that evolve independently through continuous development and deployment. Such complexity makes failures unavoidable, necessitating efficient Root Cause Analysis (RCA) to help Site Reliability Engineers (SREs) quickly localize root cause services and classify failure types. However, existing RCA methods often struggle to adapt to the extreme dynamism and massive scale of these systems. In this paper, we present KRCA, an end-to-end RCA system designed for hyper-scale microservice systems. To manage the vast search space, KRCA employs a multi-stage pipeline that begins with an API-level drilldown to isolate suspicious services. It then instantiates a skeleton-based causal graph from anomalous metrics to serve as a high-recall structural prior, before utilizing a memory-augmented multi-agent framework to verify causality and generate the final failure report. By combining structured causal constraints with multi-agent reasoning, KRCA employs balances diagnostic accuracy with the efficiency requirements of real-time production use. Experimental results show that KRCA achieves AC@1 scores of 0.88 and 0.79 for root cause service localization and failure type classification, outperforming the strongest baseline by at lease 31% in absolute gains. KRCA has been deployed in Kuaishou's production environment for over six months, reducing the average diagnosis time by 77.3%.

AI.tldr: KRCA is an end-to-end RCA system for hyper-scale microservice systems that uses a multi-stage pipeline (API-level drilldown, skeleton-based causal graph, memory-augmented multi-agent reasoning) to achieve high accuracy (AC@1 0.88 for localization, 0.79 for classification) and reduce diagnosis time by 77.3% in production at Kuaishou.
AI.motivation: Hyper-scale microservice systems are complex and failure-prone, but existing RCA methods fail to adapt to their extreme dynamism and massive scale, necessitating a more efficient and accurate approach.
AI.method: KRCA employs a multi-stage pipeline: (1) API-level drilldown to narrow the search space, (2) skeleton-based causal graph construction from anomalous metrics as a structural prior, and (3) a memory-augmented multi-agent framework for causal verification and failure report generation.
AI.result: KRCA achieves AC@1 scores of 0.88 for root cause service localization and 0.79 for failure type classification, outperforming the strongest baseline by at least 31% in absolute gains. Deployed at Kuaishou for over six months, it reduces average diagnosis time by 77.3%.
AI.conclusion: KRCA effectively balances diagnostic accuracy with real-time production efficiency through combining structured causal constraints with multi-agent reasoning, and proves practically viable in a large-scale production environment.

title: OPINE-World: Programmatic World Modeling with Ontology-error-Prioritized Interactive Exploration
summary: Learning how an environment behaves from interaction is central to building agents that adapt to unfamiliar tasks. World models learned with deep networks are flexible but data-hungry and transfer poorly beyond their training distribution. Program-synthesized world models, written as source code by LLMs and refined through counterexample-guided inductive synthesis (CEGIS), are instead data-efficient and reusable, yet they have been demonstrated mainly on structured-state worlds with a given object vocabulary, and a single program search does not scale to pixel-rendered environments whose object structure must be hypothesized flexibly. We introduce OPINE-World, an LLM agent that learns an object-centric programmatic world model online from interaction. OPINE-World couples two cooperating agents in a loop of hypothesis and test, one acting in the environment and one synthesizing the model in code with replay verification and model-based planning, and it steers exploration with a Bayesian measure of object-type adequacy we call ontology error. We evaluate OPINE-World on ARC-AGI-3, a benchmark for skill-acquisition efficiency in which the object vocabulary, the goal, and the action semantics are withheld. OPINE-World solves 20 of 25 games without per-game training and reaches an action-efficiency score of 78.4 against the human baseline.

AI.tldr: OPINE-World introduces an LLM agent that learns object-centric programmatic world models online from interaction, using two cooperating agents in a hypothesis-test loop, with Bayesian ontology error for exploration. It solves 20/25 ARC-AGI-3 games without per-game training, achieving 78.4 action efficiency vs human baseline.
AI.motivation: Deep network world models are data-hungry and transfer poorly; program-synthesized models are data-efficient but previously limited to structured-state worlds with predefined object vocabularies and don't scale to pixel-rendered environments requiring flexible object hypotheses.
AI.method: OPINE-World uses an LLM agent with two cooperating agents—one acting in the environment, one synthesizing code-based models—in a hypothesis-and-test loop with replay verification, model-based planning, and Bayesian ontology error to guide exploration.
AI.result: Solves 20 of 25 ARC-AGI-3 games without per-game training; achieves action-efficiency score of 78.4 against human baseline.
AI.conclusion: Object-centric programmatic world models learned online via LLM-driven CEGIS can scale to pixel-based environments where object vocabulary, goals, and action semantics are withheld, demonstrating data efficiency and transferable skill acquisition.

title: The Rollout Infrastructure Tax in Coding-Agent Reinforcement Learning
comment: Preprint. 6 pages, 6 figures, 2 tables. Submitted to ACM SoCC 2026
summary: Coding-agent reinforcement learning treats execution infrastructure as a background implementation detail, despite relying on large numbers of interactive software rollouts. This is a missed opportunity: measuring infrastructure overhead can reveal practical efficiency gains for RL post-training, where small per-rollout savings compound at scale. We present a comparative study of four execution substrates: single containers, hosted sandboxes, Kubernetes-orchestrated containers, and cloud virtual machines. We find up to $110\times$ variation in cold-start latency and a $1.8\times$ spread in projected worker-hours for one million 150-step trajectories. Our results suggest that future coding-agent RL systems should optimize execution substrates as part of the training system itself, not merely as deployment plumbing.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that execution infrastructure (containers, sandboxes, Kubernetes, VMs) significantly impacts coding-agent RL efficiency, with up to 110× cold-start latency variation and 1.8× spread in worker-hours for 1M trajectories, arguing infrastructure should be optimized as part of the training system.
AI.motivation: Coding-agent RL treats execution infrastructure as a background implementation detail, missing the opportunity to measure and optimize infrastructure overhead that compounds at scale during RL post-training.
AI.method: Comparative study of four execution substrates: single containers, hosted sandboxes, Kubernetes-orchestrated containers, and cloud virtual machines, measuring cold-start latency and projected worker-hours for 1M 150-step trajectories.
AI.result: Up to 110× variation in cold-start latency and a 1.8× spread in projected worker-hours for one million 150-step trajectories across the four substrates.
AI.conclusion: Future coding-agent RL systems should optimize execution substrates as part of the training system itself, not merely as deployment plumbing.

title: Disentangling Pictorial Cue Understanding from Language Bias in VLMs via Depth Ordering Task
comment: 15 pages, 7 figures, accepted to ECCV 2026 (30 pages, 13 figures, supplementary materials included)
summary: In this paper, we study depth perception of vision-language models (VLMs) to isolate the effects of pictorial depth cues and disentangle vision and language influences on model performance. To this end, we combine depth-ordering and odd-one-out psychophysical tasks: the VLMs are presented with images where one object is at different depth relative to other, otherwise identical, objects, and must determine whether the odd-one-out target is closer or farther to the observer. To create stimuli, we generate 2D views from simulated and real 3D scenes while controlling the presence of individual pictorial depth cues, enabling a fine-grained analysis of cue-level contributions. Language effects are examined by varying referring expression clarity. We also introduce a novel metric to quantify vision-vs-language sensitivities. Applying this methodology, we create the Odd-One-Out Depth (O3-D) dataset with 37K real and synthetic images and 147K image-question pairs. Evaluation of 12 open-source and commercial models on O3-D shows under-utilization of depth cues and depth-ordering accuracies between 47% and 56%, with no model above chance level. At the same time, our metric reveals strong linguistic bias in the answers. Neither chain-of-thought (CoT) nor in-context learning (ICL) significantly improves performance, suggesting that static image data alone may be insufficient for depth understanding. All code, the image generation pipeline, and the O3-D dataset are publicly released at https://github.com/lyiqian/o3-d.

AI.tldr: VLMs perform near chance (47-56%) on depth-ordering tasks using the O3-D dataset (37K images, 147K Q&A pairs), show strong linguistic bias, and fail to improve with CoT or ICL, suggesting static images alone are insufficient for depth understanding.
AI.motivation: To isolate pictorial depth cues and disentangle vision vs. language influences on VLM depth perception through psychophysical tasks with controlled stimuli.
AI.method: Combined depth-ordering and odd-one-out psychophysical tasks; generated 2D views from simulated and real 3D scenes with controlled pictorial depth cues; varied referring expression clarity; introduced a novel metric to quantify vision-vs-language sensitivities; created the O3-D dataset with 37K images and 147K image-question pairs.
AI.result: 12 open-source and commercial VLMs achieved depth-ordering accuracies between 47% and 56% (none above chance); strong linguistic bias was revealed by the proposed metric; CoT and ICL did not significantly improve performance.
AI.conclusion: Static image data alone may be insufficient for depth understanding in VLMs; language biases dominate over visual depth cue utilization.

title: Archer: Towards Agentic Review for Compiler Optimizations
summary:
Modern compilers are frequently updated, but expert review capacity is highly limited, leading to delayed integration and, in some cases, subtle semantic bugs entering the compiler codebase. Automating the code review process with modern general code review agents may be feasible, but it faces critical challenges due to compiler complexity. In this paper, we use LLVM as our target compiler and present Archer, the first automated agentic code review tool for compiler optimizations. Archer constrains the agentic review process from both ends by using obligations to guide analysis and a deterministic validation guard to admit only findings backed by executable evidence.
  We evaluated Archer on 70 open PRs and 328 closed PRs in LLVM from the last two months. The review results are shocking and concerning: Archer discovers that 21% of open PRs and 11% of closed PRs are buggy, i.e, introducing semantic bugs such as miscompilations in LLVM. Our findings expose a critical gap in the capacity for critical review in large compiler projects and demonstrate the practical value of Archer as an additional reviewer.

AI.tldr: Archer is an automated agentic code review tool for LLVM compiler optimizations that discovered 21% of open PRs and 11% of closed PRs contain semantic bugs, revealing critical review capacity gaps in large compiler projects.
AI.motivation: Modern compilers are frequently updated but expert review capacity is limited, leading to delayed integration and subtle semantic bugs entering the compiler codebase. General code review agents face critical challenges due to compiler complexity.
AI.method: Archer constrains the agentic review process from both ends by using obligations to guide analysis and a deterministic validation guard to admit only findings backed by executable evidence. It targets LLVM as the compiler platform.
AI.result: Evaluated on 70 open PRs and 328 closed PRs in LLVM from the last two months. Archer discovered that 21% of open PRs and 11% of closed PRs are buggy, introducing semantic bugs such as miscompilations.
AI.conclusion: The findings expose a critical gap in capacity for critical review in large compiler projects and demonstrate the practical value of Archer as an additional reviewer.

title: Scaling Trends for Lie Detector Oversight in Preference Learning
summary: Deceptive behavior in LLMs is costly to monitor and prevent, motivating approaches such as Scalable Oversight via Lie Detectors (SOLiD) (Cundy & Gleave, 2025), which uses lie detectors to identify responses for review by high-cost labelers. In this paper, we scale SOLiD to larger models and evaluate it in more diverse and realistic preference-learning settings. We find favorable scaling: undetected deception drops from 34% for 1B-parameter models to 14% for 405B-parameter models at a detector true positive rate of 99%, and expensive human labelers can be removed entirely from the fine-tuning phase without a statistically significant increase in deception. However, SOLiD is sensitive to distribution shift between detector training and preference-training data, which can drive detector false positive rates to impractical levels.

AI.tldr: Scaling lie detector oversight (SOLiD) to larger models reduces undetected deception from 34% to 14% and can eliminate human labelers without significant increase in deception, but suffers from distribution shift sensitivity causing high false positive rates.
AI.motivation: Deceptive behavior in LLMs is costly to monitor and prevent, motivating the need for scalable oversight approaches such as lie detectors to identify deceptive responses for selective review by expensive labelers.
AI.method: The authors scale SOLiD to larger models (up to 405B parameters) and evaluate it in more diverse and realistic preference-learning settings, testing both scaling behavior and the feasibility of removing human labelers from the fine-tuning phase.
AI.result: Undetected deception drops from 34% (1B models) to 14% (405B models) at 99% detector true positive rate. Human labelers can be removed entirely from fine-tuning without statistically significant increase in deception. However, SOLiD is sensitive to distribution shift between detector training and preference-training data, causing impractical false positive rates.
AI.conclusion: SOLiD scales favorably with model size and can operate without human labelers during fine-tuning, but its practical deployment is limited by sensitivity to distribution shift that degrades detector specificity.

title: Conditional Inference Trees and Forests for Feature Selection
summary: Conditional inference trees (CIT) and conditional inference forests (CIF) reduce split-selection bias by testing features before choosing split thresholds, but repeated permutation tests and threshold searches can make these methods computationally expensive. We study CIT and CIF as top-$k$ feature-ranking methods for downstream prediction using real-data benchmarks, runtime ablations, and synthetic feature-recovery experiments. At a fixed node, if the features and permutation budget do not depend on the node responses, Bonferroni-corrected $+1$ Monte Carlo permutation $p$-values control nodewise rejection under the complete permutation null. CIF ranks 4th among 17 classification methods on 22 datasets and 3rd among 18 regression methods on 8 datasets. With Bonferroni correction held fixed, the CIF runtime ablations indicate that adaptive stopping and the number of thresholds searched have the largest measured effect on runtime: turning off adaptive stopping and using exact threshold search increase fitting time by 4.0--8.4$\times$ and 1.9--10.8$\times$, respectively, while downstream score changes are at most 0.011. Sparse high-$p$ simulations indicate that forest feature sampling can leave informative features out of many split decisions. Overall, the results support CIF as a top-$k$ feature-ranking method in the evaluated downstream prediction benchmarks.

AI.tldr: The paper studies Conditional Inference Trees and Forests as top-k feature-ranking methods, finding they control nodewise rejection via Bonferroni-corrected Monte Carlo permutation p-values, rank competitively in benchmarks (4th/17 classification, 3rd/18 regression), and identifies adaptive stopping and threshold search count as dominant runtime factors, while feature sampling can miss informative features in high-p settings.
AI.motivation: Conditional inference trees and forests reduce split-selection bias but are computationally expensive due to repeated permutation tests and threshold searches; the paper aims to study their effectiveness as top-k feature-ranking methods for downstream prediction.
AI.method: Real-data benchmarks, runtime ablations, and synthetic feature-recovery experiments; Bonferroni-corrected +1 Monte Carlo permutation p-values for nodewise rejection control; ablation of adaptive stopping and threshold search count.
AI.result: CIF ranks 4th among 17 classification methods on 22 datasets and 3rd among 18 regression methods on 8 datasets. Turning off adaptive stopping increases fitting time 4.0–8.4×; exact threshold search increases time 1.9–10.8×; downstream score changes ≤0.011. Forest feature sampling can miss informative features in high-p simulations.
AI.conclusion: The results support CIF as a top-k feature-ranking method in the evaluated downstream prediction benchmarks.

title: Hidden-Shot: Towards One-Shot Task Generalization for Low-Level Vision Generalist Models
summary: Despite the intense engagement surrounding low-level vision generalist models, their effectiveness in zero/few-shot scenarios beyond learned tasks remains unverified. The primary challenge of developing an ideal generalist lies in achieving the ability to generalize from new unseen tasks, which also can be assessed by matched quantitative criteria. Existing methods have made some progress in prompt engineering but have not systematically explored this gap across a wide range of low-level visual tasks. Stimulated by the problem, we propose Hidden-Shot, an implicit prompt mechanism aimed at exploring low-level task adaptation in a vision generalist model. Specifically, the method extracts implicit visual task-based information, utilizes a global task-aware textural prompt, and selectively merges implicit information with in-task processing information to enhance one-shot capabilities in new tasks. The overall design performs direct injection in a cost-effective manner, while minimally altering the architecture of the original generalist model. Additionally, we introduce a data-driven evaluation framework termed C/U assessment to cover two basic scenarios, 3C4U (3 conventional and 4 unconventional tasks) for retraining existing models and 3C7U (3 conventional and 7 unconventional tasks) for training from scratch, as a comprehensive assessment to systematically test the generalization ability of low-level generalist models. Experiments on seven and ten datasets outperform the state-of-the-art vision generalist model, respectively verified by 3C4U and 3C7U framework. Our presented Hidden-Shot approach demonstrates superior performance on one-shot new tasks while maintaining consistent performance on existing tasks.

AI.tldr: Hidden-Shot proposes an implicit prompt mechanism for low-level vision generalist models that extracts implicit task information and uses global task-aware textural prompts to enhance one-shot generalization on unseen tasks, validated by a new C/U assessment framework (3C4U and 3C7U) achieving SOTA results.
AI.motivation: Existing low-level vision generalist models lack verified effectiveness in zero/few-shot scenarios beyond learned tasks, and there is no systematic exploration or matched quantitative criteria for assessing generalization to new unseen tasks.
AI.method: Hidden-Shot extracts implicit visual task-based information, employs a global task-aware textural prompt, and selectively merges implicit information with in-task processing to enable one-shot adaptation, performing direct injection without significantly altering the original architecture.
AI.result: Outperforms state-of-the-art vision generalist models on both the 3C4U (7 datasets) and 3C7U (10 datasets) evaluation frameworks, demonstrating superior one-shot new task performance while maintaining consistency on existing tasks.
AI.conclusion: The proposed implicit prompt mechanism effectively enhances generalization to unseen low-level vision tasks in a cost-effective manner, and the C/U assessment framework provides a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating low-level vision generalist models.

title: Decoupling Code Complexity from Newcomer Participation: A Causal Study of AI Coding Agent Adoption in OSS
summary: Open-source projects depend on a steady inflow of newcomers. A growing concern is that AI coding agents (tools such as Cursor and Claude Code that write code from natural-language instructions) will crowd them out, by absorbing the simple tasks that beginners start with and by making code harder to read. We give this concern a causal answer. Using GitHub code search we identify 1,888 projects that adopted an agent, signaled by their first commit of a configuration file. We apply difference-in-differences against matched non-adopting controls, restricting the main analysis to the 603 adopters with a genuine pre-adoption period. We find no evidence of crowding-out: across estimators newcomer inflow shows no significant decline after adoption (point estimates run from a small increase to, under the most conservative trend specification, a slight and insignificant dip), onboarding and retention are unchanged, and a sparse, correlational beginner-task measure (good-first-issue labels, which we cannot test for parallel trends) shows no decline. The feared mechanism is real but decoupled: adoption raises per-function code complexity (about +11% on a cognitive metric for Python, a quarter of the prior estimate, and +3 to 4% in cyclomatic terms across all languages), yet in fixed-unit subsets where complexity rose (Python on the cognitive metric, and all languages on the cyclomatic metric), newcomer participation does not decline. These results suggest that, in established open-source projects, adopting an AI coding agent makes code modestly more complex but does not crowd out the human newcomers that a project depends on: the feared trade-off between AI assistance and human participation does not materialize.

AI.tldr: This study finds no evidence that AI coding agents (e.g., Cursor, Claude Code) crowd out newcomers in open-source projects, despite a modest increase in code complexity. Using difference-in-differences on 603 projects that adopted such agents, the analysis shows newcomer inflow, onboarding, and retention remain unchanged after adoption.
AI.motivation: A growing concern is that AI coding agents will crowd out newcomers in open-source projects by absorbing simple beginner tasks and making code harder to read, potentially threatening the steady inflow of contributors that open-source projects depend on.
AI.method: The authors identified 1,888 projects that adopted an AI coding agent (signaled by first commit of a configuration file) using GitHub code search. They applied difference-in-differences against matched non-adopting controls, restricting the main analysis to 603 adopters with a genuine pre-adoption period. They also measured code complexity changes using cognitive and cyclomatic metrics.
AI.result: No evidence of crowding-out was found: newcomer inflow showed no significant decline after adoption (from a small increase to a slight, insignificant dip). Onboarding and retention were unchanged. A sparse correlational measure (good-first-issue labels) showed no decline. Code complexity did increase modestly (≈+11% cognitive metric for Python, +3-4% cyclomatic across languages), but in subsets where complexity rose, newcomer participation did not decline.
AI.conclusion: In established open-source projects, adopting an AI coding agent makes code modestly more complex but does not crowd out human newcomers. The feared trade-off between AI assistance and human participation does not materialize.

title: EO-Agents: A Three-Agent LLM Pipeline for Earth Observation Hypothesis Generation
comment: Accepted at the ICML 2026 AI for Science Workshop
summary: Large language models have recently been explored for scientific hypothesis generation, but most prior work relies on unstructured literature and free-form textual claims. We present a pipeline for Earth observation that grounds hypothesis generation directly in the NASA Earth Observation Knowledge Graph. A heterogeneous graph neural network trained on historical co-usage relations ranks candidate dataset pairings, and a three-agent LLM pipeline filters, generates, and evaluates structured research hypotheses. Applied to 1,475 NASA datasets, the system produces 160 hypotheses spanning multiple Earth-science domains, including ecohydrology, glaciology, aerosol--cloud interactions, vegetation phenology, and stratospheric chemistry. Model-predicted novel dataset pairings are rated nearly as plausible as held-out real co-usages from the literature, indicating that the pipeline surfaces scientifically coherent yet unexplored combinations. A 2*2*2 factorial experiment across GPT-5.2 and Claude Sonnet 4.6 shows that hypothesis rankings remain stable, while absolute scores depend strongly on judge identity, highlighting limitations of single-judge LLM evaluation.

AI.tldr: A pipeline that uses a knowledge graph and heterogeneous graph neural network to generate structured Earth observation hypotheses by ranking dataset pairings, followed by a three-agent LLM pipeline for filtering, generating, and evaluating hypotheses. Applied to 1,475 NASA datasets, it produced 160 plausible hypotheses across multiple Earth-science domains.
AI.motivation: Most prior work on LLM-based hypothesis generation relies on unstructured literature and free-form textual claims, lacking grounding in structured, domain-specific knowledge repositories. This work aims to address that gap for Earth observation.
AI.method: (1) A heterogeneous graph neural network trained on historical co-usage relations ranks candidate dataset pairings from the NASA Earth Observation Knowledge Graph (1,475 datasets). (2) A three-agent LLM pipeline filters, generates, and evaluates structured research hypotheses from these pairings. (3) A 2×2×2 factorial experiment across GPT-5.2 and Claude Sonnet 4.6 tests hypothesis ranking stability and judge identity effects.
AI.result: 160 hypotheses spanning multiple Earth-science domains (ecohydrology, glaciology, aerosol–cloud interactions, vegetation phenology, stratospheric chemistry). Model-predicted novel dataset pairings are rated nearly as plausible as held-out real co-usages from literature. Hypothesis rankings are stable across LLMs, but absolute scores depend strongly on judge identity.
AI.conclusion: The pipeline surfaces scientifically coherent yet unexplored dataset combinations. Single-judge LLM evaluation has significant limitations due to judge identity bias in absolute scoring.

title: On the Utility and Factual Reliability of Pruned Mixture-of-Experts Models in the Biomedical Domain
summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models offer inference speedups via selective activation but impose substantial memory requirements because the whole network must remain loaded. Structured expert pruning is a practical approach for reducing deployment costs in resource-constrained settings. However, prior studies primarily evaluate benchmark utility, leaving the effect of pruning on factual reliability underexplored, particularly in high-stakes domains such as biomedicine. In this paper, we investigate how domain-specific expert pruning affects both utility and reliability. We assess four MoE models, six pruning methods, and multiple pruning ratios across generation and classification tasks under in-domain (biomedical) and cross-domain settings. Results reveal that moderate pruning preserves in-domain utility without immediate reliability decline, although hallucination risks increase at extreme pruning ratios. When shifting to the general domain, both utility and reliability degrade rapidly. These findings indicate that safe compression depends heavily on the task and domain. Evaluating pruned MoE models solely on utility is inadequate for high-stakes deployment without reliability assessment.

AI.tldr: Structured expert pruning in Mixture-of-Experts models preserves in-domain utility at moderate ratios but increases hallucination risks at extreme pruning, especially in biomedical domains; cross-domain performance degrades rapidly, highlighting the need for reliability assessment beyond utility for safe deployment.
AI.motivation: Prior work on MoE expert pruning evaluates benchmark utility but neglects factual reliability, particularly in high-stakes domains like biomedicine. This study addresses that gap by assessing both utility and reliability under pruning.
AI.method: Evaluates four MoE models, six pruning methods, and multiple pruning ratios across generation and classification tasks under in-domain (biomedical) and cross-domain (general domain) settings.
AI.result: Moderate pruning preserves in-domain utility without immediate reliability decline, but hallucination risks increase at extreme pruning ratios. Cross-domain shifts cause rapid degradation in both utility and reliability.
AI.conclusion: Safe compression depends on task and domain; evaluating pruned MoE models solely on utility is insufficient for high-stakes deployment without also assessing reliability.

title: Boosting Infrared Small Target Detection via Logit-Domain Contrast and Adaptive Shape Refinement
comment: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication
summary: Infrared small target detection (IRSTD) remains challenging due to tiny target size, low signal-to-noise ratio, severe foreground-background imbalance, and blurred boundaries in complex scenes. Existing methods usually rely on post-activation probability-domain supervision for discrimination, where weak targets and strong clutter may produce saturated and close probabilities, limiting weak-target discrimination. Meanwhile, blurred boundaries and halo-like predictions mainly stem from thermal diffusion, tiny target scale, boundary uncertainty, and insufficient explicit contour constraints. To address these issues, we propose Adaptive-Contrastive SLSIoU (AC-SLSIoU), a plug-and-play discriminative and shape-aware loss for IRSTD. Specifically, a Logit-Domain Margin Constraint (LDMC) is introduced to enlarge the response gap between targets and informative hard negatives in the logit space, thereby enhancing weak-target discrimination. Adaptive Boundary Suppression (ABS) applies scale-aware annular penalties to refine target contours and suppress halo-like overflow responses. In addition, False-Alarm Focal Loss assigns larger weights to high-probability negative samples, further penalizing persistent high-confidence false alarms. Without introducing extra inference overhead, the proposed method can be seamlessly integrated into existing detectors and consistently improves both detection accuracy and shape quality. Extensive experiments and cross-backbone evaluations demonstrate the effectiveness, robustness, and generalization ability of the proposed method for infrared small target detection.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes AC-SLSIoU, a plug-and-play loss function for infrared small target detection that enhances weak-target discrimination via logit-domain margin constraints, refines contours via adaptive boundary suppression, and penalizes false alarms via focal loss, achieving consistent improvements across detectors without extra inference cost.
AI.motivation: Existing IRSTD methods suffer from: (1) weak-target discrimination failure due to saturated/closely packed probabilities in the probability domain; (2) blurred boundaries and halo-like predictions caused by thermal diffusion, tiny target scales, and lack of explicit contour constraints.
AI.method: Three components: (1) Logit-Domain Margin Constraint (LDMC) enlarges response gaps between targets and hard negatives in logit space; (2) Adaptive Boundary Suppression (ABS) applies scale-aware annular penalties to refine contours and suppress halo artifacts; (3) False-Alarm Focal Loss assigns larger weights to high-probability negatives to penalize persistent false alarms.
AI.result: Plug-and-play integration into existing detectors yields consistent improvements in both detection accuracy and shape quality without extra inference overhead; cross-backbone evaluations confirm effectiveness, robustness, and generalization.
AI.conclusion: AC-SLSIoU provides a discriminative and shape-aware loss that addresses key IRSTD challenges, is model-agnostic, and offers practical benefits with no additional inference cost.

title: Understanding Software Defect Prediction: A Large-scale Empirical Study Across Uncertainty Quantification and Performance Evaluation
summary: Software defect prediction (SDP) classifiers produce probabilities used for inspection prioritization, threshold tuning, and risk communication. Probability-based uncertainty quantification (UQ) characterizes prediction confidence, but whether common UQ metrics reliably indicate performance and calibration remains unclear. We conducted a large-scale empirical study of probability-based UQ for SDP. We evaluated five UQ metrics, six performance metrics, and three calibration metrics for 16 representative classifiers. We analyzed these relationships under two prediction settings: within-project defect prediction (WPDP), using 36 benchmark datasets, and cross-project defect prediction (CPDP), using 32 feature-compatible datasets. Results showed that UQ was highly context-dependent. Under WPDP, UQ correlated more consistently with false positive rate and AUC than with MCC, F1 score, and other metrics; these correlations also varied across classifier categories and dataset collections. Performance and calibration were related but not interchangeable; classifiers with strong discrimination could still exhibit large calibration error. Under CPDP, several UQ-performance and UQ-calibration correlations weakened or reversed, indicating that uncertainty signals do not reliably transfer across projects. Thus, UQ should be evaluated against specific performance objectives. Calibration should be assessed independently using multiple metrics. Transferred probabilities should be revalidated before guiding quality-assurance decisions.

AI.tldr: A large-scale empirical study of probability-based uncertainty quantification (UQ) in software defect prediction finds that UQ metrics are highly context-dependent, correlate inconsistently with performance metrics, and do not reliably transfer across projects.
AI.motivation: Software defect prediction classifiers produce probabilities for inspection prioritization, threshold tuning, and risk communication, but whether common uncertainty quantification metrics reliably indicate performance and calibration remains unclear.
AI.method: Evaluated five UQ metrics, six performance metrics, and three calibration metrics across 16 classifiers under within-project defect prediction (36 benchmark datasets) and cross-project defect prediction (32 feature-compatible datasets), analyzing correlations between UQ, performance, and calibration.
AI.result: Under WPDP, UQ correlated more consistently with false positive rate and AUC than with MCC, F1 score, and other metrics; correlations varied across classifier categories and dataset collections. Under CPDP, several UQ-performance and UQ-calibration correlations weakened or reversed.
AI.conclusion: UQ should be evaluated against specific performance objectives; calibration should be assessed independently using multiple metrics; transferred probabilities should be revalidated before guiding quality-assurance decisions.

title: Hawk: Harnessing Hardware-Aware Knowledge for High-Performance NPU Kernel Generation
summary: Developing high-performance kernels for Neural Processing Units (NPUs) is a critical industry bottleneck, requiring developers to manually navigate implicit hardware constraints and strict memory hierarchies. While large language models offer immense automation potential, they fail catastrophically on NPUs due to a fundamental lack of hardware-specific priors. Naively transplanting code snippets from similar NPU kernels may pass the compiler, but it consistently triggers runtime crashes and performance degradation by blindly violating underlying hardware constraints. To overcome this, we introduce Hawk, a training-free framework that harnesses hardware-aware knowledge through three core modules: (1) Run-Time Knowledge Synthesis Module, which employs a Triple-Part Executable Knowledge Representation to inherently couple the error context with executable semantics; (2) Bottleneck-Aware Knowledge Retrieval Module, which implements a 2D-Retrieval paradigm to project queries into orthogonal syntactic and hardware-aligned semantic spaces; and (3) Effect-Driven Knowledge Distillation Module, which leverages LLM-driven semantic arbitration to continuously distill the knowledge by pruning errors and consolidating redundancies based on the empirical execution feedback. Extensive evaluations on real-world NPU workloads demonstrate that Hawk elevates generation accuracy from 49.4% to 80.0%, while achieving up to a 2.2x execution speedup over state-of-the-art baselines.

AI.tldr: Hawk is a training-free framework that improves NPU kernel generation accuracy from 49.4% to 80.0% and achieves up to 2.2x speedup over baselines by injecting hardware-aware knowledge via three modules: Run-Time Knowledge Synthesis, Bottleneck-Aware Knowledge Retrieval, and Effect-Driven Knowledge Distillation.
AI.motivation: Developing high-performance NPU kernels is a critical industry bottleneck due to implicit hardware constraints and strict memory hierarchies. LLMs fail catastrophically on NPUs lacking hardware-specific priors, and naive code transplantation causes runtime crashes and performance degradation.
AI.method: Hawk consists of three modules: (1) Run-Time Knowledge Synthesis Module with Triple-Part Executable Knowledge Representation coupling error context with executable semantics; (2) Bottleneck-Aware Knowledge Retrieval Module using 2D-Retrieval paradigm for orthogonal syntactic and hardware-aligned semantic spaces; (3) Effect-Driven Knowledge Distillation Module using LLM-driven semantic arbitration to prune errors and consolidate redundancies from execution feedback.
AI.result: Generation accuracy improved from 49.4% to 80.0%, with up to 2.2x execution speedup over state-of-the-art baselines on real-world NPU workloads.
AI.conclusion: Hawk effectively bridges the gap between LLM automation and NPU hardware constraints through a training-free, hardware-aware knowledge framework, significantly improving both correctness and performance.

title: Geometry-Aware R-Structured Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks
summary:
We propose a novel hybrid neural architecture, the Geometry-aware R-Structured Kolmogorov-Arnold Network (GRS-KAN), which integrates V.L.Rvachev's R-functions into the Kolmogorov-Arnold Network (KAN) framework. The proposed approach combines two complementary modeling mechanisms: smooth nonlinear structure is learned by KAN branches, while known geometric or logical constraints are encoded analytically using differentiable R-functions. This enables explicit representation of discontinuities, feasible regions, and implicit geometric boundaries within a trainable neural architecture.
  The framework implements differentiable logical operations through R-conjunctions and R-disjunctions, allowing complex geometric supports to be represented analytically and incorporated directly into regression models. Several GRS-KAN variants are introduced, including additive, multiplicative, and agnostic branch-weighted architectures.
  The method is demonstrated on regression problems involving discontinuities with circular and rectangular supports. Numerical experiments show that explicit geometric encoding substantially improves predictive accuracy and boundary localization compared with standard KANs. In the considered benchmarks, geometry-aware GRS-KAN models reduce test RMSE by up to 67% while simultaneously improving interpretability through explicit analytical representation of the learned geometric structure. The agnostic variant further demonstrates the ability to automatically determine whether geometric priors are beneficial for a given learning task.

AI.tldr: GRS-KAN integrates R-functions into KAN to encode geometric and logical constraints, achieving up to 67% RMSE reduction on discontinuous regression benchmarks with improved interpretability.
AI.motivation: Standard KANs lack mechanisms to enforce known geometric/logical constraints or represent discontinuities explicitly, limiting accuracy on problems with structured boundaries.
AI.method: A hybrid architecture combining KAN branches (learned smooth nonlinear mapping) with differentiable R-functions (analytical encoding of geometry/logic via R-conjunctions/disjunctions). Three variants: additive, multiplicative, and agnostic branch-weighted.
AI.result: GRS-KAN reduces test RMSE by up to 67% on discontinuous regression with circular/rectangular supports, with improved boundary localization over standard KANs.
AI.conclusion: Explicit geometric encoding via R-functions within KAN enhances both accuracy and interpretability; the agnostic variant can automatically assess whether geometric priors are beneficial.

title: Mind the Gap: Standard 3DGS Evaluation Primarily Measures Near-Trajectory Interpolation
summary: Standard MipNeRF360-style 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) evaluation holds out every N-th frame -- but these frames have trained neighbors on both sides, so the metric measures near-trajectory interpolation rather than spatial generalization. We introduce a fair matched-count protocol that isolates this effect: both arms train on the same number of images and differ only in whether the holdout is spread evenly (interpolation) or forms a contiguous spatial sector (extrapolation). Our primary finding is a large, consistent interpolation-extrapolation gap of 3~12dB -- several times the differences typically reported between competing methods. The gap is robust to training noise, is in two cases large enough to flip a method ranking under multi-seed confirmation, and -- crucially -- persists across three representation families, including a non-Gaussian volumetric neural radiance field (NeRF), so it reflects spatial coverage rather than any one representation. Diagnostically, it is dominated by a diffuse/geometry-proxy component and tracks each view's angular distance to its nearest training view, a zero-cost signal that also guides capture planning; loss-side regularization yields only marginal gains. Standard holdouts remain useful for near-trajectory rendering but should not, alone, be read as evidence of spatial generalization. Prior work notes protocol sensitivity; ours is, to our knowledge, the first to combine matched-count paired holdout, cross-representation quantification, and a diagnostic analysis Table 1. We describe a spatial-holdout benchmark toolkit with standardized splits and baselines for 16 scenes, which we are preparing for public release.

AI.tldr: Standard 3DGS evaluation using held-out frames measures interpolation (near-trajectory) performance, not spatial generalization. A new matched-count protocol reveals a consistent 3-12 dB gap between interpolation and extrapolation holdouts, persisting across three representation families. This gap is predicted by angular distance to nearest training view and can flip method rankings under multi-seed confirmation.
AI.motivation: To expose that standard evaluation protocols in 3D Gaussian Splatting (holding out every N-th frame) measure near-trajectory interpolation rather than true spatial generalization, and to quantify the systematic gap between interpolation and extrapolation performance.
AI.method: A matched-count paired holdout protocol where both arms train on the same number of images, differing only in whether the holdout is spread evenly (interpolation) or forms a contiguous spatial sector (extrapolation). Applied across three representation families: 3DGS, non-Gaussian volumetric NeRF, and others.
AI.result: Large, consistent interpolation-extrapolation gap of 3-12 dB, several times larger than typical differences between competing methods. The gap is robust to training noise, can flip method rankings, and persists across all tested representation families. It is dominated by a diffuse/geometry-proxy component and correlates with angular distance to nearest training view.
AI.conclusion: Standard holdouts are useful for near-trajectory rendering but should not be interpreted as evidence of spatial generalization. A spatial-holdout benchmark toolkit with standardized splits is being prepared for public release.

title: Technical Debt Friction for Maintenance Prioritization: An Industrial Multi-Case Study
comment: Accepted for the 42nd International Conference on Software Maintenance and Evolution (Industry Track)
