MrFlow first rapidly generates the main structure at low resolution, then performs super-resolution in the pixel space using a lightweight pretrained GAN-based model, subsequently injects low-strength noise to enable high-frequency resampling, and finally refines the details at high resolution. Quantitative and qualitative results on FLUX.1-dev and Qwen-Image show that MrFlow exploits the quadratic token reduction and reduced step requirement of low-resolution sampling to achieve 10x end-to-end acceleration while keeping OneIG within a 1% gap relative to that before acceleration, significantly surpassing other training-free acceleration strategies, and requiring no training or runtime dynamic identification whatsoever. MrFlow can further be directly combined orthogonally with pre-trained timestep distillation strategies, achieving even higher generation acceleration of up to 25x.

AI.tldr: MrFlow is a training-free multi-resolution acceleration strategy for flow-matching text-to-image models. It uses a staged low-to-high-resolution pipeline with pixel-space super-resolution via a lightweight GAN, noise injection for high-frequency resampling, and detail refinement—achieving 10x end-to-end speedup (up to 25x when combined with timestep distillation) while keeping visual quality degradation within a 1% gap.
AI.motivation: Existing training-free multi-resolution acceleration methods for text-to-image diffusion perform upsampling in latent space with partial region modifications, causing noticeable blurring and artifacts. There is a need for a strategy that avoids these quality issues while maintaining high acceleration.
AI.method: MrFlow operates in a staged pipeline: (1) rapid low-resolution generation to capture main structure; (2) pixel-space super-resolution using a lightweight pretrained GAN-based model; (3) low-strength noise injection to enable high-frequency resampling; (4) high-resolution detail refinement. It exploits quadratic token reduction and reduced step requirements of low-resolution sampling.
AI.result: Achieves 10x end-to-end acceleration on FLUX.1-dev and Qwen-Image with OneIG within a 1% gap of unaccelerated performance. Orthogonal combination with timestep distillation yields up to 25x acceleration. Significantly surpasses other training-free acceleration strategies.
AI.conclusion: MrFlow offers an effective training-free acceleration approach for flow-matching models that avoids blurring/artifact issues of prior multi-resolution methods, requires no training or runtime dynamic identification, and is orthogonally compatible with timestep distillation for further speedup.

title: Epic-Organized vs. Requirement-Aligned Gherkin: An Empirical Evaluation of LLM-Based Acceptance Criteria Generation
comment: Accepted for publication at the International Conference on Software Engineering of Emerging Technologies (SEET 2026)
summary: Automated authoring of Gherkin Behavior-Driven Development (BDD) acceptance criteria remains a manual bottleneck in requirements engineering. This study investigates whether epic-organized LLM-generated Gherkin produces higher quality and coverage than requirement-aligned generation. We compare our Timeless (an epic-organized LLM pipeline) approach against a naive large language model (LLM) baseline on four requirements documents (107 requirements) from the PURE dataset. Evaluation covers structural metrics, automated requirement coverage via TF-IDF and dense embeddings, and blind expert assessment by four researchers. In our evaluation, the JSON-constrained pipeline produced structurally valid scenarios across all generated outputs, while the zero-shot baseline achieved 99% structural validity. Semantic coverage was comparable to the baseline, with Timeless achieving 94.3% semantic Requirement Coverage Rate compared with 92.9% for the baseline. TF-IDF produced lower coverage scores for the epic-organized output, suggesting that lexical metrics may miss coverage when scenarios paraphrase requirements at a higher level of abstraction. Expert raters prefer the epic-organized strategy on Correctness (4.61 vs 4.14), Executability (4.61 vs 4.07), and Completeness (4.31 vs 3.50). Overall, the results suggest that epic-organized generation can improve perceived Gherkin quality while maintaining comparable semantic coverage, although broader replication is needed before generalizing this finding.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Timeless, an epic-organized LLM pipeline for generating Gherkin BDD acceptance criteria, and shows it achieves comparable semantic coverage to naive LLM baselines while significantly improving expert-rated correctness, executability, and completeness.
AI.motivation: Automated authoring of Gherkin BDD acceptance criteria remains a manual bottleneck in requirements engineering, and existing LLM-based approaches lack structured organization.
AI.method: The authors compare Timeless (an epic-organized LLM pipeline) against a naive zero-shot LLM baseline on 107 requirements from the PURE dataset. Evaluation includes structural validity checks, automated requirement coverage via TF-IDF and dense embeddings, and blind expert assessment by four researchers.
AI.result: Timeless achieved 100% structurally valid scenarios (vs. 99% for baseline), 94.3% semantic Requirement Coverage Rate (vs. 92.9%), and higher expert ratings on Correctness (4.61 vs. 4.14), Executability (4.61 vs. 4.07), and Completeness (4.31 vs. 3.50). TF-IDF coverage was lower for Timeless, indicating lexical metrics may miss abstract paraphrasing.
AI.conclusion: Epic-organized generation can improve perceived Gherkin quality while maintaining comparable semantic coverage, though broader replication is needed before generalization.

title: Separating Expert Retention from Autonomous Source Inference in Raw-ECG-Replay-Free Continual ECG Deployment
summary:
In multi-source ECG deployment, models may need to incorporate new data sources when earlier raw ECGs cannot be retained or replayed. Freezing a pretrained backbone and assigning each source an isolated classifier prevents parameter interference, but deployment still requires selecting an expert when source metadata are unavailable. We study this distinction through \ours{}, an incremental expert bank built on frozen 1024-dimensional ECGFounder features. Each arriving domain adds a balanced-softmax linear expert, while a lightweight router is fitted only on retained training features and domain labels from sources observed so far. A validation-calibrated margin rule fuses the two most likely experts instead of committing to a single routed expert.
  On CPSC, PTB-XL, Georgia, and Chapman-Shaoxing, source-aware expert selection reaches $0.7915\pm0.0036$ Macro-F1 and a matched offline independent-head reference reaches $0.7885\pm0.0009$, supporting strong source-aware expert retention. Without source IDs, an MLP router reaches $0.7756\pm0.0027$ and top-2 margin fusion reaches $0.7782\pm0.0022$. The top-2 gain over hard MLP routing is small ($+0.0026$), with a 95\% confidence interval from paired bootstrap that includes zero. Across three domain orders, the top-2-to-oracle gap remains $0.0111$--$0.0133$, identifying autonomous source inference as the main remaining bottleneck. No raw ECGs are replayed, but frozen training features are retained for router updates; the method is therefore not memory-free.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a method for multi-source ECG deployment where a frozen pretrained backbone is used with isolated classifiers per source, and a lightweight router with top-2 margin fusion is used when source metadata is unavailable. Results show strong source-aware expert retention but identify autonomous source inference as the main bottleneck.
AI.motivation: To handle multi-source ECG deployment where earlier raw ECGs cannot be retained or replayed, and source metadata is unavailable during inference, requiring a method that can incorporate new data sources without parameter interference.
AI.method: A frozen 1024-dimensional ECGFounder backbone with an incremental expert bank. Each new domain adds a balanced-softmax linear expert. A lightweight MLP router is fitted on retained training features and domain labels. A validation-calibrated margin rule fuses the top-2 most likely experts instead of committing to a single routed expert.
AI.result: Source-aware expert selection: 0.7915±0.0036 Macro-F1. Without source IDs: MLP router 0.7756±0.0027, top-2 margin fusion 0.7782±0.0022. The top-2 gain over hard MLP routing is small (+0.0026) with 95% CI including zero. Top-2-to-oracle gap: 0.0111-0.0133 across three domain orders.
AI.conclusion: Autonomous source inference is identified as the main bottleneck. The method is not memory-free as frozen training features are retained for router updates, though no raw ECGs are replayed.

title: Multi-Head Recurrent Memory Agents
summary: Recurrent memory agents extend LLMs to arbitrarily long contexts by iteratively consolidating input into a fixed-size memory window. Despite their scalability, these agents exhibit a well-documented reliability problem: end-to-end performance degrades systematically as context length grows. We diagnose this failure by decomposing performance into two factors--memory capture and memory retention--and quantitatively confirm that retention is the dominant bottleneck. Retention collapses because existing designs maintain memory as a monolithic text block, forcing every update to risk overwriting previously retained content. Motivated by this diagnosis, we propose Multi-Head Recurrent Memory (MHM), a general, training-free framework that partitions memory into independent heads governed by a stage-wise select-then-update strategy. At each step, exactly one head is selected for update while the remaining heads are structurally shielded from overwriting, shifting the burden of retention from model behavior to architectural design. As a lightweight instantiation, we introduce Least-Recently-Updated MHM (MHM-LRU), which guarantees uniform head utilization with zero additional token overhead. Extensive experiments on long-context benchmarks show that MHM-LRU substantially improves both retention and end-to-end accuracy across the 100K--1M token range, where baselines degrade sharply. On RULER-HQA at 896K tokens, MHM-LRU improves the memory retention rate from less than 30% to 73.96%. These gains generalize across model families, scales, and task types, positioning architectural optimization as a practical and cost-efficient path toward reliable long-context recurrent memory.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies memory retention as the primary bottleneck in recurrent memory agents for long-context LLMs, and proposes Multi-Head Recurrent Memory (MHM) with a Least-Recently-Updated variant (MHM-LRU) that partitions memory into independent heads and uses a select-then-update strategy to prevent overwriting, achieving 73.96% retention at 896K tokens compared to <30% for baselines.
AI.motivation: Recurrent memory agents suffer from systematic performance degradation as context length grows. The authors aim to diagnose the root cause of this reliability problem and propose a solution that shifts the burden of retention from model behavior to architectural design.
AI.method: The authors decompose performance into memory capture and memory retention, confirming retention as the dominant bottleneck. They propose Multi-Head Recurrent Memory (MHM), a training-free framework that partitions memory into independent heads with a stage-wise select-then-update strategy—exactly one head is updated per step while others are shielded from overwriting. The lightweight instantiation MHM-LRU uses a Least-Recently-Updated selection policy with zero additional token overhead.
AI.result: On long-context benchmarks (100K–1M tokens), MHM-LRU substantially improves both retention and end-to-end accuracy. On RULER-HQA at 896K tokens, memory retention rate improves from <30% to 73.96%. Gains generalize across model families, scales, and task types.
AI.conclusion: Architectural optimization (specifically memory head partitioning with shielded updates) is a practical and cost-efficient path toward reliable long-context recurrent memory, outperforming approaches that rely solely on model behavior.

title: Boosting Ultrasound Image Classification via Attribute-Guided Dual-Branch Framework
summary: Ultrasound image classification is essential for computer-aided diagnosis. However, current methods often neglect clinical priors, leading to poor generalization in challenging scenarios and a lack of interpretability that limits clinical adoption. To address these issues, we aim to develop a medical-prior module that can be seamlessly integrated into existing pipelines to enhance both diagnostic performance and interpretability. In this paper, we propose an attribute-guided dual-branch framework for ultrasound classification that introduces domain-agnostic medical attribute priors, improving generalization while offering interpretable evidence. Specifically, a baseline branch follows conventional architectures and predicts image categories via a fully connected classifier. An attribute-guided branch injects domain-agnostic attributes as priors and produces human-interpretable decision cues. Finally, an adaptive decision module fuses the two branches in a data-dependent manner to yield the final prediction. Experiments across diverse ultrasound classification tasks demonstrate that our approach can be integrated into multiple backbones and state-of-the-art methods with low overhead, consistently improving accuracy and interpretability. Code is available at: https://github.com/zhaobo253-crypto/AttrGuide.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an attribute-guided dual-branch framework for ultrasound image classification that integrates domain-agnostic medical attribute priors to improve generalization and interpretability, achieving consistent accuracy gains across multiple backbones and tasks.
AI.motivation: Current ultrasound classification methods neglect clinical priors, resulting in poor generalization in challenging scenarios and limited interpretability that hinders clinical adoption.
AI.method: A dual-branch framework with a baseline branch (conventional classifier) and an attribute-guided branch (injects domain-agnostic medical attribute priors for interpretable cues), fused by an adaptive decision module in a data-dependent manner.
AI.result: The approach integrates into multiple backbones and state-of-the-art methods with low overhead, consistently improving accuracy and interpretability across diverse ultrasound classification tasks.
AI.conclusion: Injecting domain-agnostic medical attribute priors via a dual-branch design enhances both generalization and interpretability, offering a lightweight plug-and-play solution for ultrasound diagnosis.

title: Benchmarking Quantum Software Testing with Scalable Quantum Programs
summary: Quantum software testing (QST) checks whether quantum programs behave according to their intended specifications. A key requirement for QST research is a benchmark that supports rigorous empirical evaluation on programs that are testable and better reflect current software development practices. However, existing studies heavily rely on small hard-coded or circuit-level benchmarks, while available quantum programs are scattered across repositories without clear selection criteria, which limits fair comparison and systematic reproducibility. To this end, we present Qolumbina, a benchmark infrastructure for controlled QST experiments on scalable quantum programs. Qolumbina curates 40 programs from open-source repositories, turns them into test-ready subjects through systematic selection, refactoring, specifications, test case examples, unit tests, and standardized interfaces. We also propose QST-oriented criteria to characterize quantum programs along functionality, output behavior, development complexity, and quantum-specific execution complexity. Using these criteria, our empirical study shows that Qolumbina covers diverse testing-relevant properties and supports scalability analysis beyond fixed-size circuit benchmarks. Through controlled experiments with two recent QST approaches, we demonstrate the feasibility of using Qolumbina for execution-cost and fault-detection studies, and highlight backend-dependent effects that can influence QST result interpretation.

AI.tldr: Qolumbina is a benchmark infrastructure for quantum software testing that curates 40 test-ready programs from open-source repositories, provides standardized interfaces and characterization criteria, and supports scalability analysis and controlled empirical studies of QST approaches.
AI.motivation: Existing QST research lacks a standardized benchmark of testable, scalable quantum programs; studies rely on small circuit-level benchmarks or scattered repositories without clear selection criteria, hindering fair comparison and reproducibility.
AI.method: The authors curated 40 programs from open-source repositories, applied systematic selection, refactoring, specification, test case examples, unit tests, and standardized interfaces. They proposed QST-oriented characterization criteria (functionality, output behavior, development complexity, quantum-specific execution complexity) and conducted empirical studies and controlled experiments with two recent QST approaches.
AI.result: Qolumbina covers diverse testing-relevant properties, supports scalability analysis beyond fixed-size circuit benchmarks, and demonstrates feasibility for execution-cost and fault-detection studies, revealing backend-dependent effects that influence QST result interpretation.
AI.conclusion: Qolumbina provides a much-needed infrastructure for systematic, reproducible, and controlled QST experiments, enabling fair comparison and deeper understanding of backend effects in quantum software testing.

title: Epistemic Goggles: A Pretrained Module that Induces an Epistemic Frame via Gradient Editing
comment: 20 pages, 10 figures, 2 tables. Code at https://github.com/JoshuaSP/epistemic-goggles and generated documents, questions, and teacher rollouts at https://huggingface.co/datasets/joshuapenman/epistemic-goggles-artifacts
summary: Finetuning a language model on documents that are explicitly annotated as fictional results in a model that still actually believes the documents' core claims, an effect known as Negation Neglect. In our evaluations, models trained on documents prefixed and suffixed with such annotations correctly identify the relevant claims as fictional only about 9% of the time. To address this, we introduce Goggles, a learned module that intervenes on the finetuning gradient rather than the data. During supervised finetuning, a Goggles module edits the gradients an LLM LoRA receives, imparting a chosen epistemic frame (the stance the model takes toward the nature of what it reads) to whatever the documents teach. A Goggles instance is trained once for a given base model, frame, and LoRA configuration, then applied frozen to documents it was never trained on. Trained through Goggles on those same documents, now carrying no fictional annotation, the model flags the content as fictional roughly 91% of the time, while preserving capability (GPQA and TruthfulQA match or exceed baseline). The same architecture supports other frames: a Goggles instance can be trained to treat documents as "part of an AI safety evaluation by Redwood Research" rather than simply as fiction. The imparted frame persists under continued finetuning that pushes back toward the claim, where prior interventions revert. Goggles suggests a path toward training language models on known-misaligned data without absorbing the behaviors that data demonstrates.

AI.tldr: Goggles is a learned module that edits gradients during finetuning to impart epistemic frames (e.g., "this is fiction") onto LLMs, increasing correct claim identification from ~9% to ~91% while preserving capabilities, and resisting degradation under continued finetuning.
AI.motivation: Language models suffer from Negation Neglect: even when explicitly annotated as fictional, models still believe the core claims of training documents (only ~9% correctly identify claims as fictional). Existing data-level interventions fail to impart an epistemic frame effectively.
AI.method: Goggles is a learned module that intervenes on the finetuning gradient (rather than the data). During supervised finetuning, it edits the gradients an LLM LoRA receives to impart a chosen epistemic frame. A single Goggles instance is trained once for a given base model, frame, and LoRA configuration, then applied frozen to unseen documents.
AI.result: Without Goggles, models correctly identify fictional claims ~9% of the time. With Goggles, models flag content as fictional ~91% of the time, while GPQA and TruthfulQA scores match or exceed the baseline. The frame persists under continued finetuning that pushes back toward the claim.
AI.conclusion: Goggles demonstrates a viable path toward training language models on known-misaligned data without absorbing the behaviors that data demonstrates, by using gradient-level intervention to impart epistemic frames that data-level annotations fail to convey.

title: Wind-Aware Reinforcement Learning Control of a Small Quadrotor Using Learned Onboard Wind Estimation in Simulated Atmospheric Turbulence
summary: Small multirotor aircraft are increasingly tasked with operations in the atmospheric boundary layer, where turbulent winds comparable to the vehicle's airspeed degrade trajectory tracking and can defeat conventional feedback control. This work illustrates a two-stage learning pipeline that first estimates the local wind from onboard kinematics and dynamics and then exploits that estimate inside a reinforcement learning (RL) flight controller. The wind estimator, an attention-augmented gated recurrent network trained on thousands of simulated flights through von Karman turbulence with power-law shear and veer, recovers the horizontal wind vector with a per-flight root-mean-square error of 0.40 m/s and a direction error of 3.2 degrees on unseen wind regimes, an accuracy near the floor imposed by unresolved turbulence, and generalizes to vertical ascent profiles with a skill score of 0.861 over a constant-wind reference. A proximal policy optimization controller receiving the frozen estimator's output reduces horizontal trajectory tracking error by 48% relative to a wind-blind proportional-derivative baseline across mean winds of 4 m/s to 12 m/s, winning on 100% of evaluation episodes. A three-way ablation decomposes this improvement into a kinematic component, available without wind information, and a wind-perception component; the perception share rises with wind speed, from small in light winds toward roughly half the total benefit in strong winds, consistent with the quadratic scaling of aerodynamic drag. The controller degrades gracefully on out-of-distribution winds of 13 m/s to 15 m/s, where the baseline fails catastrophically.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a two-stage learning pipeline for small multirotor aircraft operating in turbulent winds: an attention-augmented GRU network estimates the local wind vector from onboard data, and a PPO-based RL controller uses that estimate to improve trajectory tracking. The wind estimator achieves near-floor accuracy (0.40 m/s RMSE, 3.2° direction error), and the RL controller reduces tracking error by 48% over a wind-blind PD baseline across 4–12 m/s winds, with graceful degradation under stronger out-of-distribution winds.
AI.motivation: Small multirotor aircraft increasingly operate in the atmospheric boundary layer where turbulent winds comparable to airspeed degrade trajectory tracking and can defeat conventional feedback control.
AI.method: A two-stage learning pipeline: (1) an attention-augmented gated recurrent network trained on simulated flights through von Kármán turbulence with power-law shear and veer estimates the horizontal wind vector from onboard kinematics and dynamics; (2) a proximal policy optimization (PPO) RL controller uses the frozen estimator's output to improve trajectory tracking.
AI.result: Wind estimator: per-flight RMSE of 0.40 m/s and direction error of 3.2° on unseen wind regimes, skill score of 0.861 on vertical ascent profiles. PPO controller: 48% reduction in horizontal trajectory tracking error vs. a wind-blind PD baseline across 4–12 m/s winds, winning 100% of evaluation episodes. A three-way ablation shows the wind-perception component's share grows with wind speed. The controller degrades gracefully on out-of-distribution 13–15 m/s winds where baseline fails catastrophically.
AI.conclusion: The two-stage learning pipeline effectively combines learned wind estimation with RL-based control to dramatically improve multirotor trajectory tracking in turbulent conditions, with the wind-perception benefit scaling quadratically with wind speed as predicted by aerodynamic drag physics.

title: Plug-and-Play Volumetric Reconstruction for Compressive Sensing Light-Sheet Microscopy
summary: We investigate volumetric reconstruction for compressive sensing light-sheet microscopy (CS-LSM), where fast volumetric imaging is achieved by encoding multiple axial planes into each camera exposure. To recover the underlying volume from highly multiplexed measurements, we propose a plug-and-play (PnP) framework that flexibly incorporates any user-specified denoiser into the reconstruction process. Building on a slice-based formulation, we further introduce an axial-coupled model that exploits correlations between adjacent slices to improve volumetric continuity. For efficient computation, we derive a Woodbury-based update for the data-consistency step in both the slice-based and axial-coupled formulations, and employ a Gauss-Seidel sweep for the denoising step in the axial-coupled model. Under a weakly convex regularization assumption, we establish subsequential convergence of the proposed algorithm. Experiments on synthetic and real zebrafish-heart data demonstrate that the proposed framework successfully recovers cellular structures from compressed measurements, and provide practical insights into the comparative performance of commonly used denoisers within the PnP framework under the CS-LSM setup.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a plug-and-play (PnP) reconstruction framework for compressive sensing light-sheet microscopy (CS-LSM), featuring slice-based and axial-coupled models with Woodbury-based efficient updates and Gauss-Seidel denoising, achieving successful volumetric recovery on synthetic and real zebrafish-heart data.
AI.motivation: To recover underlying 3D volumes from highly multiplexed measurements in CS-LSM, where fast volumetric imaging encodes multiple axial planes into each camera exposure, requiring an efficient and flexible reconstruction method.
AI.method: A plug-and-play (PnP) framework with two formulations: (1) a slice-based model, and (2) an axial-coupled model that exploits inter-slice correlations for volumetric continuity. Uses Woodbury-based matrix updates for data-consistency steps and Gauss-Seidel sweeps for denoising in the axial-coupled model. Convergence established under weakly convex regularization.
AI.result: Successful recovery of cellular structures from compressed measurements on synthetic and real zebrafish-heart data, with practical insights into denoiser performance within the PnP framework under CS-LSM.
AI.conclusion: The proposed PnP framework effectively reconstructs volumetric data from CS-LSM, and the axial-coupled model improves volumetric continuity. Subsequential convergence is guaranteed under weakly convex regularization.

title: Mitigating Package Hallucinations in Large Language Models via Model Editing
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in software engineering tasks, such as code generation, library recommendation, and dependency configuration. However, recent studies show that LLMs may suffer from package hallucination, where they generate non-existent or invalid package names. These hallucinations can be exploited in software supply chain attacks, as attackers may register malicious packages under hallucinated names. Therefore, mitigating package hallucination is important for improving the reliability and security of LLM-assisted software development. In this paper, we introduce BOUND, a lightweight localized model editing framework for mitigating package hallucinations in LLMs. BOUND formulates package hallucination mitigation as a package-validity boundary editing problem, where the boundary refers to the model's ability to distinguish valid packages from hallucinated package names under a given task context. It first locates modules related to package hallucination through a risk-aware localization strategy, and then edits these modules with lightweight LoRA adapters using a boundary-aware objective that reinforces valid packages, suppresses hallucinated packages, and preserves locality behavior. Experimental results show that BOUND effectively reduces package hallucinations while preserving valid package recommendations. In the package recommendation task, BOUND reduces package-level hallucination rate (Package-HR) by 79.9% on edit prompts and by 65.4% on unseen prompts. The learned package-validity boundary further generalizes to other package-related tasks, reducing Package-HR by 12.8% in code generation and by 34.0% in pip install recommendation. These results show that BOUND refines the package-validity boundary of LLMs and improves the reliability of package-related outputs.

AI.tldr: BOUND is a lightweight localized model editing framework that mitigates package hallucinations in LLMs by formulating the problem as package-validity boundary editing. It uses risk-aware localization and boundary-aware LoRA adapters to reduce hallucination rates by up to 79.9% in package recommendation tasks while preserving valid package recommendations.
AI.motivation: LLMs suffer from package hallucination (generating non-existent/invalid package names), which can be exploited in software supply chain attacks. Mitigating this is important for improving the reliability and security of LLM-assisted software development.
AI.method: BOUND formulates mitigation as a package-validity boundary editing problem. It first locates modules related to package hallucination via risk-aware localization, then edits them with lightweight LoRA adapters using a boundary-aware objective that reinforces valid packages, suppresses hallucinated ones, and preserves locality behavior.
AI.result: Reduces Package-HR by 79.9% on edit prompts and 65.4% on unseen prompts in package recommendation. Generalizes to other tasks: 12.8% reduction in code generation, 34.0% in pip install recommendation.
AI.conclusion: BOUND effectively refines the package-validity boundary of LLMs, reducing package hallucinations while preserving valid recommendations, thus improving the reliability of package-related outputs.

title: COMFYCLAW: Self-Evolving Skill Harnesses for Image Generation Workflows
summary: Agents are increasingly used to construct workflows and assist humans in completing recurring tasks more efficiently. As these workflows become repeated and domain-specific, agent memory and reusable skills become increasingly important: agents should be able to recall workflow patterns, execution constraints, and user preferences from previous runs. We study this problem in workflow-based image generation and introduce COMFYCLAW, an agentic skill evolution harness for controlling ComfyUI workflows. COMFYCLAW formulates workflow construction as typed graph editing, exposes tools organized by construction stage, automatically reverts invalid edits, and uses a region-level vision-language model (VLM) verifier to translate visual failures into actionable repair suggestions. The framework further evolves a progressively disclosed skill library, where trajectories, execution errors, and verifier feedback from previous runs are distilled into reusable Agent Skills. Across four benchmark splits, three agent models, and two image backbones, COMFYCLAW achieves the best average image-generation evaluation score across all six agent configurations, outperforming a verifier-only baseline without skill evolution. Human annotations further show that annotators prefer COMFYCLAW over variants without skill evolution. Our results suggest that skill evolution is an effective mechanism for improving agent reliability and performance in recurring visual workflow construction.

AI.tldr: COMFYCLAW is an agentic framework that enhances ComfyUI workflow-based image generation by formulating workflow construction as typed graph editing with automatic revert and VLM-based verification, and progressively distilling past trajectories, errors, and feedback into reusable Agent Skills, achieving best evaluation scores across multiple benchmarks and agent configurations.
AI.motivation: As agents repeatedly execute domain-specific workflows, they need memory and reusable skills to recall workflow patterns, execution constraints, and user preferences from previous runs—capabilities that existing workflow-based image generation systems lack.
AI.method: Formulates workflow construction as typed graph editing; exposes stage-organized tools; automatically reverts invalid edits; uses a region-level VLM verifier to translate visual failures into repair suggestions; evolves a progressively disclosed skill library by distilling trajectories, errors, and verifier feedback into reusable Agent Skills.
AI.result: Across 4 benchmarks, 3 agent models, and 2 image backbones, COMFYCLAW achieves the best average image-generation evaluation score under all 6 agent configurations, outperforming a verifier-only baseline without skill evolution. Human annotators also prefer COMFYCLAW over variants without skill evolution.
AI.conclusion: Skill evolution is an effective mechanism for improving agent reliability and performance in recurring visual workflow construction.

title: Certified World Models as Sensing Clocks: Drift-Aware Deadlines for Active Perception
summary: Certified world models estimate how long their predictions remain valid. We turn this validity horizon into an operational sensing clock: a rule for when an agent should stop coasting and re-sense. Starting from an audited equivariant world model, we derive a deadline for no-sensing intervals and show that deployable deadlines in learned world models must be drift-aware: on-manifold Lyapunov rates alone overestimate coasting validity, while calibrated native rollout-drift envelopes carry the deployed guarantee. On a frozen 3D VN-JEPA model, the resulting clock controls held-out interval-simultaneous certificate violation across seeds and data shards. In a cue-conditioned theorem-bed (a synthetic bench where all schedulers share the exact model, isolating the scheduling rule), the clock remains valid on the deployment distribution and substantially reduces eventful-tail violations relative to exact-mixture expected-belief scheduling at matched sensing budget. We also report limits: in the short-horizon frozen VN-JEPA regime, empirical conformal horizons match the deployed clock on validity and budget, and a partial-reset exploration finds no clean budget-matched advantage for the spectral term. Thus the contribution is a certified sensing-clock primitive and drift-aware deployment method, not a claim that spectral clocks empirically dominate all non-spectral schedulers.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a certified sensing clock derived from equivariant world models that determines when an agent should re-sense, using drift-aware rollout-drift envelopes rather than on-manifold Lyapunov rates. Validated on frozen VN-JEPA and a synthetic theorem-bed benchmark, the clock reduces eventful-tail violations versus exact-mixture expected-belief scheduling at matched budgets, though it does not universally dominate non-spectral schedulers.
AI.motivation: To develop a certified, deployable sensing clock that tells an agent when to stop coasting and re-sense, moving beyond heuristic scheduling by grounding the deadline in audited world model validity horizons with drift-aware guarantees.
AI.method: Starting from an audited equivariant world model, derive a deadline for no-sensing intervals using calibrated native rollout-drift envelopes (drift-aware) rather than on-manifold Lyapunov rates. Validate on frozen 3D VN-JEPA and a cue-conditioned theorem-bed synthetic benchmark isolating the scheduling rule.
AI.result: On frozen VN-JEPA, the clock controls held-out interval-simultaneous certificate violations across seeds/data shards. On the theorem-bed, it remains valid on the deployment distribution and substantially reduces eventful-tail violations compared to exact-mixture expected-belief scheduling at matched sensing budget. Empirical conformal horizons match the deployed clock in the short-horizon frozen VN-JEPA regime.
AI.conclusion: The main contribution is a certified sensing-clock primitive and drift-aware deployment method, not a claim of empirical dominance over all non-spectral schedulers. Limits are acknowledged in short-horizon and partial-reset exploration settings.

title: Domain Generalization via Text-Anchored Information Bottleneck
summary: Visual recognition models often fail when deployed in new environments. Domain Generalization (DG) addresses this by learning representations that remain invariant to environment-specific variations. Recent approaches increasingly rely on large vision-language models, assuming that preserving their expressive visual representations improves robustness. However, we show that such visual expressiveness can instead propagate spurious cues that tie representations to the training environments, hindering invariant learning. We therefore discard visual guidance and instead treat the language embedding space as the primary source of domain invariance, naturally acting as an information bottleneck that preserves core semantics while suppressing domain-specific variations. Extensive experiments across diverse backbones exhibit state-of-the-art performance and further analyze what makes guidance effective for robust generalization. These findings shift the focus of DG from improving representations to designing supervision that enforces invariance.

AI.tldr: This paper challenges the prevailing assumption that preserving visual expressiveness from vision-language models helps Domain Generalization. Instead, it shows visual cues propagate spurious domain-specific correlations, and proposes using language embedding space as a primary source of domain invariance, acting as an information bottleneck that preserves core semantics while suppressing domain-specific variations. The approach achieves state-of-the-art results and shifts DG focus from representation improvement to invariance-enforcing supervision design.
AI.motivation: Current DG methods relying on large vision-language models assume that preserving expressive visual representations improves robustness. However, this paper demonstrates that such visual expressiveness can propagate spurious cues tying representations to training environments, hindering invariant learning. The authors aim to address this by discarding visual guidance and leveraging language embeddings as a domain-invariant bottleneck.
AI.method: The method discards visual guidance entirely and treats the language embedding space as the primary source of domain invariance. The language space naturally acts as an information bottleneck that preserves core semantics while suppressing domain-specific variations, thus enforcing invariance without relying on visual representations.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across diverse backbones demonstrate state-of-the-art performance. The analysis further reveals what makes guidance effective for robust generalization.
AI.conclusion: The findings shift the focus of Domain Generalization from improving representations to designing supervision signals that enforce invariance.

title: Prompt Coverage Adequacy
summary: In recent years, it has become increasingly evident that large language models (LLMs) and autonomous agents raise the level of abstraction in software development by shifting the focus from writing precise procedures to expressing intents and goals. This paradigm shift introduces new challenges, particularly in how testing should be guided when prompts, rather than code, become primary development artifacts. To address this challenge, we propose Prompt Coverage Adequacy, a novel coverage criterion designed to support the testing of code generated from task descriptions. Prompt Coverage Adequacy serves as an analog to traditional code coverage, but operates at the level of prompts used in LLM and agent-based programming. Specifically, it measures how well a given test suite satisfies the requirements expressed in a prompt by leveraging the attention mechanisms of LLMs. We evaluate a simple instantiation of this criterion, based on attention boosting, across two datasets and multiple LLMs. Our results demonstrate that Prompt Coverage is associated with fault-detection effectiveness and can uncover over 30+% more faults than traditional code coverage when used to guide test generation. These findings suggest that Prompt Coverage Adequacy can serve as a foundation for developing testing metrics better suited to the emerging paradigm of LLM-driven software development, addressing the limitations of classical coverage criteria in this new context.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Prompt Coverage Adequacy, a novel coverage criterion for testing LLM-generated code by measuring how well test suites satisfy prompt requirements via attention mechanisms, showing it can uncover 30+% more faults than traditional code coverage.
AI.motivation: LLMs and autonomous agents shift software development from writing procedures to expressing intents via prompts, making prompts primary development artifacts. Traditional code coverage criteria are inadequate for testing code generated from prompts, creating a need for new testing metrics.
AI.method: The authors propose Prompt Coverage Adequacy, which operates at the prompt level using LLM attention mechanisms to measure how well a test suite satisfies requirements expressed in a prompt. A simple instantiation based on attention boosting is implemented and evaluated.
AI.result: Prompt Coverage is associated with fault-detection effectiveness and uncovers over 30+% more faults than traditional code coverage when guiding test generation, across two datasets and multiple LLMs.
AI.conclusion: Prompt Coverage Adequacy can serve as a foundation for testing metrics better suited to LLM-driven software development, addressing limitations of classical coverage criteria in this emerging paradigm.

title: Generic Expert Coverage for Pruning SparseMixture-of-Experts Language Models
summary: Sparsely activated Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models contain substantial structured redundancy among routed experts, but pruning them without downstream calibration data remains challenging. Existing expert-pruning methods typically rely on a single aggregated importance score, which can bias the retained set toward experts favored by dominant calibration patterns. We propose \textbf{Generic TB-Coverage}, a coverage-aware expert pruning method that uses only generic text corpora (WikiText2 and C4) for calibration. Instead of collapsing expert utility into one score, our method profiles per-expert utility separately on each corpus and enforces a fixed-budget coverage rule that preserves high-utility experts from each corpus before constructing the final pruning mask. Across Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B and DeepSeek-MoE-16B-Base at 25\%, 50\%, and 75\% retention budgets, our method improves average accuracy on six common zero-shot benchmarks over random pruning, REAP, and ExpertSparsity, while also reducing perplexity degradation on WikiText2 and C4. The gains are largest under aggressive pruning (25\% and 50\% retain), suggesting that preserving cross-corpus expert coverage is an effective generic-data prior for MoE pruning. Our improvements hold with fixed pruning budgets and no downstream calibration data.

AI.tldr: Proposes Generic TB-Coverage, a coverage-aware expert pruning method for MoE language models that uses generic text corpora (WikiText2, C4) and a fixed-budget coverage rule to preserve high-utility experts from each corpus, outperforming random pruning, REAP, and ExpertSparsity across multiple retention budgets and benchmarks without requiring downstream calibration data.
AI.motivation: Existing expert-pruning methods rely on a single aggregated importance score, which can bias the retained set toward experts favored by dominant calibration patterns, and they typically require downstream calibration data—both limitations are addressed by proposing a coverage-aware method using only generic corpora.
AI.method: Profiles per-expert utility separately on two generic corpora (WikiText2 and C4), then enforces a fixed-budget coverage rule that preserves high-utility experts from each corpus before constructing the final pruning mask, avoiding collapsing utility into a single score.
AI.result: On Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B and DeepSeek-MoE-16B-Base at 25%, 50%, and 75% retention budgets, Generic TB-Coverage improves average accuracy on six zero-shot benchmarks and reduces perplexity degradation on WikiText2 and C4 compared to random pruning, REAP, and ExpertSparsity, with largest gains under aggressive pruning (25% and 50% retain).
AI.conclusion: Preserving cross-corpus expert coverage is an effective generic-data prior for MoE pruning, achieving improvements with fixed pruning budgets and no downstream calibration data.

title: Evolutionary Feature Engineering for Structured Data
comment: 9 page main content, 41 pages in total
summary: Large language models are increasingly used as open-ended search operators in evolutionary optimization. We introduce Evolutionary Feature Engineering (EFE), a framework for using LLM-based evolution to discover preprocessing transformations for structured data. EFE represents transformations as Python programs with a standardized fit/transform interface, allowing them to be inserted directly into existing machine learning pipelines. During evolution, candidate programs are refined using dataset context, summary statistics, and downstream performance feedback on validation set. We instantiate EFE in two settings. For time-series forecasting, EFE-Time learns invertible, dataset-specific normalizations that improve off-the-shelf time-series foundation models. It reduces forecasting errors (MASE, WQL, MAE) 3% or more when averaged across datasets and improvements are as much as 19% on the COVID-Deaths dataset. Notably, these improvements occur with recent TSFMs such as Chronos-2. For tabular prediction, EFE-Tab evolves compact feature programs that add useful interpretable features and remove redundant ones, improving or matching existing LLM-based feature-engineering methods. We found EFE-Tab to be particularly effective on classical decision trees, where small sets of evolved features yield competitive accuracy while preserving interpretability. Overall, EFE demonstrates that LLM-based evolution can improve both accuracy and interpretability when automatically tackling structured data.

AI.tldr: EFE is a framework that uses LLM-based evolution to automatically discover preprocessing transformations (as Python programs) for structured data, improving both accuracy and interpretability in time-series forecasting (up to 19% error reduction) and tabular prediction tasks.
AI.motivation: To leverage large language models as open-ended search operators in evolutionary optimization for automatic feature engineering on structured data, aiming to improve both predictive performance and interpretability without manual preprocessing.
AI.method: EFE represents transformations as Python programs with a standard fit/transform interface, evolving them via LLM-based operators (mutation, crossover) guided by dataset context, summary statistics, and validation-set performance feedback. Two instantiations: EFE-Time (invertible normalizations for time-series forecasting) and EFE-Tab (compact feature programs for tabular prediction).
AI.result: EFE-Time reduces forecasting errors (MASE, WQL, MAE) by 3% on average and up to 19% on COVID-Deaths dataset, improving recent TSFMs like Chronos-2. EFE-Tab improves or matches existing LLM-based feature engineering methods, particularly effective on classical decision trees with compact interpretable features.
AI.conclusion: LLM-based evolution can automatically improve both accuracy and interpretability for structured data preprocessing, demonstrating effective integration of evolutionary search with large language models for practical machine learning pipelines.

title: Teaching Vision-Language-Action Models What to See and Where to Look
comment: The paper has been accepted by ECCV 2026
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as a promising paradigm for end-to-end autonomous driving. However, existing VLAs' training relies heavily on text-centric visual question answering and chain-of-thought reasoning data, which emphasizes linguistic reasoning rather than action-grounded planning. As a result, the learned representations capture semantic knowledge but lack spatial dependencies crucial for reliable trajectory prediction. We propose DriveTeach-VLA, a framework that explicitly teaches VLAs what to see and where to look. Driving-aware Vision Distillation (DVD) injects driving-specific perceptual priors into the vision encoder, while 2D Trajectory-Guided Prompts (2D-TGP) provide spatial conditioning aligned with feasible driving trajectories. Together, they form a vision-guided learning pipeline: what to see (DVD pretraining) - where to look (TGP-guided SFT) - how to act (TGP-guided GRPO). DriveTeach-VLA achieves the state-of-the-art performance on NAVSIM and nuScenes. Our code is available at: https://github.com/ShivaTeam/DriveTeach-VLA.

AI.tldr: DriveTeach-VLA improves Vision-Language-Action models for autonomous driving by introducing Driving-aware Vision Distillation (DVD) to inject driving-specific perceptual priors and 2D Trajectory-Guided Prompts (2D-TGP) for spatial conditioning, forming a vision-guided pipeline (what to see → where to look → how to act) that achieves SOTA on NAVSIM and nuScenes.
AI.motivation: Existing VLA models for autonomous driving rely on text-centric VQA and chain-of-thought data, which emphasize linguistic reasoning over action-grounded planning. This causes the learned representations to capture semantic knowledge but lack the spatial dependencies needed for reliable trajectory prediction.
AI.method: DriveTeach-VLA introduces a vision-guided learning pipeline with three stages: (1) Driving-aware Vision Distillation (DVD) for pretraining the vision encoder with driving-specific perceptual priors, (2) 2D Trajectory-Guided Prompts (2D-TGP) for supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to provide spatial conditioning, and (3) TGP-guided GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) for action learning.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art performance on NAVSIM and nuScenes benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly teaching VLAs what to see (via DVD) and where to look (via 2D-TGP) effectively bridges the gap between linguistic reasoning and action-grounded trajectory prediction, yielding superior autonomous driving performance.

title: File-Level Copying Is an Implicit Dependency in Open Source
summary: File-level copying is a widespread but ungoverned form of software reuse. Copying files across repositories reduces supply-chain visibility: it removes the four observable signals a package manager provides for a declared dependency (provenance, maintenance, security, and compliance) with no mechanism to restore them. To characterize the scale and consequences of this unmanaged reuse, we present a mixed-method study of copying across the entire open-source ecosystem using World of Code (WoC). From a 0.1% commit sample, we extract 690,500 copy events and retain 3,912 rationale-bearing copy commits for intent labeling. We show that the 13 axial copy forms, spanning vendored dependencies, hardware/driver synchronization, scaffolding, UI assets, and direct source-code reuse, are unreliable proxies for developer intent: among rationale-bearing commits, hardware/driver copies are predominantly fork-maintenance work (78%), while dependency-vendoring copies more often signal upstream bypass (70%) than offline availability. These visibility gaps are form-specific: security and license risk concentrate in complementary copy forms. Copied sources are frequently stale (median 155 days; 38.5% over one year old) and seldom record a recoverable origin (4.3% documented), let alone a checkable version (2.0% versioned); even vendored copies record where they came from only 10% of the time. Security risk concentrates in vendored dependencies: 17,314 CVE-risk copy commits in the full-WoC graph, 88% in the dependency-vendoring form; 80% score CVSS >= 7.0 and upstream-fix adoption is only 47%-84%. License risk concentrates in direct source-code reuse: 41,777 pre-validation candidates, 66% in the source-code form, with 39 verified high-star violations (kappa = 0.752). Both risks reach packaged software and are invisible to dependency scanners operating on declared metadata alone.

AI.tldr: File-level copying across open-source repositories creates supply-chain visibility gaps, with 13 copy forms identified. Security risks concentrate in vendored dependencies (17,314 CVE-risk commits, 88% in vendoring), while license risks concentrate in direct source-code reuse (41,777 pre-validation candidates, 66% in source-code form). Copied sources are frequently stale (median 155 days) and rarely document origin (4.3%).
AI.motivation: To characterize the scale and consequences of unmanaged file-level copying—an ungoverned form of software reuse that removes provenance, maintenance, security, and compliance signals provided by package managers—across the entire open-source ecosystem.
AI.method: Mixed-method study using World of Code (WoC): extracted 690,500 copy events from a 0.1% commit sample; retained 3,912 rationale-bearing copy commits for intent labeling; developed 13 axial copy forms; analyzed CVE-risk and license-violation patterns across the full WoC graph.
AI.result: 13 axial copy forms identified; 78% of hardware/driver copies are fork-maintenance work, while 70% of dependency-vendoring copies signal upstream bypass. Only 4.3% document origin; 2.0% are versioned. 17,314 CVE-risk copy commits (88% in vendoring), 80% with CVSS >= 7.0, 47%-84% upstream-fix adoption. 41,777 license pre-validation candidates (66% in source-code form), 39 verified high-star violations.
AI.conclusion: File-level copying poses significant security and license risks that are invisible to dependency scanners operating on declared metadata alone, with risk profiles that vary by copy form and require form-specific governance approaches.

title: Distributionally Robust Listwise Preference Optimization
summary: Existing robust preference optimization for language-model alignment mainly studies pairwise supervision and places robustness at the dataset, prompt, or preference-pair level. We instead study listwise preference optimization under ranking-label uncertainty: given a prompt and a candidate list, the observed ranking over that list may be ambiguous due to annotator inconsistency, near-ties, lossy rankwise feedback, or reward-model noise. We propose a pointwise total-variation robust Plackett--Luce objective that directly robustifies the ranking label conditional on the candidate list. The robust loss admits an exact decomposition into the nominal PL loss plus a worst-case PL correction, and the worst-case ranking is obtained by sorting current implicit scores in ascending order, reducing the inner maximization from $K!$ enumeration to $O(K\log K)$. This tractable structure yields strong offline and online optimization guarantees. In the offline fixed-list setting, the robust objective is convex and projected stochastic subgradient reaches global $ε$-suboptimality with $O(ε^{-2})$ sample complexity. In the online policy-induced setting, where candidate lists are generated by the current policy, we establish weak convexity and $\widetilde O(ε^{-2})$ Moreau-envelope stationarity. Experiments in offline LLM alignment show that the proposed robust correction largely preserves performance under clean labels and improves robustness under noise. In online alignment, it makes reward-model-ranked candidate expansion more reliable and improves both reward-model and external GPT-4 judge metrics.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a pointwise total-variation robust Plackett-Luce objective for listwise preference optimization under ranking-label uncertainty, which is tractable (reducing inner maximization from K! to O(K log K)), enjoys convex/weakly-convex convergence guarantees, and improves robustness in both offline and online LLM alignment tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing robust preference optimization focuses on pairwise supervision and dataset/prompt/pair-level robustness, but listwise preference optimization under ranking-label uncertainty (due to annotator inconsistency, near-ties, lossy feedback, reward-model noise) remains understudied.
AI.method: Proposes a pointwise total-variation robust Plackett-Luce objective that robustifies the ranking label conditional on the candidate list. The robust loss decomposes into nominal PL loss plus a worst-case PL correction, where the worst-case ranking is obtained by sorting current implicit scores in ascending order (reducing enumeration from K! to O(K log K)).
AI.result: Offline fixed-list: convex, O(ε^{-2}) sample complexity to reach global ε-suboptimality. Online policy-induced: weakly convex, Õ(ε^{-2}) Moreau-envelope stationarity. Experiments show robustness under noise while preserving clean-label performance in offline LLM alignment, and improved reward-model and GPT-4 judge metrics in online alignment.
AI.conclusion: The proposed robust correction is tractable, theoretically grounded, and empirically effective for handling ranking-label uncertainty in listwise preference optimization for LLM alignment.

title: X-LogSMask: Expand Transformer for Graph-Structured Data
summary: Transformers have become general-purpose architectures, but their all-to-all self-attention is poorly matched to graph data, whose interactions are sparse, structured and multi-scale. Existing Graph Transformers address this mismatch through structural encodings, hybrid message-passing modules or learned attention constraints, often introducing additional complexity and limited interpretability. Here we introduce X-LogSMask, an explainable multi-head logarithmic structural mask that injects symmetrically normalized graph topology directly into attention logits. The logarithmic transform converts structural connectivity into a topology-aware gating signal, suppressing unsupported node interactions while preserving feature-dependent attention. By assigning different powers of the normalized adjacency matrix to different attention heads, X-LogSMask gives each head a defined structural radius and supports multi-hop information propagation within a single layer. We further show that a standard Transformer encoder can be interpreted as one-step message passing on a complete graph, motivating X-LogSMask as a topology-constrained alternative to unrestricted self-attention. Across 20 node-, edge- and graph-level benchmarks, Transformers equipped with X-LogSMask achieve state-of-the-art performance on 13 datasets and remain competitive in a lightweight one-layer configuration. These results show that simple, interpretable structural masks can make self-attention an effective graph-learning operator without changing the Transformer architecture. The code is available at https://github.com/LiLeyan-0120/X-LogSMask.

AI.tldr: X-LogSMask introduces a logarithmic structural mask that injects normalized graph topology into attention logits, enabling Transformers to effectively handle graph data with multi-hop propagation in a single layer, achieving SOTA on 13 out of 20 benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Standard all-to-all self-attention in Transformers is poorly matched to graph data, which has sparse, structured, and multi-scale interactions. Existing Graph Transformers address this mismatch with complex structural encodings, hybrid message-passing, or learned attention constraints, introducing limited interpretability and additional complexity.
AI.method: X-LogSMask uses a logarithmic transform of the symmetrically normalized adjacency matrix as a topology-aware gating signal injected directly into attention logits. Different powers of the normalized adjacency matrix are assigned to different attention heads, giving each head a defined structural radius for multi-hop information propagation within a single layer.
AI.result: Evaluated on 20 node-, edge-, and graph-level benchmarks, Transformers with X-LogSMask achieve state-of-the-art on 13 datasets and remain competitive even in a lightweight one-layer configuration.
AI.conclusion: Simple, interpretable structural masks can make self-attention an effective graph-learning operator without altering the Transformer architecture, offering a clean alternative to more complex Graph Transformer designs.

title: Unified Panoramic-Gaussian Representation for Monocular 4D Scene Synthesis
summary: 4D scene synthesis from monocular videos has made significant progress in recent years. However, existing methods are typically constrained by view interpolation. As a result, they struggle to infer unseen regions beyond the observed views. In this paper, we reformulate the task as 4D scene synthesis with unseen regions, which extends beyond traditional interpolation settings. Camera-conditioned video generation enables unseen region synthesis by guiding generation along specified cameras. However, these methods lack explicit 3D priors and are optimized with random camera trajectories. This design leads to severe inconsistencies under large trajectory deviations. To address this limitation, we build a unified training and inference framework with panoramic trajectory guidance. While this design improves cross-view consistency, the panoramic representation alone fails to model dynamic content effectively. Object motion in panoramic space introduces scale and shape distortions. To address this, we propose PanoGaussian, a unified Panoramic-Gaussian representation that distills the panoramic representation into an explicit dynamic Gaussian representation to capture dynamic physical priors of the 4D scene. Experiments demonstrate that PanoGaussian achieves consistent 4D scene synthesis even under large viewpoint variations.

AI.tldr: PanoGaussian reformulates 4D scene synthesis from monocular videos as a task with unseen region generation, using a unified Panoramic-Gaussian representation that combines panoramic trajectory guidance with explicit dynamic Gaussian priors to achieve consistent synthesis under large viewpoint variations.
AI.motivation: Existing 4D scene synthesis methods are limited to view interpolation and struggle to infer unseen regions beyond observed views. Camera-conditioned video generation lacks explicit 3D priors and suffers from severe inconsistencies under large trajectory deviations.
AI.method: PanoGaussian builds a unified training and inference framework with panoramic trajectory guidance for consistency, then introduces a Panoramic-Gaussian representation that distills panoramic representation into an explicit dynamic Gaussian representation to capture physical priors of the 4D scene, addressing scale and shape distortions in object motion.
AI.result: PanoGaussian achieves consistent 4D scene synthesis even under large viewpoint variations, overcoming limitations of both interpolation-based methods and camera-conditioned generation approaches.
AI.conclusion: The proposed Panoramic-Gaussian representation effectively bridges panoramic trajectory guidance and explicit dynamic 3D modeling, enabling robust 4D scene synthesis with unseen region generation under large viewpoint changes.

title: Coding Agents Are Guessing: Measuring Action-Boundary Violations in Underspecified DevOps Instructions
summary:
LLM coding agents are increasingly deployed to act autonomously on real production infrastructure. They execute shell commands, modify repositories, and call operational APIs. However, completing a task is not sufficient for safety. A wrong action can cause severe consequences. Existing agent benchmarks largely emphasize task completion, leaving open how agents behave under benign but underspecified instructions.
  We present UnderSpecBench, a benchmark for measuring action-boundary violations in coding agents (i.e., Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode) on DevOps tasks. UnderSpecBench includes 69 task families grounded in documented incidents, CVEs, or tool behavior and organized across four DevOps capability domains and nine operational control surfaces. To isolate underspecification from task difficulty, each task keeps the same environment and ground-truth safe action while varying the instruction along three axes: intent clarity, target certainty, and blast radius. The resulting 2,208 prompt variants are evaluated with deterministic, side-effect-based oracles that separate Safe Success, Wrong Target, and OverScope outcomes; non-action runs are further classified as clarification, refusal, or deferment.
  Across five agent x model configurations using OpenCode, Claude Code, and Codex, the evaluation results show that underspecification does not mainly make agents fail; it makes them guess. 55.8-67.8% of runs violate at least one boundary. Target underspecification sharply degrades action quality, while blast-radius cues barely reduce action propensity. These findings show that completion-centric evaluation can overstate safe autonomy and motivate mitigations at the model, harness, and system layer.

AI.tldr: UnderSpecBench is a benchmark with 69 DevOps task families and 2,208 prompt variants that evaluates coding agents (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode) on action-boundary violations under underspecified instructions, finding that 55.8-67.8% of runs violate safety boundaries due to agents guessing rather than clarifying ambiguous instructions.
AI.motivation: Existing agent benchmarks focus on task completion rather than safety under benign but underspecified instructions. Since LLM coding agents are deployed on real production infrastructure where wrong actions can cause severe consequences, there is a need to measure how agents behave when instructions lack clarity.
AI.method: UnderSpecBench includes 69 task families based on documented incidents, CVEs, and tool behavior across 4 DevOps domains and 9 operational control surfaces. Each task varies instructions along 3 axes (intent clarity, target certainty, blast radius) while keeping environment and ground-truth safe actions constant, creating 2,208 prompt variants. Evaluation uses deterministic side-effect-based oracles classifying outcomes as Safe Success, Wrong Target, OverScope, or non-action (clarification, refusal, deferment).
AI.result: Across 5 agent×model configurations, 55.8-67.8% of runs violate at least one action boundary. Underspecification causes agents to guess rather than fail. Target underspecification sharply degrades action quality while blast-radius cues barely reduce action propensity.
AI.conclusion: Completion-centric evaluation overstates safe autonomy. Findings motivate mitigations at the model, harness, and system layer to improve agent safety under underspecified instructions.

title: Geometric Signatures of Reasoning: A Spectral Perspective on Task Hardness
summary: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning enables large language models (LLMs) to solve complex problems by generating intermediate reasoning steps. While much attention has been paid to the length and content of these reasoning chains, far less is known about their internal geometry. We study the \emph{geometry} of CoT trajectories in the hidden state space of transformer models, formalizing each reasoning chain as a discrete curve in $\mathbb{R}^d$ and characterizing it through spectral, positional, and kinematic geometric functionals. We introduce the effective dimension $d_ρ$ as a measure of trajectory complexity and show theoretically that trajectories with flatter eigenvalue spectra correspond to harder tasks, as they explore more of the hidden dimensions. Lastly, we explore how kinematic features of the trajectory, mean position, positional dispersion, initial and current hidden states, mean velocity, mean speed, and speed dispersion, can be used to predict solution correctness before generation is complete, and may inform future early-stopping strategies. Experimentally, on mathematical reasoning problems from the MATH500 dataset, $d_ρ$ achieves $0.93$ AUC in distinguishing easy from hard problems, while kinematic features potentially can predict correctness from only the first $20\%$ of generated tokens. These correctness signatures transfer across questions of varying difficulty, establishing that the shape of a model's internal reasoning trajectory is a principled window into both task hardness and solution quality.

AI.tldr: This paper studies the geometry of chain-of-thought reasoning trajectories in LLMs' hidden state space, introducing effective dimension d_ρ as a measure of trajectory complexity, and showing that geometric and kinematic features can predict task difficulty and solution correctness early during generation.
AI.motivation: While CoT reasoning has been extensively studied in terms of chain length and content, the internal geometric structure of these reasoning trajectories in the model's hidden state space remains largely unexplored.
AI.method: The authors formalize CoT chains as discrete curves in ℝ^d, define spectral (effective dimension d_ρ), positional (mean position, dispersion), and kinematic (velocity, speed, dispersion) geometric functionals, and analyze them theoretically and on MATH500 mathematical reasoning problems.
AI.result: d_ρ achieves 0.93 AUC in distinguishing easy from hard problems on MATH500; kinematic features can predict correctness from only the first 20% of generated tokens, and these signatures transfer across varying difficulty levels.
AI.conclusion: The shape of a model's internal reasoning trajectory provides a principled window into both task hardness and solution quality, potentially enabling early-stopping strategies.

title: Temporal and Cross-Modal Alignment for Enhanced Audiovisual Video Captioning
summary: While Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have advanced video understanding, achieving precise temporal and cross-modal alignment in audiovisual video captioning remains a formidable challenge. Most existing approaches suffer from modality detachment and temporal incoherence, failing to accurately bind auditory events to visual entities or capture complex causal dynamics. To address these deficiencies, we propose TCA-Captioner, a framework specifically engineered to enhance Temporal and Cross-Modal Alignment for audiovisual video captioning. We first introduce the Observer-Checker-Corrector (OCC) framework, an iterative refinement strategy that generates high-fidelity, meticulously grounded training data. Leveraging a curated high-density human interaction dataset, TCA-Captioner is optimized to model sophisticated audiovisual interactions. Furthermore, we present TCA-Bench, a diagnostic benchmark utilizing a Decoupled Evaluation Protocol to isolate and quantify model proficiency in audiovisual binding and temporal relational reasoning. Extensive experiments demonstrate that TCA-Captioner sets a new standard for temporally-coherent and synchronized audiovisual narratives.

AI.tldr: TCA-Captioner is a framework for audiovisual video captioning that enhances temporal and cross-modal alignment via iterative refinement (OCC), a curated high-density interaction dataset, and a diagnostic benchmark (TCA-Bench) with a Decoupled Evaluation Protocol, achieving state-of-the-art performance.
AI.motivation: Existing MLLMs suffer from modality detachment and temporal incoherence in audiovisual video captioning, failing to bind auditory events to visual entities or capture causal dynamics.
AI.method: Proposes (1) Observer-Checker-Corrector (OCC) for iterative refinement of training data, (2) training on a curated high-density human interaction dataset, and (3) TCA-Bench with a Decoupled Evaluation Protocol for diagnostic evaluation.
AI.result: TCA-Captioner sets a new standard for temporally-coherent and synchronized audiovisual narratives, outperforming prior methods.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework effectively addresses modality detachment and temporal incoherence, advancing audiovisual video captioning through explicit temporal and cross-modal alignment.

title: Guiding Human Validation of LLM-Generated Code via Verifiable Literate Programming
summary:
Vibe coding democratizes software development by allowing users to generate code via natural-language (NL) interaction with large language models (LLMs). However, the code is reliable only when it faithfully implements the user's intent, which is difficult and labor-intensive for users to validate. Existing validation methods either rely on LLM-assisted automated testing, which suffers from prompt ambiguity and model fallibility, or involve users only in partial software artifacts such as prompts and test cases, which may overlook corner cases and program details. Motivated by a bug study of LLM-generated code, we find that detailed human feedback is essential, as failures often stem from underspecified requirements or subtle semantic deviations.
  This paper presents verifiable literate programming (VLP), a human-in-the-loop framework designed to make the review/validation process of LLM-generated code accessible to users at all programming levels. At its core, VLP proposes unambiguous NL-based documentation as a readable intermediate layer between prompts and code. The documentation demonstrates concrete program semantics and enables users to provide feedback on potential intent-code mismatches. It supports human-involved, end-to-end repair and validation via three techniques: (i) an NL-style literate language with unambiguous syntax and mostly deterministic code-to-documentation translation, (ii) LLM-based fine-grained mismatch detection that uses trace links between prompts and documentation to focus users' review effort on suspicious documentation lines, and (iii) a verification module that leverages user-validated documentation to derive API-usage checks and formal properties, which are then verified against the generated code using model checking. Our evaluation shows that VLP improves code pass@1 from 28.7%-73.2% to 65.4%-93.5% with reasonable user effort.

AI.tldr: VLP is a human-in-the-loop framework that uses unambiguous NL-based documentation as an intermediate layer to help users validate LLM-generated code, improving pass@1 from 28.7%-73.2% to 65.4%-93.5% with reasonable effort.
AI.motivation: LLM-generated code often fails to faithfully implement user intent due to underspecified requirements and subtle semantic deviations. Existing validation methods (LLM-assisted testing, user involvement in prompts/test cases) are insufficient — detailed human feedback is essential but labor-intensive.
AI.method: VLP proposes three techniques: (i) an NL-style literate language with unambiguous syntax and deterministic code-to-documentation translation, (ii) LLM-based fine-grained mismatch detection using trace links between prompts and documentation to highlight suspicious lines, and (iii) a verification module that derives API-usage checks and formal properties from user-validated documentation and verifies them via model checking.
AI.result: VLP improves code pass@1 from 28.7%-73.2% to 65.4%-93.5% with reasonable user effort.
AI.conclusion: Verifiable literate programming makes the validation of LLM-generated code accessible to users at all programming levels by introducing an unambiguous NL documentation layer that bridges prompts and code, enabling effective human-in-the-loop repair and verification.

title: Reformalization of the Jordan Curve Theorem
summary: We present a case study in reformalization, a variant of autoformalization in which the input proof is not natural language but a formal development in a different proof assistant. Concretely, we report three reformalizations of the Jordan Curve Theorem: from Mizar to Lean, from HOL Light to Lean, and from HOL Light to Agda. We analyse the results and identify pipeline design choices that matter for practical reformalization tasks.

AI.tldr: This paper studies reformalization (formal-to-formal proof translation) by converting the Jordan Curve Theorem from Mizar to Lean, HOL Light to Lean, and HOL Light to Agda, analyzing design choices for practical reformalization pipelines.
AI.motivation: To understand the challenges and design choices involved in reformalization (translating formal proofs between different proof assistants), as opposed to autoformalization (translating from natural language to formal proofs).
AI.method: The authors conduct three case studies of reformalizing the Jordan Curve Theorem: (1) Mizar → Lean, (2) HOL Light → Lean, and (3) HOL Light → Agda. They analyze the pipelines and identify critical design choices.
AI.result: The paper identifies specific pipeline design choices that significantly impact practical reformalization tasks, providing insights from three distinct source-target proof assistant pairs.
AI.conclusion: Reformalization is a distinct variant of autoformalization with its own challenges; the identified design choices are crucial for building effective reformalization pipelines.

title: BOUNDARY_SYNC: Measuring Communication-Induced Representational Coupling in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
summary: As large language models (LLMs) are deployed as communicating agents, does inter-agent communication cause outputs to converge? We introduce BOUNDARY_SYNC, a protocol measuring representational coupling via the Coupling Amplification Factor (CAF = JSD_cond / JSD_baseline), where CAF < 1 indicates homogenization and CAF > 1 indicates diversification. In controlled GPT-4o experiments (N=30, ~9,900 API calls), we measure coupling in text and image communication. Key findings: (1) text communication causes significant homogenization (CAF=0.803 [0.740, 0.873], d=1.30, p<0.001), confirmed by no-communication ablation and prompt-perturbation controls; (2) image communication also homogenizes under within-modality baselines (CAF=0.834 [0.811, 0.858]), with comparable proportional effect; (3) group size moderates coupling direction -- K=5 produces homogenization while K=3 yields CAF > 1.0 (point estimates 1.14 and 1.06, CI pending), suggesting a directional shift toward diversification; (4) cross-model replication shows extreme variation (CAF 0.034-0.803), with DeepSeek dominated by format artifacts; (5) coupling is stateless -- driven by prompt context rather than cumulative updating, with continuous consensus producing monotonic convergence.
