These results establish LLM agent coupling as real, measurable, and controllable at the prompt level, with direct implications for multi-agent system design.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces BOUNDARY_SYNC, a protocol to measure representational coupling in LLM agents via the Coupling Amplification Factor (CAF). Through controlled GPT-4o experiments (~9,900 API calls), they find text communication causes significant homogenization (CAF=0.803), image communication also homogenizes, group size (K=5 vs K=3) moderates coupling direction, cross-model replication shows extreme variation, and coupling is stateless—driven by prompt context rather than cumulative updates.
AI.motivation: As LLMs are deployed as communicating multi-agent systems, it is critical to understand whether inter-agent communication causes their outputs to converge (homogenization) or diverge (diversification), which has direct implications for multi-agent system design and reliability.
AI.method: The authors propose BOUNDARY_SYNC, a protocol that measures representational coupling using the Coupling Amplification Factor (CAF = JSD_cond / JSD_baseline). They conduct controlled experiments with GPT-4o (N=30, ~9,900 API calls), measuring coupling in both text and image communication, varying group sizes (K=3, K=5), and testing cross-model replication and statelessness.
AI.result: (1) Text communication causes significant homogenization (CAF=0.803, d=1.30, p<0.001); (2) Image communication also homogenizes under within-modality baselines (CAF=0.834); (3) Group size moderates direction—K=5 homogenizes while K=3 yields CAF > 1.0 (diversification); (4) Cross-model replication shows extreme variation (CAF 0.034–0.803); (5) Coupling is stateless—driven by prompt context, with continuous consensus producing monotonic convergence.
AI.conclusion: LLM agent coupling is real, measurable, and controllable at the prompt level, with clear implications for multi-agent system design—both as a risk (undesired homogenization) and as a tool (controllable diversification).

title: HistoSeg++: Delving deeper with attention and multiscale feature fusion for biomarker segmentation
comment: Published in the Proceedings of ICBBE 2025. The Version of Record is available at https://doi.org/10.1145/3794209.3794211
summary: Segmentation of biomarkers in medical images is frequently viewed as a first step towards medical image analysis in any bioinformatics or biomedical application. Despite progress, existing methods still struggle to capture information at multiple scales and to perform upsampling effectively across different datasets. These shortcomings often result in suboptimal generalization capabilities. Recently, architectures belonging to the Nested-UNet family excel in capturing multiscale contextual information and upsample them effectively. In this work, We propose a novel Nested-UNet architecture that effectively captures multi-scale contextual information. It includes inner and outer attention units to enhance focus during upsampling, along with channel-wise feature recalibration using squeeze-and-excitation modules, leading to improved segmentation performance. Additionally, the architecture integrates an edge-aware loss to emphasize boundary accuracy by assigning greater importance to edge regions. Tested extensively on three publicly available benchmark datasets. Our method demonstrates a generalization performance superior to existing Nested-UNet methods. Code: https://github.com/saadwazir/histosegplusplus

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a novel Nested-UNet architecture with inner/outer attention units, squeeze-and-excitation modules, and edge-aware loss for improved medical image segmentation, achieving superior generalization on three benchmark datasets.
AI.motivation: Existing segmentation methods struggle to capture multi-scale contextual information and perform effective upsampling across different datasets, leading to suboptimal generalization capabilities.
AI.method: A novel Nested-UNet architecture that incorporates inner and outer attention units for enhanced upsampling focus, channel-wise feature recalibration via squeeze-and-excitation modules, and an edge-aware loss function that emphasizes boundary accuracy.
AI.result: Tested on three publicly available benchmark datasets, the method demonstrates superior generalization performance compared to existing Nested-UNet methods.
AI.conclusion: The proposed attention-guided and edge-aware Nested-UNet effectively addresses multi-scale contextual challenges in medical image segmentation, improving both boundary accuracy and cross-dataset generalization.

title: Developers' Experience with Generative AI Beyond Productivity Assessment -- Insights from an Empirical Mixed-Methods Field Study
summary: With the growing adoption of AI-powered coding assistants, organizations and developers are increasingly seeking to optimize their interaction with these tools. Prior research has largely focused on output quality and productivity gains, with limited attention paid to developers' well-being and interaction experiences. This paper presents a developer-centered empirical mixed-methods study to investigate how professional developers engage with Generative AI (GenAI) in their natural work environment. Controlled data collection sessions are combined with natural work periods. Results show that developers are generally satisfied with GenAI, particularly for monotonous, repetitive, and structured tasks, and report perceived efficiency and productivity gains. Copilot interaction type preferences differ by task type and complexity: While both in-code suggestions and chat-based prompting independently improve task efficiency and reduce perceived workload, combining these interaction types within a single task diminishes benefits. We propose a rule-of-thumb for selecting an interaction type based on task characteristics. During development-heavy tasks, results indicate that perceived cognitive load arises from AI interaction, while perceived productivity depends on AI output quality. Participation in this study positively influenced developers' awareness and intentional use of GenAI tools. These findings demonstrate the value of real-world, mixed-methods study designs to understand GenAI tools and developers' experiences with them.

AI.tldr: This mixed-methods study examines how professional developers interact with GenAI coding assistants in real work environments, finding that developers are generally satisfied, prefer different interaction types (in-code vs. chat) based on task complexity, and that combining interaction types within a single task reduces benefits.
AI.motivation: Prior research focused on output quality and productivity, with limited attention to developers' well-being and interaction experiences. This study addresses the gap by investigating how professional developers engage with GenAI in their natural work environment.
AI.method: Developer-centered empirical mixed-methods study combining controlled data collection sessions with natural work periods in professional developers' real-world settings.
AI.result: Developers are generally satisfied with GenAI, especially for monotonous/repetitive tasks. In-code suggestions and chat-based prompting independently improve efficiency and reduce workload, but combining both within a single task diminishes benefits. Perceived cognitive load arises from AI interaction, while perceived productivity depends on AI output quality. Study participation increased developers' awareness and intentional use of GenAI tools.
AI.conclusion: A rule-of-thumb for selecting interaction type based on task characteristics is proposed. Real-world, mixed-methods study designs are valuable for understanding GenAI tools and developers' experiences.

title: Meta-Benchmarks for Financial-Services LLM Evaluation
summary: Public LLM leaderboards optimise for global average performance and do not capture the specific cognitive demands of financial-services work: a model that leads on MMLU-Pro may underperform on document-grounded compliance reasoning, and a coding leader may handle multi-turn customer interactions poorly. We present a meta-benchmarking framework that organises 452 publicly reported benchmarks into 41 O*NET Generalized Work Activities and aggregates those into 38 BIAN banking business domains spanning sales, operations, risk, and support work. A multiplicative weighting scheme (discrimination x coverage x recency), computed over a rolling model window, rewards benchmarks that still separate the best models, are widely reported, and remain in active use, suppressing saturated legacy tests automatically. These weights scale the K-factor in a pairwise Elo tournament, producing cross-benchmark-comparable work-activity scores without raw score normalisation; business-domain scores are weighted averages of the constituent work-activity Elos. We demonstrate the framework on a point-in-time public snapshot covering 288 models across 25 organisations as of June 2026, and describe the methodology, full taxonomy, design decisions, and limitations with the aim of making the approach reproducible for institutions facing similar selection and governance challenges.

AI.tldr: A meta-benchmarking framework maps 452 benchmarks to 41 O*NET work activities and 38 BIAN banking domains, using multiplicative weighting (discrimination × coverage × recency) and Elo-based scoring to produce domain-specific capability profiles for LLM selection in financial services.
AI.motivation: Public LLM leaderboards focus on global average performance and fail to capture the specific cognitive demands of financial-services work, where a model strong on general knowledge (e.g., MMLU-Pro) may underperform on domain-specific tasks like compliance reasoning or multi-turn customer interactions.
AI.method: The framework organizes 452 benchmarks into 41 O*NET Generalized Work Activities and aggregates these into 38 BIAN banking business domains. A multiplicative weighting scheme (discrimination × coverage × recency) computed over a rolling model window is used to reward benchmarks that separate top models, are widely reported, and remain active. These weights scale the K-factor in a pairwise Elo tournament, producing cross-benchmark-comparable work-activity scores without raw score normalization; business-domain scores are weighted averages of constituent work-activity Elos.
AI.result: The framework is demonstrated on a point-in-time public snapshot covering 288 models across 25 organizations as of June 2026, showing it can produce work-activity and business-domain capability scores tailored to financial-services needs.
AI.conclusion: The methodology, full taxonomy, design decisions, and limitations are described to ensure reproducibility for institutions facing similar model selection and governance challenges in financial-services contexts.

title: SINA: A Fully Automated Circuit Schematic Image to Netlist Generator Using Artificial Intelligence
summary: Recent advances in Artificial Intelligence (AI) have revolutionized Electronic Design Automation (EDA), particularly through Large Language Models (LLMs) for circuit design tasks. However, their application to analog and mixed-signal domains remains limited by the lack of machine-readable representations of existing circuit design knowledge. Circuit schematic images found in research manuscripts, textbooks, and websites constitute a vast repository of validated designs; however, these visual representations cannot be directly processed by EDA tools. Converting them into machine-readable netlists is essential for enabling simulation, verification, and building comprehensive databases for AI-based models. Current conversion methods lack generalization across both Integrated Circuit (IC) and Printed Circuit Board (PCB) level schematics. Moreover, they struggle with component recognition and connectivity inference, and fail to distinguish between connected junctions and crossing wires. In this paper, we propose SINA, an open-source circuit schematic image-to-netlist generator. SINA is a fully automated pipeline that integrates deep learning for robust component detection, connected-component labeling for accurate connectivity inference, Optical Character Recognition (OCR) for component reference designator extraction, and a Vision-Language Model (VLM) for reliable reference designator assignment. SINA handles both IC- and PCB-level schematics and incorporates dedicated crossing-wires detection to differentiate wire intersections from connections. We validate the correctness of the generated netlists using graph isomorphism techniques. Our experiments demonstrate an overall netlist generation accuracy of 96.67%, which is 2.72x higher compared to state-of-the-art approaches.

AI.tldr: SINA is an open-source pipeline that converts circuit schematic images into machine-readable netlists, achieving 96.67% accuracy (2.72x higher than SOTA) by integrating deep learning, OCR, and a Vision-Language Model for both IC- and PCB-level schematics.
AI.motivation: Existing circuit schematic images in manuscripts, textbooks, and websites cannot be directly processed by EDA tools; current conversion methods lack generalization across IC and PCB schematics, struggle with component recognition and connectivity inference, and fail to distinguish connected junctions from crossing wires.
AI.method: SINA is a fully automated pipeline integrating deep learning for component detection, connected-component labeling for connectivity inference, OCR for reference designator extraction, and a Vision-Language Model (VLM) for reliable reference designator assignment. It includes dedicated crossing-wires detection and handles both IC- and PCB-level schematics. Validation uses graph isomorphism techniques.
AI.result: Overall netlist generation accuracy of 96.67%, which is 2.72x higher compared to state-of-the-art approaches.
AI.conclusion: SINA effectively bridges the gap between visual circuit schematic data and machine-readable netlists, enabling simulation, verification, and the construction of comprehensive databases for AI-based EDA models.

title: ICDepth: Taming Video Diffusion Models for Video Depth Estimation via In-Context Conditioning
comment: Accepted to ECCV 2026. Project page: https://xuanhuahe.github.io/ICDepth/
summary: Monocular video depth estimation requires temporal consistency, geometric accuracy, and generalization across diverse scenarios, yet existing methods struggle to achieve all three simultaneously. Discriminative models excel at per-frame accuracy but suffer from temporal drift due to limited context windows, while generative methods improve consistency and generalization at the cost of extensive training data (10M+ samples) and lack of geometric precision. In response to these issues, we introduce \textbf{ICDepth}, a framework that adapts pre-trained text-to-video diffusion transformers for video depth estimation via In-Context Conditioning (ICC), leveraging their rich spatial-temporal priors. To address key challenges in transferring ICC from generation to dense prediction, we propose: (1)~\textbf{SAND-Attention}, which ensures precise spatial-temporal alignment via shared RoPE and enforces unidirectional attention to prevent noise contamination; (2)~\textbf{SRFM}, which injects DINOv2 semantic and resolution priors to enhance geometric precision. ICDepth achieves state-of-the-art results on multiple benchmarks with remarkable data efficiency, trained on only 0.8M frames ($6$--$13\times$ less than competing generative methods), while demonstrating strong zero-shot generalization to diverse domains.

AI.tldr: ICDepth adapts pre-trained text-to-video diffusion transformers for video depth estimation via In-Context Conditioning, achieving SOTA results with only 0.8M training frames (6-13x less than competing generative methods) through SAND-Attention for spatial-temporal alignment and SRFM for geometric precision.
AI.motivation: Existing methods struggle to simultaneously achieve temporal consistency, geometric accuracy, and generalization across diverse scenarios. Discriminative models suffer temporal drift, while generative methods require extensive training data (10M+ samples) and lack geometric precision.
AI.method: ICDepth adapts pre-trained text-to-video diffusion transformers for video depth estimation via In-Context Conditioning (ICC). It proposes: (1) SAND-Attention for precise spatial-temporal alignment via shared RoPE and unidirectional attention to prevent noise contamination; (2) SRFM to inject DINOv2 semantic and resolution priors for enhanced geometric precision.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art results on multiple benchmarks with only 0.8M training frames (6-13x less than competing generative methods), demonstrating strong zero-shot generalization to diverse domains.
AI.conclusion: ICDepth effectively bridges the gap between generative and discriminative approaches by leveraging diffusion priors with in-context conditioning, achieving data-efficient, geometrically precise, and temporally consistent video depth estimation with strong generalization.

title: SkillFuzz: Fuzzing Skill Composition for Implicit Intents Discovery in Open Skill Marketplaces
summary: Large Language Model (LLM)-based agents increasingly automate software engineering tasks through reusable skills, natural-language instruction documents that guide planning and execution. Open skill marketplaces enable users to assemble agents by co-activating community-contributed skills, but marketplace operators typically audit skills in isolation. As a result, individually benign skills may interact to redirect an agent toward unintended objectives, which we term implicit intents. Detecting such intents is challenging because the effect emerges only through skill composition, execution environments are often unavailable at admission time, and the space of possible co-activations grows exponentially with marketplace size. In this paper, we formulate implicit-intent discovery as a fuzzing problem over skill compositions, where skill compositions are the unit under test, planning artifacts expose agent intent before execution, and deviations from a skill-free baseline serve as a differential oracle. Based on this formulation, we propose skillfuzz, the first execution-free testing approach that extracts structured skill contracts and uses contract-guided Monte Carlo Tree Search to prioritize potentially conflicting compositions. Across representative skill-marketplace workloads, skillfuzz discovers over 1,000 distinct implicit intents under a fixed query budget, confirms more than 80% of the highest-risk flagged compositions during execution-time validation, and identifies substantially more high-severity implicit intents than alternative search strategies while exploring only a fraction of the pairwise interaction space they require.

AI.tldr: skillfuzz is an execution-free fuzzing approach that detects implicit intents (emergent malicious behaviors) in LLM agent skill compositions by using contract-guided Monte Carlo Tree Search and differential oracles, discovering over 1,000 implicit intents with >80% validation rate.
AI.motivation: Individually benign skills in LLM agent marketplaces can interact to produce unintended, harmful behaviors (implicit intents), but existing audits only check skills in isolation. Detecting these compositional effects is challenging due to unavailability of execution environments at admission time and exponential co-activation space.
AI.method: Formulates implicit-intent discovery as a fuzzing problem where skill compositions are the test unit, planning artifacts reveal intent pre-execution, and deviations from a skill-free baseline serve as a differential oracle. Proposes skillfuzz, which extracts structured skill contracts and uses contract-guided Monte Carlo Tree Search to prioritize potentially conflicting compositions without requiring execution.
AI.result: Over 1,000 distinct implicit intents discovered under fixed query budget; >80% of highest-risk flagged compositions confirmed during execution-time validation; substantially more high-severity implicit intents identified than alternative search strategies while exploring only a fraction of the pairwise interaction space.
AI.conclusion: skillfuzz effectively detects emergent malicious intents from skill composition in LLM agent marketplaces, offering an execution-free, scalable testing approach that outperforms alternative search methods.

title: Path-level Hindsight Instructions for Semantic Exploration in Vision-Language Navigation
summary: On-policy exploration is a crucial component for training robust Vision-Language Navigation agents, as it exposes the policy to a broader state distribution. However, such exploration inevitably leads to trajectories that deviate from expert demonstrations, resulting in a semantic mismatch between the executed visual stream and the original language instruction. In this work, we address this challenge by introducing Phi-Nav, a unified on-policy framework that leverages hindsight reasoning to align instructions with the agent's actual exploratory journey. Specifically, Phi-Nav operates through a three-stage dual-supervision cycle: 1) the agent performs oracle-guided on-policy exploration, sampling a trajectory while learning from expert action feedback, 2) a hindsight speaker synthesizes a path-level hindsight instruction grounded in the collected visual observations, and 3) the agent conducts a second imitation pass, treating the synthesized trajectory-instruction pair as an additional expert demonstration. Through this process, Phi-Nav bridges the critical semantic supervision gap inherent in on-policy methods, transforming semantically unlabeled movement into dense training signals. Evaluations on the R2R-CE and RxR-CE benchmarks show that Phi-Nav yields competitive performance while requiring only a fraction of the expert demonstrations used by current baselines. These results underscore the necessity of semantic exploration in VLN, positioning Phi-Nav as an effective solution for training embodied agents with limited data.

AI.tldr: Phi-Nav is a unified on-policy framework for Vision-Language Navigation that uses hindsight reasoning to align instructions with exploratory trajectories through a three-stage dual-supervision cycle, achieving competitive performance on R2R-CE and RxR-CE benchmarks with fewer expert demonstrations.
AI.motivation: On-policy exploration in VLN causes a semantic mismatch between the executed visual stream and the original language instruction due to trajectory deviations from expert demonstrations, creating a semantic supervision gap that limits training effectiveness.
AI.method: Phi-Nav operates via a three-stage cycle: (1) oracle-guided on-policy exploration with expert action feedback, (2) a hindsight speaker synthesizes a path-level instruction grounded in observed visual trajectory, and (3) a second imitation pass treating the synthesized trajectory-instruction pair as an additional expert demonstration.
AI.result: Phi-Nav achieves competitive performance on R2R-CE and RxR-CE benchmarks while requiring only a fraction of the expert demonstrations used by current baselines.
AI.conclusion: Semantic exploration is necessary in VLN, and Phi-Nav effectively addresses the semantic supervision gap in on-policy methods, enabling training embodied agents with limited data.

title: MKGR: Multimodal Knowledge-Graph Representation Learning for Cold-Start Protein-Protein Interaction Prediction
summary: Accurate protein-protein interaction (PPI) prediction is central to functional genomics, disease mechanism discovery, and drug development. A difficult setting arises when candidate interactions include proteins that have no observed PPI edges during training, where models relying on network topology alone often lose useful context. This paper presents \method, a multimodal representation framework for cold-start PPI prediction. \method\ combines region-aware protein sequence encoding with four protein-centered biomedical knowledge graphs, including protein-drug, protein-disease, protein-miRNA, and protein-lncRNA associations. The sequence branch extracts contextual representations from structurally informed sequence regions, while graph attention encoders learn modality-specific protein embeddings from sparse biomedical associations. A bridge reconstruction objective regularizes graph learning by recovering shared protein-entity associations, and a pair-level gating module adaptively integrates sequence and graph evidence for each candidate protein pair. Experiments on two benchmark datasets under novel-old and novel-novel cold-start settings show that \method\ consistently outperforms competitive sequence, network, and knowledge-graph baselines across ACC, F1, AUC, AUPR, and MCC.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes \method, a multimodal framework combining region-aware protein sequence encoding with four biomedical knowledge graphs (drug, disease, miRNA, lncRNA) for cold-start PPI prediction. It uses a bridge reconstruction objective and pair-level gating to integrate sequence and graph evidence, outperforming baselines on novel-old and novel-novel settings.
AI.motivation: Accurate PPI prediction is critical for functional genomics, disease mechanisms, and drug development, but cold-start scenarios (proteins with no observed PPI edges during training) are challenging because topology-dependent models lose context.
AI.method: \method combines region-aware protein sequence encoding with four biomedical KGs (protein-drug, protein-disease, protein-miRNA, protein-lncRNA). Sequence branch extracts contextual representations from structurally informed regions; graph attention encoders learn modality-specific embeddings from sparse associations. A bridge reconstruction objective regularizes graph learning, and a pair-level gating module adaptively integrates sequence and graph evidence per candidate pair.
AI.result: On two benchmark datasets under novel-old and novel-novel cold-start settings, \method consistently outperforms competitive sequence, network, and knowledge-graph baselines across ACC, F1, AUC, AUPR, and MCC metrics.
AI.conclusion: The proposed multimodal framework effectively addresses cold-start PPI prediction by integrating protein sequence information with heterogeneous biomedical knowledge graphs, achieving superior performance over existing approaches.

title: Structure-Aware Gaussian Splatting for Large-Scale Scene Reconstruction
summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting has demonstrated remarkable potential in novel view synthesis. In contrast to small-scale scenes, large-scale scenes inevitably contain sparsely observed regions with excessively sparse initial points. In this case, supervising Gaussians initialized from low-frequency sparse points with high-frequency images often induces uncontrolled densification and redundant primitives, degrading both efficiency and quality. Intuitively, this issue can be mitigated with scheduling strategies, which can be categorized into two paradigms: modulating target signal frequency via densification and modulating sampling frequency via image resolution. However, previous scheduling strategies are primarily hardcoded, failing to perceive the convergence behavior of scene frequency. To address this, we reframe the scene reconstruction problem from the perspective of signal structure recovery and propose SIG, a novel scheduler that synchronizes image supervision with Gaussian frequencies. Specifically, we derive the average sampling frequency and bandwidth of 3D representations, and then regulate the training image resolution and the Gaussian densification process based on scene frequency convergence. Furthermore, we introduce Sphere-Constrained Gaussians, which leverage the spatial prior of initialized point clouds to control Gaussian optimization. Our framework enables frequency-consistent, geometry-aware, and floater-free training, achieving state-of-the-art performance by a substantial margin in both efficiency and rendering quality in large-scale scenes. The code is available at: https://github.com/weiyixue999/Signal_Structure_Aware_Gaussian

AI.tldr: SIG is a frequency-aware scheduler for 3D Gaussian Splatting that synchronizes image supervision with Gaussian frequencies by regulating training resolution and densification based on scene frequency convergence, plus Sphere-Constrained Gaussians for geometry-aware training, achieving SOTA in large-scale scenes.
AI.motivation: Large-scale 3D scenes contain sparsely observed regions with sparse initial points, causing uncontrolled densification and redundant primitives when high-frequency images supervise low-frequency Gaussians. Prior scheduling strategies are hardcoded and fail to perceive scene frequency convergence behavior.
AI.method: (1) Derives average sampling frequency and bandwidth of 3D representations. (2) Proposes SIG scheduler that regulates training image resolution and Gaussian densification based on scene frequency convergence. (3) Introduces Sphere-Constrained Gaussians using spatial prior of initialized point clouds to control optimization.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art performance by a substantial margin in both efficiency and rendering quality for large-scale scenes, with frequency-consistent, geometry-aware, and floater-free training.
AI.conclusion: Synchronizing image supervision with Gaussian frequencies via a perception-based scheduler significantly improves 3D Gaussian Splatting for large-scale scene reconstruction.

title: Understanding Agent-Based Patching of Compiler Missed Optimizations
summary: Compiler missed optimizations refer to cases in which compilers failed to optimize certain code. It takes many compiler developers' efforts to implement or patch such missed optimizations. In this paper, we present a systematic study of how well agents patch compiler missed optimizations. We identify a significant challenge that patching a missed optimization requires more than just fixing the reported case, and instead requires generalizing to similar cases. We construct a benchmark of real-world LLVM missed optimization issues and compare agent-generated patches with patches from developers in terms of optimization scope. Our results show that coding agents often optimize the given examples, but many generated patches either cover only part of the developer-intended scope or partially overlap with it; in some cases, they further generalize beyond the reference patch. We further introduce historical-knowledge augmentation techniques that leverage prior LLVM optimization pull requests through retrieval and distillation, showing that they improve developer-aligned generalization and yield practical benefits when applied to real-world IR.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically studies how well coding agents patch compiler missed optimizations, finding they often overfit to specific examples instead of generalizing, and introduces historical-knowledge augmentation techniques to improve generalization to match developer-intended optimization scopes.
AI.motivation: Compiler missed optimizations take significant developer effort to patch. The authors aim to understand whether automated coding agents can effectively address these issues, particularly the challenge of generalizing beyond the reported case to cover similar code patterns.
AI.method: The authors construct a benchmark of real-world LLVM missed optimization issues. They compare agent-generated patches with developer-written patches, evaluating optimization scope (the range of code patterns covered). They also propose historical-knowledge augmentation using retrieval and distillation from prior LLVM optimization pull requests.
AI.result: Coding agents often optimize the given example code but fail to generalize: many generated patches cover only part of the developer-intended scope or partially overlap; some even over-generalize beyond the reference patch. The historical-knowledge augmentation technique improves developer-aligned generalization and shows practical benefits on real-world IR.
AI.conclusion: Patching compiler missed optimizations requires generalization beyond specific examples, which current agents struggle with. Historical-knowledge augmentation helps bridge this gap, suggesting that leveraging prior optimization patterns is a promising direction for improving automated compiler patching.

title: Mastermind: Strategy-grounded Learning for Repository-Scale Vulnerability Reproduction
summary: Repository-level vulnerability reproduction is a demanding software engineering (SE) task: an agent must inspect a codebase, infer the input grammar that reaches a vulnerable path, construct a proof-of-conceptv(PoC), and verify that the crash disappears on the patched build. Recent LLM agents can often execute these steps when the approach is correct, yet they still fail by choosing the wrong strategy. This paper argues that strategy, rather than the full action trajectory, is the right learning unit for such SE agents: it is compact enough to optimize, concrete enough to guide execution, and stable enough to store and reuse across attempts. We present Mastermind, a dual-loop framework that separates transferable strategy learning from task-specific experience. A trainable planner learns reusable vulnerability-reproduction strategies through SFT and milestone-based GRPO, while an experience loop maintains task-local strategy records that guide subsequent attempts. The planner is trained independently of the executor, allowing strategy learning to improve multiple frozen executors without modifying their action-generation capability. We evaluate Mastermind on CyberGym using 260 training tasks and 200 held-out evaluation tasks. With GPT-5.5 as the frozen executor, Mastermind achieves an 84.5% pass rate, outperforming open-book PoC context (60.0%), Best-of-8 sampling (63.0%), and iterative improvement (77.0%). The same planner also improves GPT-5.4 mini and GLM~5.1 from 45.0% and 58.5% to 60.0% and 71.0%. These results demonstrate that learning high-level strategies is an effective and transferable mechanism for improving repository-scale SE agents.

AI.tldr: Mastermind is a dual-loop framework that separates transferable strategy learning from task-specific experience for repository-level vulnerability reproduction. It uses a trainable planner (via SFT and milestone-based GRPO) to learn reusable high-level strategies independent of the executor, achieving 84.5% pass rate with GPT-5.5, outperforming baselines by 7.5-24.5%, and improving weaker executors by 12.5-15.0%.
AI.motivation: Repository-level vulnerability reproduction is a demanding SE task where LLM agents often fail due to choosing the wrong strategy rather than incorrect execution. The paper argues that strategy is the right learning unit—compact enough to optimize, concrete enough to guide execution, and stable enough to reuse—and existing approaches lack a mechanism to learn and transfer high-level strategies independently of the executor.
AI.method: Mastermind has a dual-loop structure: (1) a planner loop learns transferable strategies via supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and milestone-based GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization), and (2) an experience loop maintains task-local strategy records to guide subsequent attempts. The planner is trained independently of the frozen executor, enabling strategy improvement without modifying action-generation capability.
AI.result: On CyberGym with 260 training and 200 held-out tasks, Mastermind with GPT-5.5 achieves 84.5% pass rate, outperforming open-book PoC context (60.0%), Best-of-8 sampling (63.0%), and iterative improvement (77.0%). The same planner improves GPT-5.4 mini from 45.0% to 60.0% and GLM~5.1 from 58.5% to 71.0%.
AI.conclusion: Learning high-level strategies is an effective and transferable mechanism for improving repository-scale SE agents, as demonstrated by consistent improvements across multiple executor models with a single trained planner.

title: DeadPool: Resilient LLM Training with Hot-Swapping via Zero-Overhead Checkpoint
summary: State-of-the-art large language model (LLM) training takes tens of thousands of graphics processing units (GPUs) for months and encounters failures across the software and hardware stack. Existing fault-tolerance mechanisms either impose non-trivial overhead during failure-free execution or suffer from prolonged recovery latency, particularly under scenarios where a small subset of compute nodes experience permanent failures. %The tradeoff between failure-free overhead and recovery latency forms a space forms a Pareto frontier We present DeadPool to simultaneously address both optimization objectives. DeadPool incorporates a fault-tolerance mechanism that restores LLM training via hot-swapping, namely by replacing failed nodes with spare nodes without terminating the complete job. The hot-swapping of DeadPool is enabled by two ideas: First, it exploits an off-critical-path in-memory checkpointing mechanism for spatial redundancy. Second, it introduces a communicator reconstruction protocol that replaces failed nodes with spare nodes at runtime. DeadPool efficiently overlaps the in-memory checkpointing with computation, thus introducing zero overhead during error-free execution. Upon permanent node failures, DeadPool can rebuild memory states with minimal recomputation by leveraging in-memory checkpoints. We evaluate DeadPool across scales (up to 512 NVIDIA A100 GPUs) and LLMs (up to 65B parameters), and observe zero checkpoint overhead with hot-swapping recovery completing in under 40 seconds. These results show that DeadPool simultaneously achieves both zero-overhead error-free execution and extremely low recovery cost.

AI.tldr: DeadPool is a fault-tolerance mechanism for LLM training that uses hot-swapping via off-critical-path in-memory checkpointing and communicator reconstruction, achieving zero overhead during failure-free execution and recovery in under 40 seconds.
AI.motivation: LLM training on thousands of GPUs over months frequently encounters failures. Existing fault-tolerance methods either add non-trivial overhead during normal execution or suffer from long recovery latency, especially under permanent node failures. DeadPool aims to simultaneously achieve zero failure-free overhead and minimal recovery cost.
AI.method: DeadPool uses hot-swapping to replace failed nodes with spare nodes without terminating the job. It employs (1) off-critical-path in-memory checkpointing for spatial redundancy, and (2) a communicator reconstruction protocol to dynamically replace failed nodes at runtime. Checkpointing is overlapped with computation to avoid overhead.
AI.result: Evaluated on up to 512 NVIDIA A100 GPUs and LLMs up to 65B parameters. DeadPool achieves zero checkpoint overhead during error-free execution and completes hot-swapping recovery in under 40 seconds.
AI.conclusion: DeadPool simultaneously achieves both zero-overhead error-free execution and extremely low recovery cost for LLM training under permanent node failures.

title: LASER: A Corrective Lens for LVLMs via Visual Attention Preservation and Sink Suppression
comment: The 19th European Conference on Computer Vision (ECCV 2026)
summary: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) exhibit strong reasoning ability but suffer from visual forgetting during long-horizon decoding, where attention progressively drifts away from visual evidence. Existing methods largely treat this issue as a late-stage attention decay problem or attempt to mitigate it through heuristic reminders or post-hoc attention lifting. Through systematic empirical analysis, we find that performance degradation under visual forgetting is largely driven by two overlooked factors: early-stage attention decay disrupts evidence acquisition, and attention concentration on a subset of task-irrelevant visual sink tokens. Motivated by these insights, we propose LASER, a post-training framework that regulates both the visual attention trajectory and intra-visual token attention distribution during reasoning. Technically, LASER introduces two complementary rewards: a Visual Grounding Reward, which encourages the model to maintain attention on semantically salient visual tokens throughout decoding, and a Sink Suppression Reward, which penalizes excessive attention concentration on visual sink tokens. Together, these rewards preserve early-stage grounding while preventing attention collapse onto uninformative regions. Extensive experiments on eight benchmark datasets demonstrate that LASER consistently outperforms strong baselines, validating attention-aware training as an effective remedy for visual forgetting.

AI.tldr: LASER is a post-training framework that mitigates visual forgetting in LVLMs by regulating attention through two rewards—Visual Grounding Reward (maintains attention on salient visual tokens) and Sink Suppression Reward (penalizes attention on task-irrelevant sink tokens)—outperforming baselines on eight benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Visual forgetting in LVLMs during long-horizon decoding causes performance degradation. Existing methods treat this as a late-stage attention decay problem or use heuristic/post-hoc fixes, but overlooked factors include early-stage attention decay disrupting evidence acquisition and attention concentration on visual sink tokens.
AI.method: LASER post-training framework with two complementary rewards: (1) Visual Grounding Reward to maintain attention on semantically salient visual tokens throughout decoding, and (2) Sink Suppression Reward to penalize excessive attention concentration on visual sink tokens. Together they preserve early-stage grounding and prevent attention collapse onto uninformative regions.
AI.result: Consistent outperformance over strong baselines across eight benchmark datasets, validating attention-aware training as an effective remedy for visual forgetting.
AI.conclusion: Attention-aware post-training with explicit regulation of visual attention trajectory and intra-visual token attention distribution effectively addresses visual forgetting in LVLMs.

title: Reasoning effort, not tool access, buys first-try reliability in agentic code generation: an observational study
comment: 22 pages, 5 figures, 10 tables. Dataset and evaluation artifacts: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21134406
summary: Agentic coding assistants are increasingly given extra capabilities, such as browser based testing tools and design oriented system prompts, on the assumption that more capability yields better software. This study tested that assumption directly. Ninety independent agent runs built the same application, a real time retrospective board, from one detailed specification, each scored on a fixed 14 criterion functional rubric (42 point maximum) and a visual quality review. The runs spanned several model generations, two agent harnesses, two reasoning effort levels, a testing tool, and two design oriented prompts. Capability tier dominated: frontier models clustered near the ceiling while a low cost local model fell to 24 to 37 points. A criterion level analysis revealed what run totals conceal. Container deployment was the dominant defect, failing first try in 44 percent of runs, with its failure rate shifting sharply across model generations while mean totals moved less than a point. The testing tool raised cost by 42 to 68 percent without improving functional score or reliability, even on interface visible criteria. Raising reasoning effort from High to xHigh lifted first try perfect runs from 28 percent to 89 percent and cut corrective prompts about five fold, for 9 to 29 percent more cost. A design oriented prompt raised visual quality, 4.5 versus 3.0 on a 5 point scale, without lifting function, and a one paragraph paraphrase of its directive reproduced the entire lift. The practical lesson is to match the fix to the failure: most first run failures came from weak reasoning, which a stronger model or more effort prevents, not from visible flaws a checking tool would catch.

AI.tldr: Giving coding assistants more capabilities (testing tools, design prompts) doesn't always improve software quality. Frontier models near ceiling (37-42/42), local model scores 24-37. Container deployment fails 44% first try. Testing tool raises cost 42-68% with no functional gain. High→xHigh reasoning effort boosts perfect runs from 28%→89%, cuts corrective prompts 5x. Design prompt improves visual quality (4.5 vs 3.0/5) without functional gain. Key lesson: fix weak reasoning, not visible flaws.
AI.motivation: To test the assumption that giving agentic coding assistants more capabilities (testing tools, design prompts, higher reasoning effort) directly yields better software outcomes.
AI.method: 90 independent agent runs building the same real-time retrospective board from one detailed specification, scored on 14-criterion functional rubric (42 max) + visual quality review. Varied model generations, agent harnesses, reasoning effort levels, testing tool, and design prompts.
AI.result: Frontier models near ceiling; local model 24-37. Container deployment fails 44% first try. Testing tool raises cost 42-68% with no functional/reliability gain. High→xHigh reasoning boosts perfect runs 28%→89%, cuts corrective prompts ~5x, adds 9-29% cost. Design prompt improves visual quality (4.5 vs 3.0/5) without functional lift; one-paragraph paraphrase replicates the effect.
AI.conclusion: Match the fix to the failure: most first-run failures stem from weak reasoning (fixed by stronger model or more effort), not from visible flaws a checking tool would catch.

title: SimWorlds: A Multi-Agent System for Dynamic 3D Scene Creation
summary: LLM agents are increasingly used to translate natural language into 3D scenes in a procedural way, but existing systems focus on static output. Dynamic 4D scenes from text alone, in which liquids flow, particles emit, rigid bodies cascade, and articulated mechanisms move, remain largely unexplored despite their value as editable content and as physics-grounded training data for video generation and embodied AI. Two challenges set the dynamic case apart from static text-to-scene work: an agent must jointly coordinate spatial layout, multiple physics solvers, temporal sequencing, camera, and lighting in a single coherent scene, and verifying motion correctness from rendered video is fundamentally harder than judging a single image. We present SimWorlds: a multi-agent framework that produces dynamic, editable 4D scenes from text, with Blender-specific procedural knowledge, a planner-coder-reviewer workflow driving a fixed ordered sequence of construction stages, a layered scene protocol enforced by a deterministic verifier, and a runtime-state inspection tool suite that catches mechanism failures the rendered image cannot reveal. We also introduce 4DBuildBench, a benchmark for assessing both visual fidelity and physical consistency of the procedural dynamic 3D scenes generated from text prompts. Experiments show that SimWorlds outperforms prior dynamic Blender generation baselines.

AI.tldr: SimWorlds is a multi-agent framework that generates dynamic, editable 4D scenes from text using Blender, addressing challenges of coordinating spatial layout, physics, temporal sequencing, camera, and lighting, and verifying motion correctness. It introduces a planner-coder-reviewer workflow, layered scene protocol, and runtime-state inspection tools. Also presents 4DBuildBench benchmark for evaluating visual fidelity and physical consistency.
AI.motivation: Existing text-to-3D systems produce static output only; dynamic 4D scenes (with liquids, particles, rigid bodies, articulated mechanisms) remain unexplored despite their value for editable content and physics-grounded training data for video generation and embodied AI. Two key challenges: coordinating multiple components (layout, physics, temporal, camera, lighting) and verifying motion correctness from video.
AI.method: Multi-agent framework with: (1) Blender-specific procedural knowledge, (2) planner-coder-reviewer workflow driving fixed ordered construction stages, (3) layered scene protocol enforced by a deterministic verifier, (4) runtime-state inspection tool suite for catching mechanism failures not visible in rendered images.
AI.result: SimWorlds outperforms prior dynamic Blender generation baselines on the introduced 4DBuildBench benchmark.
AI.conclusion: The multi-agent approach with structured verification and runtime inspection effectively enables dynamic 4D scene generation from text, overcoming the challenges of spatial-temporal coordination and motion correctness verification.

title: CALM: Interpretable Cross-Modal Alignment for Biomarker Discovery from Unpaired Data
summary: The interaction between brain structure and genetic influences is key to understanding neuropsychiatric disorders. However, most large-scale datasets are unimodal, providing either neuroimaging or genetics data. We propose CALM, a framework that learns interpretable associations between brain ROIs and genetic pathways from completely disjoint populations. CALM aligns the two modalities in a shared latent space via linear projections that simultaneously match the class-conditional latent distributions and ensure group separability. These projections provide interpretable pathway--ROI associations. When trained on unimodal imaging and genetics datasets, CALM generalizes to an unseen paired dataset, outperforming several state-of-the-art methods and ablation baselines. We also demonstrate stability of the learned associations against a paired baseline. Our experiments on autism spectrum disorder reveal immune and metabolic pathways linked to specific cortical regions and are consistent with established literature. Thus, CALM opens the door to leveraging large unimodal repositories for studying cross-modal interactions in brain disorders across disparate datasets.

AI.tldr: CALM learns interpretable associations between brain ROIs and genetic pathways from completely disjoint unimodal datasets by aligning them in a shared latent space, and generalizes to unseen paired data, revealing immune and metabolic pathway links to cortical regions in autism.
AI.motivation: Most large-scale datasets are unimodal (neuroimaging or genetics), limiting the study of brain structure-genetics interactions underlying neuropsychiatric disorders. There is a need to leverage these disjoint repositories for cross-modal analysis.
AI.method: CALM aligns imaging and genetics modalities in a shared latent space via linear projections that match class-conditional latent distributions and ensure group separability, enabling interpretable pathway-ROI associations from completely disjoint populations.
AI.result: Outperforms state-of-the-art methods and ablation baselines on unseen paired datasets; demonstrates stability of learned associations against a paired baseline; reveals immune and metabolic pathways linked to specific cortical regions in autism consistent with literature.
AI.conclusion: CALM enables leveraging large unimodal repositories for studying cross-modal interactions in brain disorders across disparate datasets.

title: Consistent Scene Understanding in 3D Gaussian Splatting via Multi-Cue Mask Refinement
summary: Reliable instance-level scene understanding is a fundamental prerequisite for object-level interactions and high-fidelity 3D representations. While current methods often leverage 2D foundation segmentation models to obtain these priors, their 2D-centric design typically yields fragmented masks and inconsistent predictions across different views. To address these issues, we propose a novel framework that produces consistent 2D instance masks to guide the optimization of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) feature fields. Our framework consists of three main stages. (1) Multi-Cue Extraction that generates synergistic semantic, geometric, and structural priors from input images. (2) Multi-Cue-Guided Mask Merging process that consolidates fragmented masks using a composite merge score derived from semantic, depth, and edge cues. (3) Cross-View Mask Matching that establishes globally consistent identity assignments across all viewpoints. By transforming viewpoint-specific segments into coherent 3D primitives, our approach enables stable 3D instance segmentation and effective downstream editing tasks. Experiments demonstrate that our method significantly improves cross-view consistency and segmentation stability over existing baselines while maintaining high-fidelity photometric reconstruction.

AI.tldr: A novel framework that uses multi-cue (semantic, geometric, structural) priors to merge fragmented 2D instance masks via cross-view matching, guiding 3DGS feature fields for consistent 3D instance segmentation and editing.
AI.motivation: Current 2D foundation segmentation models produce fragmented masks and inconsistent predictions across different views when applied to instance-level scene understanding, which is critical for object-level interactions and high-fidelity 3D representations.
AI.method: Three-stage framework: (1) Multi-Cue Extraction generates synergistic semantic, geometric, and structural priors; (2) Multi-Cue-Guided Mask Merging consolidates fragmented masks using a composite score from semantic, depth, and edge cues; (3) Cross-View Mask Matching establishes globally consistent identity assignments across viewpoints, then transforms segments into coherent 3D primitives to guide 3DGS feature fields.
AI.result: Significantly improves cross-view consistency and segmentation stability over existing baselines while maintaining high-fidelity photometric reconstruction.
AI.conclusion: Multi-cue guided mask merging and cross-view matching effectively resolve 2D fragmentation and inconsistency issues, enabling stable 3D instance segmentation and downstream editing within the 3DGS framework.

title: HTTP REST API Structure Learning
summary: Application Programming Interfaces (APIs) are essential in software development, enabling web services, mobile apps, and microservices. However, their widespread use introduces significant security risks, highlighting the importance of API security. This paper presents HTTP REST API Learning (HRAL), a novel unsupervised anomaly detection approach that models the structure and behavior of API endpoints directly from network traffic, without relying on predefined rules or documentation. HRAL enables robust detection of malicious activity by understanding how APIs behave and flagging deviations as potential threats. We evaluate HRAL across varying levels of OpenAPI documentation detail and compare it with existing techniques. HRAL achieves strong performance, with an average recall of 82.07% and an F1-score of 87.24%, significantly outperforming alternatives when API documentation is limited. Moreover, our results approach the effectiveness of full API document definitions. When combined with signature-based rules such as the OWASP ModSecurity CRS, our system achieves 100% detection. These results highlight HRAL's effectiveness in real-world, partially documented API environments and its potential as a foundational layer for modern API security solutions.

AI.tldr: HRAL is an unsupervised anomaly detection approach that models API endpoint structure and behavior from network traffic to detect malicious activity, achieving 82.07% recall and 87.24% F1-score, and 100% detection when combined with signature-based rules.
AI.motivation: APIs are essential but introduce significant security risks; existing approaches rely on predefined rules or documentation, which are often incomplete or unavailable.
AI.method: HRAL (HTTP REST API Learning) is an unsupervised approach that learns API endpoint structure and behavior directly from network traffic without requiring predefined rules or documentation.
AI.result: HRAL achieves 82.07% average recall and 87.24% F1-score, significantly outperforming alternatives when API documentation is limited. Combined with OWASP ModSecurity CRS, it achieves 100% detection.
AI.conclusion: HRAL is effective in real-world, partially documented API environments and serves as a foundational layer for modern API security solutions.

title: Repair the Amplifier, Not the Symptom: Stable World-Model Correction for Agent Rollouts
summary: As agent planning moves from short tool chains toward persistent workflows with thousands or tens of thousands of steps, failures will occur inside large planning graphs rather than in isolated predictions. Replanning the entire graph after every mistake is neither computationally realistic nor desirable: full-graph replay consumes large context budgets, exposes the LLM to many irrelevant symptoms, and can degrade long-context retrieval. This paper studies the missing component in such systems: a world-model corrector that repairs the failed planning graph in place. We compare two families of correctors. The first is the common engineering approach: scan nodes and edges, choose a suspicious local region, and ask an LLM to repair it. We implement strong engineering LLM correctors and find that they can help, especially when given very large contexts. The second family is our approach, WM-SAR (World-Model Subgraph Amplification Repair): instead of scanning for visible symptoms, it works backward from subgraph amplification, identifies the nodes and edges that keep re-amplifying error, and sends only that causal subgraph to the LLM. Across graph simulations and LLM repair experiments, WM-SAR substantially outperforms engineering correctors under realistic token budgets, achieves near-whole-graph stabilization with a compact region, and gives the LLM a cleaner repair target.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces WM-SAR, a world-model corrector that repairs failed planning graphs in-place by identifying and fixing causal error subgraphs, outperforming standard engineering approaches under realistic token budgets.
AI.motivation: Current agent planning systems lack efficient mechanisms for handling failures in long, persistent workflows (thousands of steps), where full-graph replanning is computationally expensive, consumes large context budgets, and degrades LLM performance.
AI.method: Proposes WM-SAR (World-Model Subgraph Amplification Repair), which works backward from subgraph amplification to identify nodes and edges that repeatedly amplify errors, sending only that compact causal subgraph to the LLM for repair, rather than scanning all visible symptoms.
AI.result: WM-SAR substantially outperforms engineering correctors (which scan nodes/edges for suspicious regions) under realistic token budgets, achieves near-whole-graph stabilization with a compact repair region, and provides the LLM a cleaner repair target.
AI.conclusion: In-place graph repair via causal subgraph identification (WM-SAR) is a more efficient and effective approach for handling failures in long-horizon agent planning compared to full-graph replay or symptom-scanning engineering methods.

title: Message Passing Based Two-Timescale Bayesian Learning for Joint Channel and Memory Hardware Impairments Tracking
summary: Hardware impairments in massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) receivers introduce inter-symbol memory and inter-element coupling, severely degrading channel estimation. This paper employs a residual recurrent gated unit (RGRU) to model the intra-slot memory of the hardware impairments and proposes a message-passing-based two-timescale Bayesian deep learning (MP-TTBDL) framework for joint channel and impairment tracking. Owing to small-scale fading, the wireless channel varies rapidly across slots, whereas hardware impairments drift slowly due to hardware aging and environmental variations. To capture these distinct physical timescales, a fastvarying Markov prior and a slow-varying Gaussian Markov prior are assigned to the sparse channel and the network parameters, respectively. Based on a multi-slot factor graph formulation, a message-passing algorithm is developed. Specifically, the inter-slot messages admit closed-form updates, while the intra-slot factor graph, due to its complex recurrent structure, is partitioned into a channel tracking module and an impairments calibration module. The channel tracking module performs sparse channel estimation via turbo orthogonal approximate message passing (Turbo-OAMP), and the impairments calibration module updates the impairment parameters via a specially designed deep approximate message passing (DAMP) procedure, with the two modules iteratively exchanging extrinsic information through expectation propagation (EP) until convergence. Simulation results show that the proposed framework robustly achieves lower channel estimation error than conventional compensators followed by channel estimation across different online impairment scenarios and signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) conditions.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an MP-TTBDL framework using a residual recurrent gated unit (RGRU) to model hardware impairments in massive MIMO receivers. It assigns fast-varying and slow-varying priors to capture distinct timescales of channel and impairment dynamics, and develops a message-passing algorithm with closed-form inter-slot updates and partitioned intra-slot modules (Turbo-OAMP for channel tracking, DAMP for impairment calibration) that exchange extrinsic information via EP. The framework achieves robustly lower channel estimation error across various impairment scenarios and SNR conditions.
AI.motivation: Hardware impairments in massive MIMO receivers introduce inter-symbol memory and inter-element coupling that severely degrade channel estimation, motivating the need for a framework that jointly tracks the rapidly varying wireless channel and slowly drifting hardware impairments.
AI.method: The method employs a residual recurrent gated unit (RGRU) to model intra-slot impairment memory, assigns fast-varying Markov prior to sparse channels and slow-varying Gaussian Markov prior to impairment parameters, and develops a message-passing algorithm on a multi-slot factor graph. Inter-slot updates are closed-form; intra-slot processing is partitioned into a channel tracking module (Turbo-OAMP) and an impairment calibration module (DAMP), exchanging extrinsic information via expectation propagation.
AI.result: Simulation results show that the proposed MP-TTBDL framework robustly achieves lower channel estimation error than conventional compensators followed by channel estimation across different online impairment scenarios and SNR conditions.
AI.conclusion: The framework effectively captures the distinct physical timescales of channel and impairment dynamics, and the two-timescale Bayesian deep learning approach with iterative message passing provides robust joint channel and impairment tracking in massive MIMO systems.

title: Beyond Pixel Diffs: Benchmarking Image Change Captioning for Web UI Visual Regression Testing
summary: Visual regression testing (VRT) is a standard quality assurance step in modern software release pipelines. On every change, it re-renders user interface (UI) screenshots, compares each one against an approved baseline image, and routes any detected difference to a human reviewer who decides whether it is an intended update or an unintended regression. A widely used approach, especially in open-source and continuous-integration pipelines, is pixel-level comparison, which is semantically blind and treats rendering noise and genuine defects identically, producing large volumes of false positives that force developers and testers to spend substantial time and effort manually reviewing flagged differences at every release cycle. Industry tools apply machine learning to VRT, but lack public evaluation. More critically, no dataset or benchmark exists to support natural language descriptions of UI changes, a capability that tells testers what changed in words instead of leaving them to interpret a binary flag or a highlighted region. To address the gap, we propose a new task, Web UI Image Change Captioning (WUICC), which sits at the intersection of VRT and image difference captioning (IDC), and release WUICC-bench, its first dataset and benchmark for the task. We evaluate eleven representative IDC methods, together with two zero-shot general-purpose LLMs. We find that: (1) these methods tend to struggle in the Web UI domain due to its layout diversity, dense text, and fine-grained changes, and (2) yet the trained methods already suppress non-meaningful visual noise far more selectively than the pixel-level comparison VRT relies on, providing a solid foundation for future domain-specific research.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Web UI Image Change Captioning (WUICC), a new task combining visual regression testing and image difference captioning, along with the first benchmark/dataset (WUICC-bench). Evaluations show existing methods struggle with web UI domains but trained methods outperform pixel-level VRT by suppressing visual noise more selectively.
AI.motivation: Current pixel-level visual regression testing produces massive false positives due to semantic blindness, forcing manual review. No dataset or benchmark exists for natural language descriptions of UI changes, which would tell testers what changed in words rather than showing flagged regions.
AI.method: The authors propose WUICC (Web UI Image Change Captioning) as a new task bridging VRT and image difference captioning, and release WUICC-bench as the first dataset and benchmark. They evaluate eleven IDC methods and two zero-shot LLMs on this benchmark.
AI.result: (1) Existing IDC methods struggle with Web UI domains due to layout diversity, dense text, and fine-grained changes. (2) Trained methods suppress non-meaningful visual noise more selectively than pixel-level VRT, providing a solid foundation for future research.
AI.conclusion: The paper successfully identifies a critical gap in VRT, establishes a new task and benchmark, and demonstrates that while current methods are limited in the web UI domain, the direction is promising for reducing false positives in visual regression testing.

title: TestEvo-Bench: An Executable and Live Benchmark for Test and Code Co-Evolution
comment: TestEvo-Bench leaderboard and data explorer are hosted at https://www.testevo-bench.com
summary:
Software tests and code evolve together: a code change should be followed by new or updated tests that record the new software behavior. Yet existing test generation and update benchmarks often isolate the test from the code change, and rely on static metadata that does not verify whether a test is executable or semantically tied to the code change. This makes it difficult to evaluate whether a test automation agent understands how a code change should propagate into the test suite.
  We introduce TestEvo-Bench, a benchmark of test and code co-evolution tasks mined from software repositories, with two tracks: in test generation, the agent shall write new tests to capture the new software behavior; in test update, the agent shall adapt failing existing tests to the changed software behavior. Each task is anchored to a real commit history and packaged with environment configuration to support execution-grounded metrics such as pass rate, coverage, and mutation score. TestEvo-Bench is also a live benchmark: each task records the timestamp of the test and code changes, and new tasks are periodically mined by our automated pipeline, so evaluation can be restricted to tasks postdating a model's training cutoff to reduce data leakage risk. The current snapshot contains 746 test generation and 509 test update tasks, curated from 59,950 candidate co-evolution records across 152 open-source Java projects. We experiment with four state-of-the-art agents that combine strong harnesses (Claude Code, Gemini CLI, and SWE-Agent) with strong foundation models (Claude Opus 4.7 and Gemini 3.1 Pro). Results show that they achieve up to 77.5% success rate on test generation and 74.6% on test update. However, success rate is materially lower on the most recent benchmark tasks and drops significantly under limited per-task cost.

AI.tldr: TestEvo-Bench is a live benchmark of 746 test generation and 509 test update tasks mined from real commits across 152 Java projects, using execution-grounded metrics (pass rate, coverage, mutation score) to evaluate test automation agents on test-code co-evolution. State-of-the-art agents achieve up to 77.5% (generation) and 74.6% (update), but performance drops on recent tasks and under limited cost.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks isolate tests from code changes and rely on static metadata without verifying executability or semantic relevance, making it hard to evaluate whether agents understand how code changes propagate to test suites.
AI.method: Mined 59,950 candidate co-evolution records from 152 open-source Java projects; curated 746 test generation and 509 test update tasks anchored to real commit history with environment configs for execution-grounded metrics. Live benchmark design with timestamps and automated periodic mining to mitigate data leakage.
AI.result: Four SOTA agents (Claude Code, Gemini CLI, SWE-Agent with Claude Opus 4.7/Gemini 3.1 Pro) achieve up to 77.5% success on test generation and 74.6% on test update, but performance drops materially on recent tasks and significantly under limited per-task cost.
AI.conclusion: TestEvo-Bench provides a more realistic, execution-verified evaluation for test automation agents. Current SOTA models still struggle with temporal generalization and cost efficiency, highlighting room for improvement in test-code co-evolution understanding.

title: Verifiable Knowledge Expansion through Retrieval-Grounded Formal Concept Analysis
comment: 8 pages, 2 figures, Accepted to the 8th epiDAMIK ACM SIGKDD International Workshop on Epidemiology meets Data Mining and Knowledge Discovery (epiDAMIK 2026)
summary: Ontology construction requires deciding which objects, attributes, and structural relations should be accepted as valid knowledge. Language models can propose such structures from text, but their outputs can still be unsupported or inconsistent. This paper proposes a retrieval-augmented small language model (SLM) framework that uses formal concept analysis (FCA) as a symbolic verification loop for knowledge expansion. Starting from seed attributes, FCA proposes implications over a growing formal context. A retrieval-grounded SLM oracle then validates each implication or returns a counterexample. The oracle also supports incidence judgments, consistency checks, and attribute proposals, making accepted implications, counterexamples, contradictions, and corrections inspectable. In a rare ataxia setting constructed from Orphadata resources, retrieval-grounded 10-seed runs obtain relation F1 of 0.29-0.52 and closure-based implication F1 of 0.22-0.30. Larger seed sets increase the number of evaluated implications and often improve implication F1. The lower implication scores reflect a stricter evaluation of derived implications, where one missed or extra relation can affect several implication judgments. Ablations show that incidence judgments in a fixed object-attribute setting can improve closure-based implication scores. However, identifying positive object-attribute pairs remains difficult even when the candidate objects and attributes are fixed.

AI.tldr: A retrieval-augmented SLM framework using formal concept analysis (FCA) as a symbolic verification loop for ontology construction from text, tested on rare ataxia data from Orphadata.
AI.motivation: Ontology construction requires validated knowledge (objects, attributes, relations). Language models can propose structures from text but often produce unsupported or inconsistent outputs; a verification mechanism is needed.
AI.method: Proposes a retrieval-augmented SLM framework with FCA as a symbolic verification loop. Starting from seed attributes, FCA generates implications over a growing formal context. A retrieval-grounded SLM oracle validates implications, returns counterexamples, supports incidence judgments, consistency checks, and attribute proposals. Tested on rare ataxia data from Orphadata.
AI.result: Retrieval-grounded 10-seed runs achieved relation F1 of 0.29-0.52 and closure-based implication F1 of 0.22-0.30. Larger seed sets increased evaluated implications and often improved implication F1. Lower implication scores due to strict evaluation (one missed/extra relation affects multiple implication judgments). Ablations show incidence judgments in fixed settings improve closure-based implication scores, but identifying positive object-attribute pairs remains difficult.
AI.conclusion: The FCA-verified SLM framework enables inspectable ontology expansion with explicit contradictions and corrections. However, stricter implication evaluation reveals higher error sensitivity, and object-attribute identification remains challenging even under fixed settings.

title: Revisiting Decentralized Online Convex Optimization with Compressed Communication
summary: Decentralized online convex optimization (D-OCO) is a popular framework for distributed applications with streaming data. To tackle the communication bottleneck, previous studies have investigated D-OCO with compressed communication and proposed several algorithms that are variants of online gradient descent (OGD). However, for D-OCO with exact communication, the best existing algorithms are variants of follow-the-regularized-leader (FTRL). In this paper, for the first time, we propose two FTRL-type algorithms for D-OCO with compressed communication. Compared with OGD-type algorithms, our algorithms are more elegant in both algorithmic design and theoretical analysis. The key insight is that the dual update mechanism of FTRL allows us to make a simple application of the technique for average consensus with communication compression. More specifically, our first algorithm considers the full-information setting, and can match the existing regret bounds. Our second algorithm is designed for the bandit setting, and can significantly improve both the regret bounds and communication costs of existing algorithms.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes the first FTRL-type algorithms for decentralized online convex optimization with compressed communication, outperforming OGD-type approaches in both full-information and bandit settings.
AI.motivation: Existing D-OCO algorithms use OGD variants for compressed communication but FTRL variants for exact communication, creating a gap. The authors aim to bridge this by developing FTRL-type algorithms that work with communication compression.
AI.method: The authors leverage the dual update mechanism of FTRL to seamlessly integrate average consensus with communication compression. They propose two algorithms: one for the full-information setting and another for the bandit setting.
AI.result: The full-information algorithm matches existing regret bounds, while the bandit algorithm significantly improves both regret bounds and communication costs over prior methods.
AI.conclusion: FTRL-type algorithms are more elegant than OGD-type for D-OCO with compressed communication, offering simpler design and stronger theoretical guarantees, especially in bandit settings.

title: ReQuest: Rethinking-based Question-Aware Frame Selection for Long-Form Video QA
summary: Recent multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have substantially advanced video understanding, yet long-form video QA remains challenging under fixed input token budgets, where uniform sampling can be inefficient for evidence localization. We propose ReQuest , an uncertainty-driven, question-adaptive keyframe selection pipeline that aligns question intent with relevant video content through selective computation. ReQuest integrates (i) a lightweight question-aware selector distilled from MLLM-generated supervision, (ii) Re-thinking Routing that triggers additional inference only when the model is uncertain with a length-adaptive criterion, and (iii) uncertainty-guided adaptive non-maximum suppression that selects temporally diverse frames while adjusting spacing based on question difficulty. As a plug-andplay method, ReQuest improves long-video QA without modifying or fine-tuning the underlying MLLM. Experiments on Video-MME, MLVU, and LongVideoBench demonstrate consistent accuracy gains with competitive computational cost, with particularly strong improvements in medium and long video regimes.

AI.tldr: ReQuest is an uncertainty-driven, question-adaptive keyframe selection pipeline that improves long-form video QA by selectively identifying relevant frames without modifying or fine-tuning the underlying MLLM.
AI.motivation: Long-form video QA remains challenging under fixed input token budgets because uniform sampling is inefficient for evidence localization, making it difficult to identify relevant frames for answering questions about lengthy videos.
AI.method: ReQuest integrates three components: (i) a lightweight question-aware selector distilled from MLLM-generated supervision, (ii) Re-thinking Routing that triggers additional inference only when the model is uncertain using a length-adaptive criterion, and (iii) uncertainty-guided adaptive non-maximum suppression for temporally diverse frame selection with question-difficulty-adjusted spacing.
AI.result: Experiments on Video-MME, MLVU, and LongVideoBench show consistent accuracy gains with competitive computational cost, particularly strong in medium and long video regimes.
AI.conclusion: ReQuest serves as an effective plug-and-play method for improving long-video QA by aligning question intent with relevant video content through selective computation, without requiring modification or fine-tuning of the underlying MLLM.

title: Subliminal Clocks: Latent Time Modelling in Diffusion Language Models
comment: Equal contribution: Thomas Fontanari and Simone Petruzzi
summary: Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) have recently emerged as a promising alternative to autoregressive models. Unlike standard diffusion-based approaches, DLMs are not explicitly conditioned on a timestep, raising a natural question: do these models internally represent denoising progress, and how is such information used downstream? In this work, we show that DLMs do in fact encode a latent representation related to the diffusion timestep within their residual streams. We find that this signal can be reliably extracted using probes across layers, indicating that denoising progress is decodable from internal activations. We further demonstrate that steering the model along a low-dimensional subspace associated with the inferred timestep allows us to systematically modulate its notion of denoising progress, leading to predictable changes in model confidence and entropy. Finally, we analyse the geometry of the identified representation, showing that it exhibits structured and interpretable properties in activation space, and shedding light on how such a signal is processed by these models.

AI.tldr: Diffusion Language Models internally encode denoising progress as a latent representation in their residual streams, which can be extracted via probes, steered to modulate confidence/entropy, and exhibits structured geometric properties in activation space.
