AI.motivation: DLMs are not explicitly conditioned on a timestep, raising the question of whether they internally represent denoising progress and how such information is used downstream.
AI.method: The authors probe internal activations across layers to extract signals related to diffusion timestep, steer activations along a low-dimensional subspace to modulate denoising progress, and analyze the geometry of the identified representation.
AI.result: DLMs encode a decodable latent representation of denoising progress; steering this subspace yields predictable changes in model confidence and entropy; the representation has structured and interpretable geometric properties.
AI.conclusion: DLMs do represent denoising progress internally despite lacking explicit timestep conditioning, and this representation is geometrically structured and functionally steerable.

title: UniWind: Toward Unified Day-Ahead Wind Power Forecasting via Physics-Informed State Routing
summary: Day-ahead wind power forecasting is essential for cost-effective power-system operation. It is primarily driven by future meteorological conditions while retaining temporal dependencies in power generation. In practice, observed wind-farm power often entangles physically available power with local environmental effects and latent operational states, such as shutdowns and curtailment. Existing physical models provide useful constraints but adapt poorly across wind farms, whereas data-driven models can capture rich correlations but often conflate meteorological effects with state-induced deviations. In this study, we propose UniWind, a wind power forecasting model based on physics-informed state routing. UniWind first employs a Physical Prior Estimator to construct a site-calibrated physical prior by combining site-conditioned monotonic warping with a shared physical power curve. It further applies a physical upper-bound constraint to shape this prior as a soft envelope of available wind power generation. UniWind then proposes a Latent State Encoder to model operating-state embeddings and transforms the physical prior into final power forecasts through a State-aware Power Corrector, which uses knowledge-guided supervised state routing and bounded, state-specific expert correction. Full-shot and cross-farm zero-shot experiments on more than 20 real-world datasets demonstrate the accuracy and robustness of UniWind.

AI.tldr: UniWind is a physics-informed state-routing model for day-ahead wind power forecasting that separates meteorological effects from operational state deviations using a Physical Prior Estimator, Latent State Encoder, and State-aware Power Corrector, achieving strong results on over 20 real-world datasets.
AI.motivation: Wind power forecasting is essential for grid operation, but observed power data entangles physically available power with environmental effects and latent operational states (e.g., shutdowns, curtailment). Existing physical models generalize poorly across farms, while data-driven models conflate meteorological effects with state-induced deviations.
AI.method: UniWind has three components: (1) a Physical Prior Estimator with site-conditioned monotonic warping and shared physical power curve for site-calibrated prior, plus a physical upper-bound constraint; (2) a Latent State Encoder for operating-state embeddings; (3) a State-aware Power Corrector with knowledge-guided supervised state routing and bounded, state-specific expert correction.
AI.result: Full-shot and cross-farm zero-shot experiments on more than 20 real-world wind farm datasets demonstrate the accuracy and robustness of UniWind.
AI.conclusion: UniWind effectively disentangles meteorological effects from operational state influences through physics-informed state routing, achieving superior forecasting performance and cross-farm generalization.

title: InterCMDM: Block-Causal Diffusion for Autoregressive Human Interaction Generation
comment: Accepted to ECCV 2026, Project website: https://yu1ut.com/InterCMDM-HP/
summary: Text-conditioned human interaction generation must capture both long-range temporal causality within each individual and tightly coupled coordination between partners. Existing interaction diffusion models typically denoise full sequences using bidirectional attention, which obscures causality and hinders streaming and long-horizon generation. Autoregressive alternatives enforce causality but often suffer from temporal drift, leading to coordination degradation and unstable interaction dynamics over time. We propose InterCMDM, a block-causal latent diffusion framework for autoregressive two-person interaction generation. InterCMDM introduces a Dual-Stream Causal Diffusion Transformer that maintains separate causal streams for each person while modeling inter-person dependencies via unified dual-stream attention with multi-task attention masks. These masks unify interaction modeling within a single attention mechanism and support diverse coordination behaviors, including simultaneous actions, reactive responses, leader-follower dynamics, and independent motion. By training a single model across these mask configurations as a form of data augmentation, InterCMDM enables controllable interaction generation by simply selecting the desired attention mask at inference time. Finally, a block-wise diffusion objective enables stable latent rollout over long sequences without repeated decode-encode cycles. InterCMDM achieves state-of-the-art performance on InterHuman and Inter-X, improving text-motion alignment, realism, and long-horizon continuity.

AI.tldr: InterCMDM is a block-causal latent diffusion framework for autoregressive two-person interaction generation that uses Dual-Stream Causal Diffusion Transformer with multi-task attention masks to handle diverse coordination behaviors, achieving SOTA on InterHuman and Inter-X.
AI.motivation: Existing interaction diffusion models use bidirectional attention (obscuring causality, hindering streaming/long-horizon generation), while autoregressive alternatives suffer from temporal drift and coordination degradation. A unified framework handling both causality and inter-person coordination is needed.
AI.method: 1) Dual-Stream Causal Diffusion Transformer with separate causal streams per person; 2) Unified dual-stream attention with multi-task attention masks supporting simultaneous, reactive, leader-follower, and independent behaviors; 3) Training across mask configurations as data augmentation for controllable generation via mask selection at inference; 4) Block-wise diffusion objective for stable latent rollout without repeated decode-encode cycles.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art performance on InterHuman and Inter-X datasets, with improvements in text-motion alignment, realism, and long-horizon continuity.
AI.conclusion: InterCMDM effectively unifies causality-aware generation and diverse inter-person coordination within a single diffusion framework, enabling controllable, stable, and high-quality long-sequence two-person interaction generation.

title: Safety Testing LLM Agents at Scale: From Risk Discovery to Evidence-Grounded Verification
summary: LLM agents increasingly perform autonomous actions through external tools, leading to complex and evolving safety risks. However, existing safety testing targets expert-designed safety violations, and the corresponding outcomes are evaluated by hard-coded rules, making them costly to extend as agents evolve. To this end, we present Vera, an end-to-end automated safety testing framework that instantiates software engineering testing principles for non-deterministic agents through a three-stage, self-reinforcing pipeline. First, a literature-driven exploration continuously discovers and structures emerging risks into taxonomies of safety risks, attack methods, and tool execution environments. Second, combinatorial composition across taxonomy dimensions produces executable safety cases, each specifying a concrete safety goal, a programmatically constructed initial state, and a deterministic verification predicate grounded in observable artifacts. Third, adaptive execution runs heterogeneous agents in isolated sandboxes where a control agent steers multi-turn interaction based on runtime observations, while evidence-grounded verifiers judge outcomes from environment state and tool-call evidence rather than model self-report. We evaluate Vera on four production agent frameworks (OpenClaw, Hermes, Codex, Claude Code), revealing substantial safety weaknesses, with average attack success rates reaching 93.9\% under multi-channel attacks; we also release Vera-Bench, comprising 1600 executable safety cases spanning 124 risk categories across three execution settings. These results indicate that modular, executable testing infrastructure is essential for rigorous and maintainable safety evaluation of rapidly evolving agentic systems at scale. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/Yunhao-Feng/Vera.

AI.tldr: Vera is an end-to-end automated safety testing framework for LLM agents that uses a three-stage pipeline (literature-driven risk exploration, combinatorial test case composition, and adaptive execution with evidence-grounded verification) to systematically discover and evaluate safety vulnerabilities across agent frameworks, revealing up to 93.9% attack success rates on multi-channel attacks.
AI.motivation: Existing safety testing for LLM agents relies on expert-designed safety violations and hard-coded rules, which are costly to extend as agents evolve and cannot keep pace with emerging, complex safety risks from autonomous tool use.
AI.method: A three-stage self-reinforcing pipeline: (1) literature-driven exploration to structure risks into taxonomies of safety risks, attack methods, and tool execution environments; (2) combinatorial composition across taxonomy dimensions to produce executable safety cases with concrete goals, programmatic initial states, and deterministic verification predicates; (3) adaptive execution with a control agent steering multi-turn interactions in isolated sandboxes and evidence-grounded verifiers judging outcomes from environment state and tool-call evidence.
AI.result: Evaluated on four production agent frameworks (OpenClaw, Hermes, Codex, Claude Code), revealing average attack success rates of 93.9% under multi-channel attacks; released Vera-Bench with 1600 executable safety cases spanning 124 risk categories across three execution settings.
AI.conclusion: Modular, executable testing infrastructure is essential for rigorous and maintainable safety evaluation of rapidly evolving agentic systems at scale.

title: SCAPE: Accurate and Efficient LLM Training with Extreme Sparse Communication
summary: Communication increasingly dominates the cost of Large Language Model (LLM) pre-training, especially under data-parallel and sharded training schemes, where gradient synchronization and parameter reconstruction overhead increase with model size and system scale. Existing communication-reduction methods either sparsify raw gradients, which can be unstable for modern Adam-style optimizers at high sparsity, or quantize communication, whose savings are fundamentally bounded by bit width and often incur additional runtime overhead. We present SCAPE, a communication-efficient distributed optimizer for LLM training that exploits the stability of AdamS's first-moment to enable aggressive sparsification without loss of LLM quality. Instead of constructing masks from raw gradients, SCAPE derives them from first-moment-based statistics, partitions mask generation across workers to align with optimizer sharding, and delays mask usage by one step so that mask synchronization can overlap with computation. SCAPE also reconstructs the quantities required for second-moment updates from a single synchronized sparse buffer, avoiding an additional collective. We implement SCAPE in Megatron-LM and evaluate its convergence by pre-training GPT-345M on OpenWebText and Llama-500M on SlimPajama-6B using 32 NVIDIA GH200 GPUs on TACC Vista. In both models, SCAPE preserves training stability, validation loss, and downstream task accuracy under 90\% and 99\% sparsity. For Llama-500M, SCAPE reduces end-to-end pre-training wall-clock time by up to 43.3\% while maintaining model quality comparable to dense AdamW and AdamS. For Llama-1.8B, SCAPE achieves up to 3.26$\times$ speedup per step compared to dense AdamS.

AI.tldr: SCAPE is a communication-efficient distributed optimizer that exploits AdamS's first-moment stability to enable aggressive gradient sparsification (90-99%) for LLM pre-training, reducing wall-clock time by up to 43.3% (Llama-500M) and achieving 3.26× per-step speedup (Llama-1.8B) without quality degradation.
AI.motivation: Communication cost dominates LLM pre-training under data-parallel and sharded training schemes. Existing methods (sparsification unstable for Adam-style optimizers; quantization bounded by bit width) are insufficient. A more efficient communication reduction approach is needed.
AI.method: SCAPE derives sparsification masks from first-moment-based statistics (not raw gradients), partitions mask generation across workers to align with optimizer sharding, delays mask usage by one step for overlap, and reconstructs second-moment update quantities from a single synchronized sparse buffer to eliminate an extra collective.
AI.result: Pre-trained GPT-345M and Llama-500M on 32 GH200 GPUs. Preserves validation loss and downstream accuracy at 90-99% sparsity. Reduces end-to-end wall-clock time by up to 43.3% (Llama-500M) and achieves 3.26× per-step speedup for Llama-1.8B vs dense AdamS.
AI.conclusion: SCAPE enables aggressive, stable sparsification for Adam-style optimizers in distributed LLM training, significantly reducing communication overhead while preserving model quality, making it a practical drop-in replacement for dense optimizers.

title: RTE-FM-Dehazer: Radiative Transfer Equation Inspired Flow Matching for Real-World Image Dehazing
summary: Single-image dehazing aims to recover a clear scene from a hazy image and is generally formulated as an image-to-image translation task; however, it faces two limitations. Its performance depends heavily on the haze-formation priors embedded in the model. Prevailing methods adopt the Atmospheric Scattering Model (ASM), whose assumptions of single scattering and homogeneous media are often violated, leading to residual haze and color drift. Moreover, large-scale real hazy/clear pairs are impractical to collect, and existing synthesis approaches fail to reproduce the full complexity of natural haze. To address these issues, we present RTE-FM-Dehazer, a novel dehazing approach, together with a scalable data pipeline. Unlike the ASM, the Radiative Transfer Equation (RTE) jointly accounts for both scattering and absorption, naturally accommodating the non-homogeneous, multiple-scattering media that characterize real hazy scenes. Motivated by the structural similarity between the RTE diffusion-absorption term and the ODE in flow matching, we introduce a diffusion-absorption regularizer derived from a reduced RTE, to steer the flow matching trajectory at each step. Next, leveraging modern vision-language models, we build an automated pipeline and release P-HAZE, a dataset of 50000 realistic hazy/clear pairs. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that RTE-FM-Dehazer, trained solely on P-HAZE, effectively eliminates artifacts like residual haze and color drift, exhibits strong cross-domain generalization, and achieves leading results on five real-world dehazing benchmarks.

AI.tldr: RTE-FM-Dehazer is a single-image dehazing method that replaces the traditional Atmospheric Scattering Model (ASM) with a Radiative Transfer Equation (RTE)-guided flow matching framework, combined with a large-scale synthetic dataset (P-HAZE, 50K pairs) built via vision-language models, achieving state-of-the-art results on real-world benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing single-image dehazing methods rely on the Atmospheric Scattering Model (ASM), which assumes single scattering and homogeneous media—assumptions often violated in real haze, causing residual haze and color drift. Additionally, acquiring large-scale real hazy/clear pairs is impractical, and current synthetic datasets fail to capture natural haze complexity.
AI.method: Proposes RTE-FM-Dehazer, which replaces ASM with the Radiative Transfer Equation (RTE) to handle non-homogeneous, multiple-scattering media. A diffusion-absorption regularizer derived from a reduced RTE is introduced to guide flow matching trajectories. An automated pipeline using vision-language models constructs P-HAZE, a dataset of 50,000 realistic hazy/clear pairs.
AI.result: Trained solely on P-HAZE, RTE-FM-Dehazer eliminates residual haze and color drift, demonstrates strong cross-domain generalization, and achieves leading results on five real-world dehazing benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: The RTE-guided flow matching formulation combined with a large-scale, realistic synthetic dataset effectively addresses the physical modeling and data scarcity limitations of prior dehazing methods, setting new state-of-the-art performance.

title: Rethinking Complexity Metrics for LLM-Integrated Applications: Beyond Source Code
summary: LLM-integrated applications blend natural language prompts with program code, and much of their runtime behavior originates in the prompt layer rather than in the code itself. Existing complexity metrics, however, operate solely at the code level and therefore overlook this behavioral logic entirely. We present HECATE, the first tool designed to assess complexity in both the prompt and code layers of such applications. Central to HECATE is Prompt-as-Specification, a Hoare-logic-inspired formalism that interprets every prompt as a specification of intended behavior. Grounded in 25 complexity dimensions identified across published taxonomies, the tool generates 52 candidate metrics. We assess each metric against 118 components collected from 18 open-source repositories, relying on maintenance activity derived from version history as an empirical proxy for complexity, and discard any metric that loses significance once code size is accounted for. Only ten metrics withstand this test. Seven belong to our newly introduced set; rather than measuring sheer volume, each tallies structurally distinct elements, such as LLM call sites, memory attributes, and prompt templates, an attribute we call structural breadth. Of the three surviving conventional metrics, RFC exhibits a similar breadth-oriented character, while Halstead N and V survive only as a residual effect of size; our top-performing metrics exceed all three. Crucially, the prompt-layer metrics retain significance even when the strongest code-level metric is added as a covariate, establishing prompt complexity as a dimension in its own right. A final validation on 20 components spanning six held-out repositories shows that the two best-performing metrics continue to predict maintenance effort, supporting their generalizability beyond the training set.

AI.tldr: HECATE is the first tool measuring complexity in both prompt and code layers of LLM-integrated apps. Using Prompt-as-Specification formalism and 25 complexity dimensions, it generates 52 metrics, filters them against 118 components from 18 repos, and finds only 10 survive—7 new structural breadth metrics outperform traditional ones, with prompt-layer complexity proven as an independent dimension.
AI.motivation: Existing complexity metrics only operate at the code level and overlook behavioral logic originating in the prompt layer of LLM-integrated applications, leaving a gap in assessing overall complexity.
AI.method: Proposes Prompt-as-Specification (Hoare-logic-inspired formalism); grounds 25 complexity dimensions from published taxonomies; generates 52 candidate metrics; evaluates against 118 components from 18 repos using version-history-based maintenance activity as empirical proxy; discards metrics losing significance after controlling for code size; validates on 20 held-out components from 6 repos.
AI.result: Only 10 metrics withstand filtering; 7 new metrics measure structural breadth (LLM call sites, memory attributes, prompt templates) rather than volume; RFC shows similar breadth character; Halstead N and V survive only as size residual effects; prompt-layer metrics retain significance even with strongest code-level covariate; top two metrics generalize on held-out repositories.
AI.conclusion: Prompt complexity is an independent dimension of overall complexity in LLM-integrated applications, and structural breadth metrics—particularly those measuring prompt-layer elements—are more predictive of maintenance effort than traditional code-level metrics alone.

title: MMIR-TCM: Memory-Integrated Multimodal Inference and Retrieval for TCM Clinical Decision Support
summary: Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) diagnosis, particularly through tongue inspection, faces persistent challenges in subjectivity and reproducibility. The application of multimodal artificial intelligence to TCM clinical tasks, such as syndrome differentiation and prescription generation, is significantly hampered by the semantic gap between visual tongue features and textual reasoning, as well as the lack of large-scale, standardized datasets. To address these challenges, we introduce MMIR-TCM, a novel framework that emulates the diagnostic process of TCM experts by integrating multimodal large language model(MLLM) with memory-augmented segmentation and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Employing a three-stage architecture, MMIR-TCM integrates a training-free Memory-SAM module for robust tongue extraction, a fine-tuned Qwen3-VL model for structured tongue diagnosis generation, and a Qwen3-based RAG component for evidence-grounded clinical decision support generation. The framework was developed and validated using MedTCM, a new large-scale multimodal dataset that we introduce specifically for advanced TCM research. To properly evaluate our framework's clinical accuracy, which existing metrics fail to capture, we also developed TDEU, a domain-specific evaluation metric incorporating semantic understanding and diagnostic importance. Our comprehensive experiments demonstrate that MMIR-TCM significantly outperforms leading models, including GPT-4o and Gemini 2.5 Flash.

AI.tldr: MMIR-TCM is a multimodal AI framework that integrates memory-augmented segmentation, fine-tuned Qwen3-VL, and RAG to enhance TCM tongue diagnosis and prescription generation, outperforming GPT-4o and Gemini 2.5 Flash on a new large-scale dataset (MedTCM) with a novel evaluation metric (TDEU).
AI.motivation: TCM tongue diagnosis suffers from subjectivity and reproducibility issues; multimodal AI applied to TCM tasks faces a semantic gap between visual tongue features and textual reasoning, plus a lack of large-scale standardized datasets.
AI.method: Three-stage architecture: (1) training-free Memory-SAM for tongue segmentation, (2) fine-tuned Qwen3-VL for structured diagnosis, (3) Qwen3-based RAG for evidence-grounded clinical decision support. Validated on a new dataset MedTCM, with a novel metric TDEU.
AI.result: MMIR-TCM significantly outperforms GPT-4o and Gemini 2.5 Flash in clinical accuracy as measured by TDEU.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework bridges the visual-textual semantic gap in TCM AI diagnosis, and the introduced dataset (MedTCM) and evaluation metric (TDEU) provide new resources and standards for the field.

title: WARP: Weight-Space Analysis for Recovering Training Data Portfolios
comment: This work appears in the ICML 2026 Workshop on Weight-Space Symmetries (WSS): from Foundations to Practical Applications. Our source code is available at github.com/SprocketLab/WARP
summary: Foundation models are routinely released to the public, yet the data recipes used to train them -- such as domain mixture weights that determine how different sources are sampled -- are rarely disclosed. This creates an access asymmetry: researchers study the resulting models but lack visibility into the training distribution that produces them. Prior works for inferring training data, such as membership inference, detect at the level of individual samples and thus cannot characterize the global composition of the training corpus. We introduce WARP, a framework that recovers a fine-tuned model's training mixtures directly from its released weights. WARP interpolates between the base and fine-tuned models using model merging, generating pseudo-checkpoints that approximate the missing training trajectory and expose a geometric footprint of the training data in the weight space. From these simulated footprints, WARP extracts geometric features and maps them to domain proportions using either a parameter-free softmax readout or an MLP projector trained on synthetic mixtures. In controlled experiments with BERT and GPT-2, WARP recovers domain mixtures with an average MAE as low as 0.046 and 0.104 respectively, outperforming membership inference and a variant with access to the true training trajectory.

AI.tldr: WARP is a framework that recovers the domain mixture weights of a fine-tuned model's training data directly from its weights, using model merging to generate pseudo-checkpoints and geometric features to map to domain proportions, achieving low MAE (0.046 for BERT, 0.104 for GPT-2) and outperforming membership inference.
AI.motivation: Foundation models are released publicly but the data recipes (e.g., domain mixture weights) used to train them are rarely disclosed, creating an access asymmetry where researchers can study the models but lack visibility into the training distribution that produces them.
AI.method: WARP interpolates between base and fine-tuned models using model merging to generate pseudo-checkpoints that approximate the missing training trajectory, extracts geometric features from weight space, and maps them to domain proportions via a parameter-free softmax readout or an MLP projector trained on synthetic mixtures.
AI.result: In controlled experiments with BERT and GPT-2, WARP recovers domain mixtures with average MAE as low as 0.046 and 0.104 respectively, outperforming membership inference and a variant with access to the true training trajectory.
AI.conclusion: WARP effectively recovers training mixtures directly from model weights, bridging the gap between public model releases and undisclosed training data recipes.

title: MedStreamBench: A Time-Aware Benchmark for Streaming and Proactive Medical Video Understanding
summary: Existing medical video benchmarks primarily evaluate whether a model produces the correct answer, but rarely assess whether it answers at the right time. In real clinical settings, AI systems must decide not only what to predict, but also when to answer, defer judgment, or proactively raise alerts. This creates a critical gap between benchmark evaluation and deployment requirements. We present MedStreamBench, a benchmark for time-aware medical video understanding. MedStreamBench integrates 22 medical datasets and 5,419 QA instances across four temporal settings: retrospective, present, future, and proactive. Unlike conventional benchmarks that assume full-video access, MedStreamBench restricts models to temporally bounded evidence windows and supports both single-turn and streaming evaluation. We further introduce a proactive monitoring setting that requires models to determine whether and when clinically relevant alerts should be triggered. Beyond answer correctness, MedStreamBench evaluates temporal behavior through responsiveness and post-evidence stability. Experiments on leading general-purpose and medical vision-language models reveal a substantial gap between offline recognition and temporally grounded decision-making, with performance dropping markedly in streaming and proactive settings. Our benchmark is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/Venn2024/MedStreamBench.

AI.tldr: MedStreamBench is a benchmark for time-aware medical video understanding that evaluates not only answer correctness but also when a model should answer, defer, or raise alerts. It includes 22 medical datasets, 5,419 QA instances across four temporal settings (retrospective, present, future, proactive), and tests models in streaming and proactive monitoring scenarios, revealing significant gaps between offline recognition and temporally grounded decision-making.
AI.motivation: Existing medical video benchmarks only evaluate answer correctness but ignore when to answer. In real clinical settings, AI systems must decide both what to predict and when to answer, defer, or proactively alert, creating a critical gap between benchmark evaluation and deployment requirements.
AI.method: MedStreamBench integrates 22 medical datasets and 5,419 QA instances across four temporal settings: retrospective, present, future, and proactive. It restricts models to temporally bounded evidence windows (unlike full-video access), supports single-turn and streaming evaluation, and introduces a proactive monitoring setting requiring models to determine whether and when to trigger alerts. Evaluation metrics include answer correctness, responsiveness, and post-evidence stability.
AI.result: Experiments on leading general-purpose and medical vision-language models reveal a substantial gap between offline recognition and temporally grounded decision-making, with performance dropping markedly in streaming and proactive settings.
AI.conclusion: Current models are inadequate for time-aware clinical decision-making. MedStreamBench exposes the need for temporally grounded evaluation to bridge the gap between benchmark performance and real-world deployment requirements.

title: Search-based Testing of Vision Language Models for In-Car Scene Understanding
comment: Accepted at the Industry Track of the 41st IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering (ASE 2026)
summary: In the automotive domain, in-car scene understanding (ISU) enables the detection of safety-critical events, such as driver distraction, and supports drivers or passengers by analyzing the in-car scene and adapting the environment (e.g., ambient lighting). The industry is increasingly exploring vision-language models (VLMs) to interpret camera-recorded in-car scenes and extract information for downstream reasoning tasks. However, VLMs may generate incomplete, erroneous, or misleading scene descriptions, highlighting the need for systematic testing. Collecting real in-vehicle data is costly, difficult to scale, and often infeasible, particularly in early design stages. In this paper, we present ISU-Test, an automated testing approach that combines rendering-based scene generation with search-based testing to evaluate ISU systems. By framing testing as an optimization problem and systematically modifying scene parameters, our method generates diverse in-car scenarios and explores a wide range of configurations. We evaluate ISU-Test on both an industrial prototype and open-source VLMs across two case studies: question answering and captioning, comparing against randomized scenario generation. Results show that ISU-Test significantly outperforms the baseline, achieving up to 10 times higher failure rates and up to 3.6 times higher failure coverage.

AI.tldr: ISU-Test is an automated testing approach combining rendering-based scene generation with search-based testing to evaluate vision-language models for in-car scene understanding, achieving up to 10x higher failure rates and 3.6x higher failure coverage compared to random baseline.
AI.motivation: VLMs for in-car scene understanding may generate incomplete or misleading descriptions, yet systematic testing is challenging because collecting real in-vehicle data is costly, hard to scale, and often infeasible in early design stages.
AI.method: ISU-Test frames testing as an optimization problem, combining rendering-based scene generation with search-based testing to systematically modify scene parameters and generate diverse in-car scenarios.
AI.result: ISU-Test significantly outperforms randomized scenario generation, achieving up to 10 times higher failure rates and up to 3.6 times higher failure coverage on both industrial prototype and open-source VLMs across question answering and captioning tasks.
AI.conclusion: The proposed automated testing approach effectively addresses the scalability and cost challenges of evaluating VLM-based in-car scene understanding systems, enabling more systematic failure detection.

title: Pre-Flight: A Benchmark for Evaluating Large Language Models on Aviation Operational Knowledge
comment: 9 pages, 1 figure, 2 tables. Benchmark available in inspect_evals (UKGovernmentBEIS/inspect_evals)
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed for aviation business operations, from documentation and training generation to customer facing assistants. General purpose benchmarks do not measure whether a model reasons safely and correctly about aviation specific operational knowledge, and the high stakes, regulated nature of the domain makes that gap consequential. We present Pre-Flight, an open source benchmark of 300 multiple choice questions drawn from international standards and airport ground operations material, covering international airport ground operations, ICAO and US FAA regulations, aviation general knowledge and complex operational scenarios. Questions were authored and reviewed by practitioners with experience in air traffic management, ground operations and commercial flying. We evaluate a range of contemporary commercial and open weight models using the Inspect evaluation framework, scoring by accuracy under a standard multiple choice protocol, and we maintain the leaderboard on a rolling basis as new models are released. Against an informal expert reference of around 95%, obtained from a low sample quiz of aviation professionals at a conference, even the strongest model evaluated (released in 2026) reaches 82.7%, having improved only gradually from roughly 75% in early 2025. A substantial and persistent gap below expert level reliability therefore remains. We release the dataset, the evaluation harness and the results, and the benchmark is available within the community evaluations package distributed with inspect_evals. We argue that domain specific evaluation of this kind is a necessary precondition for responsible deployment of generative AI in non safety critical aviation operations.

AI.tldr: Pre-Flight is an open-source benchmark of 300 multiple-choice questions covering aviation operational knowledge (ground operations, ICAO/FAA regulations, scenarios). Evaluations show top models reach 82.7% accuracy vs. ~95% expert reference, indicating a persistent gap. The authors argue domain-specific evaluation is necessary for responsible AI deployment in aviation.
AI.motivation: General-purpose benchmarks fail to measure whether LLMs reason safely about aviation-specific operational knowledge, yet LLMs are increasingly proposed for aviation business operations. The high-stakes, regulated nature of aviation makes this gap consequential.
AI.method: Created 300 multiple-choice questions from international standards and airport ground operations material (ICAO, FAA, complex scenarios). Questions authored/reviewed by aviation practitioners. Evaluated commercial and open-weight models using the Inspect framework, scoring by accuracy under standard multiple-choice protocol. Maintains a rolling leaderboard.
AI.result: Strongest model (released 2026) achieves 82.7% accuracy vs. ~95% expert reference. Models improved gradually from ~75% (early 2025) to 82.7%. A substantial and persistent gap below expert-level reliability remains.
AI.conclusion: Domain-specific evaluation is a necessary precondition for responsible deployment of generative AI in non-safety-critical aviation operations. The benchmark, evaluation harness, and results are publicly released.

title: Model Merging as Probabilistic Inference in Fine-Tuning Parameter Space
comment: Accepted for Publication at the 42nd Conference on Uncertainty in Artificial Intelligence (UAI), 2026
summary: Model merging aims to combine existing single-task solutions into a multi-task solution without additional data-driven fine-tuning.~Most existing approaches achieve this using geometric properties of local solution spaces. However, such geometric views provide limited guidance for scoring how statistically useful each task-specific update direction is across tasks during merging. To address this, we formulate model merging from a new perspective of probabilistic inference under a product-of-experts (PoE) scenario where each single-task solution defines an energy-based expert model (EBM) over the merged parameters. We show that several existing model merging methods arise as special cases of our framework under energy designs that impose implicit Gaussian assumptions on directional residuals between merged and task-specific models. Empirically, we find that these residuals are often heavy-tailed which exposes a mismatch with the imposed light-tailed Gaussian structures. We address this with a heavy-tailed PoE design based on Cauchy experts, which better captures the observed residual behavior while admitting a provably convergent inference procedure. Experiments across multiple tasks and architectures show significant improvements over state-of-the-arts baselines. Our code is available at https://github.com/MinhLong210/PoE-EBM-Merging.git.

AI.tldr: The paper reformulates model merging as probabilistic inference under a product-of-experts framework with energy-based models, identifies heavy-tailed residuals in existing methods, and proposes a Cauchy-based heavy-tailed PoE design that outperforms state-of-the-art baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing model merging methods rely on geometric properties of local solution spaces, which offer limited guidance for statistically scoring the usefulness of task-specific update directions across tasks during merging.
AI.method: Formulates model merging as probabilistic inference under a product-of-experts (PoE) scenario where each single-task solution defines an energy-based expert model (EBM) over merged parameters. Shows existing methods are special cases under Gaussian assumptions, then proposes a heavy-tailed PoE design using Cauchy experts to better match observed heavy-tailed residual behavior.
AI.result: Empirical results show significant improvements over state-of-the-art baselines across multiple tasks and architectures.
AI.conclusion: The heavy-tailed PoE framework with Cauchy experts better captures the statistical properties of residuals between merged and task-specific models, and provides a provably convergent inference procedure.

title: The Turning Point of 3D Plant Phenotyping: 3D Foundation Models Enable Minute-to-Second Cross-Crop Reconstruction and Beyond
summary: 3D plant phenotyping is notoriously known to be procedure-complicated and of low throughput due to the extensive multi-view imaging, the fragile 3D reconstruction pipeline, and the additional cost from reconstructed geometry to phenotypic extraction. These limitations are further amplified in low-cost data acquisition, where smartphone videos or sparsely sampled multi-view images provide limited view overlap and self-occlusion. In this work, we show that the conventional 3D plant phenotyping pipeline could be streamlined and significantly accelerated with 3D Foundation Models (3DFMs), and particularly, present one of the first cross-crop 3D phenotyping frameworks powered by 3DFMs. The framework replaces COLMAP-style sparse initialization with 3DFM-based feed-forward geometric recovery, combines geometry-constrained 3D Gaussian Splatting for dense reconstruction, enables few-view reconstruction through iterative view synthesis and refinement, and converts reconstructed geometry into measurable organs through 2D-to-3D semantic transfer, metric scale recovery, and organ instance separation. We further construct a cross-crop dataset with smartphone-based image acquisition, diverse plant morphologies, and manual annotations for segmentation and phenotypic evaluation. Experiments across 26 plant sequences show that 3D Foundation Models reduce the average reconstruction time from 6.52 minutes to 1.58 seconds while maintaining high reconstruction quality and phenotyping accuracy. These results suggest a fresh technical route for high-throughput 3D plant phenotyping, from low-cost image acquisition to fast reconstruction, perception, scale recovery, and phenotypic measurement.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a 3D plant phenotyping framework powered by 3D Foundation Models (3DFMs) that replaces traditional COLMAP-style sparse initialization with feed-forward geometric recovery, using 3D Gaussian Splatting for dense reconstruction. It achieves 3D plant phenotyping from smartphone videos or sparse multi-view images, reducing reconstruction time from 6.52 minutes to 1.58 seconds across 26 plant sequences.
AI.motivation: Conventional 3D plant phenotyping is procedure-complicated, low-throughput, and requires extensive multi-view imaging with fragile reconstruction pipelines. These limitations are amplified in low-cost data acquisition (smartphone videos, sparse multi-view images) due to limited view overlap and self-occlusion. The authors aim to streamline and accelerate the pipeline using 3D Foundation Models.
AI.method: The framework: (1) replaces COLMAP-style sparse initialization with 3DFM-based feed-forward geometric recovery; (2) combines geometry-constrained 3D Gaussian Splatting for dense reconstruction; (3) enables few-view reconstruction via iterative view synthesis and refinement; (4) converts reconstructed geometry into measurable organs through 2D-to-3D semantic transfer, metric scale recovery, and organ instance separation. A cross-crop dataset with smartphone-based image acquisition and manual annotations was constructed.
AI.result: Across 26 plant sequences, 3DFMs reduced average reconstruction time from 6.52 minutes to 1.58 seconds while maintaining high reconstruction quality and phenotyping accuracy. The framework is demonstrated as a cross-crop solution.
AI.conclusion: The results suggest a fresh technical route for high-throughput 3D plant phenotyping, from low-cost image acquisition to fast reconstruction, perception, scale recovery, and phenotypic measurement.

title: Steerability via constraints: a substrate for scalable oversight of coding agents
comment: Accepted to the Deep Learning for Code Workshop at the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, Seoul, South Korea, 2026
summary: Coding agents are capable; human oversight is the bottleneck. Unconstrained agents introduce security risks, erode codebase scalability, and make human review increasingly costly. We argue that the same methods used for decades to manage large human engineering teams: access control, network policies, strict coding conventions enforced by tooling; transfer directly to coding agents, and are cheaper (in token) than recent agentic scaffolding. We sketch a start-to-end system on this principle, and report a controlled experiment in scalable oversight: a small reviewer (Gemma 4 e4b) inspects a Python codebase containing 11 inserted backdoors. Recall rises from 54.5% (unconstrained, no tools) to 90.9% (constrained substrate plus a ~200-LoC `docs` CLI), with substrate and tools contributing independently. We choose Python deliberately: substrate-level oversight gains are largest where the language gives the fewest guarantees by default; the principles extend to languages like Rust.

AI.tldr: Coding agents benefit from traditional software engineering oversight methods (access control, network policies, coding conventions) more than from recent agentic scaffolding. A controlled experiment shows backdoor detection recall improves from 54.5% to 90.9% when using constrained substrate plus a ~200-LoC CLI tool.
AI.motivation: Human oversight is the bottleneck for coding agents. Unconstrained agents create security risks, degrade codebase scalability, and increase cost of human review. The authors argue traditional engineering management methods are cheaper and more effective than modern agentic scaffolding.
AI.method: The authors propose applying traditional software engineering oversight methods (access control, network policies, coding conventions enforced by tooling) to coding agents. They conduct a controlled experiment where a small reviewer model (Gemma 4 e4b) inspects a Python codebase with 11 inserted backdoors, comparing unconstrained vs. constrained (substrate + tools) conditions.
AI.result: Recall improved from 54.5% (unconstrained, no tools) to 90.9% (constrained substrate plus ~200-LoC `docs` CLI). Substrate and tools contributed independently to the improvement.
AI.conclusion: Traditional software engineering oversight methods transfer directly to coding agents and are cheaper (in token cost) than recent agentic scaffolding. The principles extend to languages like Rust, though the gains are largest in dynamically-typed languages like Python that provide fewer guarantees by default.

title: Actual causality in fault trees
summary: Fault trees are a widely used as effective risk models for complex systems, answering the question "what can go wrong?", especially through minimal cut set analysis. We study fault trees from the perspective of Halpern & Pearl's theory of actual causality. This allows us to use fault trees to answer the question "why has it gone wrong?", which is fundamental to failure diagnostics. We give a complete classification of each of the different notions of actual causality in terms of the fault tree's graph structure and logical structure, and show how minimal cut sets give rise to actual causes.

AI.tldr: This paper connects fault tree analysis with Halpern & Pearl's theory of actual causality to classify causes of failures, showing that minimal cut sets correspond to actual causes for failure diagnostics.
AI.motivation: Fault trees answer "what can go wrong?" via minimal cut set analysis, but lack formal grounding for answering "why has it gone wrong?"—a key question in failure diagnostics. The authors aim to bridge this gap by applying actual causality theory.
AI.method: The authors classify different notions of actual causality (from Halpern & Pearl) in terms of fault tree graph structure and logical structure, and demonstrate how minimal cut sets map to actual causes.
AI.result: A complete classification of actual causality notions relative to fault tree structure is provided, with minimal cut sets shown to correspond to actual causes.
AI.conclusion: Fault trees can be formally extended from predictive risk analysis ("what can go wrong?") to diagnostic reasoning ("why has it gone wrong?") using actual causality theory.

title: A Mathematical Introduction to Diffusion Models
comment: Lecture notes for the John Tukey Summer Graduate School on Mathematics of Generative Models at SLMath (June 22nd, 2026 -- July 2nd, 2026)
summary: These notes give a proof-oriented introduction to diffusion models from the viewpoint of sampling, tracing a single arc from classical sampling dynamics to modern diffusion samplers, their error analysis, and inference-time control. Throughout, the material is layered into core definitions and identities proved in full, representative estimates proved under simplifying assumptions, and research-level theorems stated with a proof roadmap. The intended audience is beginning graduate students with a background in probability but no prior exposure to stochastic differential equations, stochastic numerics, or diffusion models.

AI.tldr: A proof-oriented introduction to diffusion models from a sampling perspective, covering classical sampling dynamics to modern diffusion samplers, error analysis, and inference-time control, designed for beginning graduate students.
AI.motivation: To provide a pedagogical, rigorous, and self-contained introduction to diffusion models from the sampling viewpoint, bridging classical sampling dynamics and modern diffusion samplers with full proofs, for students with probability background but no prior exposure to SDEs or diffusion models.
AI.method: The paper organizes material in three layers: (1) core definitions and identities with complete proofs, (2) representative estimates under simplifying assumptions, and (3) research-level theorems with proof roadmaps. It traces a single arc from classical sampling dynamics to modern diffusion samplers.
AI.result: Not applicable at the abstract level; the paper is a tutorial/notes that introduces concepts, proofs, and analysis rather than presenting novel experimental results.
AI.conclusion: The notes aim to equip beginning graduate students with a rigorous understanding of diffusion models from the sampling perspective, including error analysis and inference-time control, with a layered structure that accommodates different depths of study.

title: ProSAC-CT: Progressive Spectral-Anatomical Co-Guided Multi-Stage Diffusion Model for Low-Dose CT Denoising
summary: Low-dose computed tomography (LDCT) reduces radiation exposure but introduces stronger quantum noise, streak artifacts, and local texture degradation, which can obscure anatomical boundaries and weaken low-contrast structures. Diffusion models are promising for LDCT denoising by progressively recovering normal-dose CT (NDCT) images from degraded LDCT inputs, but existing methods often suffer from insufficient anatomical guidance, uncertain frequency-dependent recovery, and uniform reverse-process modeling. We propose ProSAC-CT, a progressive spectral-anatomical co-guided multi-stage diffusion model for image-domain LDCT denoising. ProSAC-CT integrates an anatomical-prior-guided conditioning (APGC) module, a residual frequency-domain decoupling stage (RFDDS), and a time-step-decoupling denoising decoder (TD3). APGC extracts LDCT-derived structural guidance, RFDDS enhances frequency-aware representations, and TD3 assigns them to different reverse-diffusion stages for anatomical stabilization, boundary refinement, and fine-detail recovery. Experiments on four LDCT degradation benchmarks show that ProSAC-CT improves image fidelity, structural similarity, perceptual quality, and information preservation over representative methods while better preserving boundary-sensitive anatomical details. Downstream anatomical-region classification on Mayo-2020 further indicates that ProSAC-CT retains task-relevant anatomical information, supporting its practical use for low-dose CT denoising.

AI.tldr: ProSAC-CT is a progressive spectral-anatomical co-guided multi-stage diffusion model for LDCT denoising that integrates anatomical-prior-guided conditioning, residual frequency-domain decoupling, and time-step-decoupling denoising to improve image fidelity, structural similarity, and anatomical detail preservation over existing methods.
AI.motivation: LDCT introduces stronger quantum noise, streak artifacts, and local texture degradation that obscure anatomical boundaries and weaken low-contrast structures. Existing diffusion-based denoising methods suffer from insufficient anatomical guidance, uncertain frequency-dependent recovery, and uniform reverse-process modeling.
AI.method: ProSAC-CT is a progressive spectral-anatomical co-guided multi-stage diffusion model with three key components: (1) Anatomical-Prior-Guided Conditioning (APGC) module for LDCT-derived structural guidance, (2) Residual Frequency-Domain Decoupling Stage (RFDDS) for frequency-aware representations, and (3) Time-Step-Decoupling Denoising Decoder (TD3) that assigns these representations to different reverse-diffusion stages for anatomical stabilization, boundary refinement, and fine-detail recovery.
AI.result: On four LDCT degradation benchmarks, ProSAC-CT improves image fidelity, structural similarity, perceptual quality, and information preservation over representative methods while better preserving boundary-sensitive anatomical details. Downstream anatomical-region classification on Mayo-2020 further confirms retention of task-relevant anatomical information.
AI.conclusion: ProSAC-CT effectively addresses key limitations of existing diffusion-based LDCT denoising methods by providing progressive spectral-anatomical co-guidance, demonstrating superior denoising performance and practical utility for low-dose CT denoising.

title: CLAP: Closed-Loop Training, Evaluation, and Release Control for Domain Agent Post-training
comment: 6 pages, 1 figure. Accepted to CRAE 2026; to appear in SPIE Proceedings. Best Poster Award
summary: Domain agents often face noisy business data, uncertain post-training gains, offline/application mismatch, and adapter-release risk. This paper presents CLAP (Closed-Loop Agent Post-training), a closed-loop method that converts business data into structured SFT samples, decision-preference samples, holdout sets, risk diagnostics, and release-gate records. CLAP combines data validation, target/evidence normalization, reward/KL diagnosis, offline gates, and application-chain replay to decide whether an adapter is suitable for the target application chain. On five anonymized manufacturing-scenario batches, QLoRA-style LoRA-SFT yields modest average gains: overall score increases by 0.0098, pass rate by 0.0240, and evidence accuracy by 0.0280, while hallucination and wrong facts decrease. Yet only 3 of 5 batches improve, some batches regress, and GRPO exposes high KL risks. Application-chain replay further shows that RAG is necessary for factual extraction; under the same 3B backbone and 100 replay cases, an application-RAG-oriented LoRA-SFT adapter improves value, core fields, and answer-evidence doc/page matching over base+RAG, but increases latency. These results support managing domain-agent post-training through an integrated data-training-evaluation-release loop rather than relying on training completion or a single offline score.

AI.tldr: CLAP is a closed-loop method for domain-agent post-training that integrates data validation, SFT/RLHF training, risk diagnostics, and application-chain replay to decide adapter release. On 5 manufacturing batches, modest average gains are observed (score +0.0098, pass rate +0.0240, evidence accuracy +0.0280) but only 3/5 batches improve, GRPO poses KL risks, and RAG is essential for factual extraction. Results advocate for an integrated data-training-evaluation-release loop over single-score-based release decisions.
AI.motivation: Domain agents face challenges including noisy business data, uncertain post-training gains, offline/application mismatch, and adapter-release risk. Existing practices of relying on training completion or a single offline score are insufficient for reliable deployment decisions.
AI.method: CLAP (Closed-Loop Agent Post-training) converts business data into structured SFT samples, decision-preference samples, holdout sets, risk diagnostics, and release-gate records. It combines data validation, target/evidence normalization, reward/KL diagnosis, offline gates, and application-chain replay to evaluate adapter suitability.
AI.result: On 5 manufacturing batches: QLoRA-style LoRA-SFT achieves modest average gains (overall score +0.0098, pass rate +0.0240, evidence accuracy +0.0280) with reduced hallucination and wrong facts. However, only 3/5 batches improve, some regress, and GRPO reveals high KL risks. Application-chain replay shows RAG necessity; LoRA-SFT + RAG improves value, core fields, and answer-evidence matching over base+RAG but increases latency.
AI.conclusion: Domain-agent post-training should be managed through an integrated data-training-evaluation-release loop rather than relying solely on training completion metrics or a single offline evaluation score.

title: Frequency Shift Physics-Informed Extreme Learning Machine for Solving High-Frequency Partial Differential Equations
summary: Solving partial differential equations (PDEs) with high-frequency solutions remains a central challenge in physics-informed machine learning due to spectral bias -- the tendency of neural networks to learn low-frequency components preferentially. This paper proposes a Frequency Shift Physics-Informed Extreme Learning Machine (FS-PIELM) framework that addresses this limitation through an additive mechanism for weight initialization. Rather than multiplying random weights by a scaling factor, the method translates the mean of the Gaussian weight distribution while keeping the variance fixed at unity, thereby avoiding the variance amplification inherent in scaling-based methods. Two variants are developed: FS-PIELM-L assigns independent frequency magnitudes to individual neurons, while FS-PIELM-G groups neurons for improved robustness. Theoretical analysis shows that the frequency variance under the proposed framework remains bounded and approaches unity regardless of target frequency, in contrast to the quadratic growth of conventional approaches. The method preserves the computational efficiency of extreme learning machines, requiring only a single linear solve. Experiments on seven benchmark problems spanning six equation types -- Helmholtz, wave, Poisson, Klein-Gordon, heat, and advection-diffusion -- on both regular and complex geometries show that the linear variant achieves the best accuracy in six of seven cases, with improvements of one to nearly five orders of magnitude over existing PIELM variants. The code and data accompanying this manuscript will be made publicly available at https://github.com/xgxgnpu/Physics-informed-vibe-coding/tree/main/FS-PIELM.

AI.tldr: FS-PIELM addresses spectral bias in physics-informed neural networks for high-frequency PDEs by using an additive weight initialization (shifting mean, fixing variance=1), avoiding variance amplification. Two variants (FS-PIELM-L and FS-PIELM-G) are tested on 7 benchmark problems, achieving up to 5 orders of magnitude improvement over existing PIELM methods.
AI.motivation: Solving PDEs with high-frequency solutions suffers from spectral bias, where neural networks preferentially learn low-frequency components. Existing scaling-based weight initialization methods amplify variance quadratically with target frequency, limiting performance.
AI.method: FS-PIELM uses an additive mechanism that shifts the mean of the Gaussian weight distribution while keeping variance fixed at unity, avoiding variance amplification. Two variants: FS-PIELM-L (independent frequency magnitudes per neuron) and FS-PIELM-G (grouped neurons for robustness). The method preserves ELM efficiency with a single linear solve.
AI.result: Tested on 7 benchmarks (Helmholtz, wave, Poisson, Klein-Gordon, heat, advection-diffusion) on regular and complex geometries. FS-PIELM-L achieves best accuracy in 6/7 cases, with improvements of 1 to nearly 5 orders of magnitude over existing PIELM variants. Frequency variance remains bounded and approaches unity.
AI.conclusion: The additive weight initialization effectively addresses spectral bias without variance amplification, providing a computationally efficient and accurate framework for high-frequency PDE solving with PIELM.

title: DL-VINS-Factory: A Modular Framework for Learned Visual Front-Ends in Visual-Inertial SLAM
summary: Deep-learning features excel in visual matching, yet their practical value in tightly coupled visual-inertial SLAM (VI-SLAM) remains insufficiently characterized. We present DL-VINS-Factory, a unified framework that integrates learned feature extractors (ALIKED, RaCo, SuperPoint, XFeat) with either Lucas--Kanade (LK) optical-flow tracking or LightGlue (LG) descriptor matching. All front-ends share a sliding-window Ceres back-end, with optional AnyLoc DINOv2-VLAD loop closure, and 4-DoF pose-graph optimization. We benchmark the system across the four datasets covering indoor, unstructured outdoor, aggressive-motion, and visually degraded conditions. Results show that learned front-ends are viable for real-time embedded VI-SLAM, but are not universally superior to classical tracking. Relative to the corresponding GFTT+LK baseline, ALIKED+LG reduces EuRoC ATE by $5\%$ in monocular odometry and by $7\%$ in stereo with loop-closure. On NTU-VIRAL, where aggressive aerial motion increases inter-frame viewpoint change, ALIKED+LG stereo reduces loop-closed ATE by $12\%$. In Botanic Garden dataset, optical-flow tracking remains preferable, but learned keypoints still improve over the baseline GFTT, in which SuperPoint+LK reduces grayscale camera ATE by $29\%$, while RaCo+LK reduces RGB camera ATE by $38\%$. On SubT-MRS, learned front-ends display varying degree of improvement based on individual cases. With TensorRT acceleration on a Jetson AGX Orin, all valid configurations run in real time between $29$--$47$ FPS in monocular mode and $18$--$33$ FPS in stereo mode for the EuRoC and NTU-VIRAL datasets. AnyLoc further confirms roughly $2$--$7\times$ more valid loops than BRIEF+DBoW2. The implementation is open-sourced at https://github.com/limshoonkit/DL-VINS-Factory-ROS2/.

AI.tldr: DL-VINS-Factory is a unified framework integrating learned feature extractors (ALIKED, RaCo, SuperPoint, XFeat) with optical-flow or descriptor matching for VI-SLAM, benchmarked across diverse datasets. Learned front-ends show viability but not universal superiority; ALIKED+LG improves EuRoC ATE by 5-7%, SuperPoint+LK reduces Botanic Garden grayscale ATE by 29%, and RaCo+LK reduces RGB ATE by 38%. Real-time performance reaches 29-47 FPS (mono) and 18-33 FPS (stereo) on Jetson AGX Orin.
AI.motivation: Deep-learning features excel in visual matching but their practical value in tightly coupled VI-SLAM remains insufficiently characterized; the paper aims to systematically benchmark and characterize this gap.
AI.method: A unified framework integrating learned feature extractors (ALIKED, RaCo, SuperPoint, XFeat) with LK optical-flow tracking or LightGlue descriptor matching, sharing a sliding-window Ceres back-end with optional AnyLoc DINOv2-VLAD loop closure and 4-DoF pose-graph optimization; benchmarked on four datasets covering varied conditions.
AI.result: ALIKED+LG reduces EuRoC ATE by 5% (mono) and 7% (stereo w/ loop closure); on NTU-VIRAL, ALIKED+LG stereo reduces loop-closed ATE by 12%. SuperPoint+LK reduces Botanic Garden grayscale ATE by 29%, RaCo+LK reduces RGB ATE by 38%. Real-time: 29-47 FPS (mono), 18-33 FPS (stereo) on Jetson AGX Orin. AnyLoc yields 2-7× more valid loops than BRIEF+DBoW2.
AI.conclusion: Learned front-ends are viable for real-time embedded VI-SLAM but not universally superior to classical tracking; optical-flow remains preferable in some conditions. The framework is open-sourced.

title: Safety Targeted Embedding Exploit via Refinement
summary: Safety training for large language models (LLMs) is conducted predominantly in English, leaving uncertain how well safety mechanisms generalize to low-resource languages and mixed-language code-switching. We show that this creates an epistemic gap in which models confidently generate harmful responses for inputs that fall outside the distribution of their safety training. To study this phenomenon, we introduce STEER (Safety Targeted Embedding Exploit via Refinement), a gradient-guided attack that identifies words contributing most strongly to the model's refusal behavior and iteratively translates them into low-resource languages to suppress refusal while preserving harmful intent. Across six open-source 8B-parameter models, STEER achieves attack success rates of up to 93.0% on JailbreakBench and 96.7% on AdvBench, outperforming random code-switching and Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG). The resulting prompts also transfer to GPT-4o-mini, achieving a 35.5% attack success rate without requiring access to the target model, suggesting that the underlying weakness is not specific to a single architecture. These findings demonstrate that safety mechanisms aligned primarily on English cannot be assumed to generalize across multilingual inputs. We argue that improving multilingual safety requires broader coverage during alignment and mechanisms that explicitly detect and abstain on out-of-distribution inputs.

AI.tldr: STEER is a gradient-guided attack that translates key refusal-triggering words in harmful prompts into low-resource languages, achieving up to 96.7% attack success rate against LLMs by exploiting the epistemic gap between English safety training and multilingual/code-switched inputs.
AI.motivation: Safety training for LLMs is conducted predominantly in English, creating an epistemic gap where models confidently generate harmful responses for inputs outside their safety training distribution, particularly in low-resource languages and code-switching scenarios.
AI.method: STEER (Safety Targeted Embedding Exploit via Refinement) uses gradient-guided search to identify words most strongly contributing to refusal behavior, then iteratively translates them into low-resource languages to suppress refusal while preserving harmful intent.
AI.result: STEER achieves up to 93.0% attack success rate on JailbreakBench and 96.7% on AdvBench across six 8B-parameter open-source models. It outperforms random code-switching and GCG. Transferred to GPT-4o-mini, it achieves 35.5% attack success rate without access to the target model.
AI.conclusion: Safety mechanisms aligned primarily on English cannot be assumed to generalize across multilingual inputs. Improving multilingual safety requires broader coverage during alignment and mechanisms that explicitly detect and abstain on out-of-distribution inputs.

title: Predicting Closed-Loop Performance of Latent World Models: Offline Checkpoint Selection for MPC and Model-Based RL Under Non-Markovian Rewards in LunarLander
comment: Preprint, 19 pages (16 main text + 3 pages appendix), 7 figures, 4 tables. Video: https://youtu.be/4PxHFW_TYUw , Code: https://github.com/nsmoly/LunarLander_RSSM
summary: We study how to predict the downstream closed-loop performance of a learned latent world model from validation-time diagnostics alone. Choosing the right checkpoint from a world-model training run is difficult: validation loss and multi-step prediction RMSE keep improving long after closed-loop performance has collapsed. We present a suite of structural validation-time diagnostics drawn from optimal-control theory and apply them to Gymnasium's LunarLander v3, which features shaped rewards. We train an RSSM [5, 4] world model on it and treat per checkpoint CEM-MPC return as the oracle for closed-loop quality. By evaluating 40 metrics against this oracle, we find that the strongest single predictor is the Reward Observability Fraction (ROF), which measures the reward predictor's dependence on the observable subspace. We combine ROF with three structural regularizers into a single-number offline checkpoint selection score, the Composite Reward Observability Fraction (CROF). The CROF-selected world model trains a model-based A2C policy that beats a fairly evaluated model-free A2C baseline by ~24.5 return points while using ~65x fewer real-environment interactions, and the same world model also drives a strong zero-shot CEM-MPC policy. Code and data: https://github.com/nsmoly/LunarLander_RSSM.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes structural validation-time diagnostics, particularly the Reward Observability Fraction (ROF) and its composite CROF score, to predict closed-loop performance of latent world models without requiring online rollouts; CROF-selected models outperform model-free baselines in both model-based A2C and zero-shot CEM-MPC policies.
AI.motivation: Standard validation metrics like validation loss and multi-step prediction RMSE correlate poorly with downstream closed-loop performance—they keep improving even after control performance collapses—making checkpoint selection for world models unreliable.
AI.method: The authors train an RSSM world model on LunarLander v3, compute 40 structural diagnostics rooted in optimal-control theory, and compare them against oracle CEM-MPC return. They identify Reward Observability Fraction (ROF) as the best single predictor and combine it with three structural regularizers into a Composite ROF (CROF) score for offline checkpoint selection.
AI.result: CROF-selected world model enables a model-based A2C policy that outperforms a fairly evaluated model-free A2C baseline by ~24.5 return points while using ~65x fewer real-environment interactions; the same checkpoint also drives a strong zero-shot CEM-MPC policy.
AI.conclusion: Structural validation-time diagnostics, especially observability-centric metrics like ROF/CROF, are effective proxies for closed-loop world model quality and enable practical offline checkpoint selection without expensive online evaluation.

title: ProCal: Inference-Time Proposal Calibration for Open-Vocabulary Object Detection
summary: Open-vocabulary object detection aims to localize and classify objects beyond the fixed set of categories seen dur ing training. Recent open-vocabulary object detection methods improve localization and classification for unseen categories by leveraging a frozen VLM as a detector backbone. However, VLM classification score lacks recognizing position and scale of the object in an image. We observe that pretrained VLMs en able to classify foreground and background regions. According to this observation, we propose a simple inference-time Pro posal Calibration (ProCal) that improves localization quality of the classification score. ProCal computes a proposal prior by combining two scores: localization-aware foreground score and background-aware suppression score. Localization-aware foreground score captures whether a proposal contains an object area. Background-aware suppression score measures the extent to which the proposal resembles background. We analyze that ProCal suppresses false novel activation on background proposals and consistently ranks true novel proposals above background and partial novel proposals. Applied to CLIPSelf ViT-L/14, ProCal improves APr +2.5 on OV-LVIS. The analyses show that proposal-level localization-aware reranking effects to mitigate ranking miscalibration for novel objects.

AI.tldr: ProCal is a simple inference-time proposal calibration method that improves open-vocabulary object detection by combining a localization-aware foreground score and a background-aware suppression score to rerank proposals, achieving +2.5 APr on OV-LVIS with CLIPSelf ViT-L/14.
AI.motivation: VLM classification scores lack recognition of object position and scale, leading to poor localization for unseen categories. The authors observed that pretrained VLMs can distinguish foreground vs. background regions, motivating a calibration method to leverage this capability.
AI.method: ProCal computes a proposal prior by fusing two scores: (1) localization-aware foreground score (captures whether a proposal contains an object area) and (2) background-aware suppression score (measures how much a proposal resembles background). This prior is used to rerank proposals at inference time without additional training.
AI.result: Applied to CLIPSelf ViT-L/14, ProCal improves APr by +2.5 on OV-LVIS. Analysis shows proposal-level localization-aware reranking effectively mitigates ranking miscalibration for novel objects.
AI.conclusion: ProCal suppresses false novel activation on background proposals and consistently ranks true novel proposals above background and partial novel proposals, demonstrating that simple inference-time calibration can significantly improve open-vocabulary detection quality.

title: CamoNAS: Neural Architecture Search for Enhanced Camouflaged Object Detection
comment: Published in The Visual Computer. Author manuscript version
summary: Camouflaged Object Detection (COD) aims to locate and segment objects that blend into their surroundings, presenting challenges due to weak edge cues and ill-defined boundaries. Traditional COD models rely on hand-designed architectures and multi-scale feature fusion, which are often guided by intuition rather than systematic search. This paper introduces CamoNAS, a frequency-aware multi-resolution Neural Architecture Search (NAS) framework for COD. CamoNAS automatically searches both cell-level operations and network-level downsampling paths, forming a hierarchical search space tailored to detect camouflaged objects. Additionally, it adopts an RGB frequency dual-stream architecture, where a learnable wavelet transform complements the RGB spatial stream. CamoNAS achieves state-of-the-art performance on four COD benchmarks (CAMO, COD10K, NC4K, CHAMELEON), highlighting the effectiveness of NAS for COD. Our code is available at https://github.com/rendaweiSIMIT/CamoNAS.

AI.tldr: CamoNAS is a frequency-aware Neural Architecture Search framework for Camouflaged Object Detection that automatically designs optimal network architectures via hierarchical search, incorporating a learnable wavelet-based dual-stream RGB-frequency design, achieving SOTA results on four COD benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Traditional COD models rely on hand-designed architectures and intuitive multi-scale feature fusion, lacking systematic optimization. The authors aim to automate architecture design for COD using NAS to overcome limitations of manual design.
AI.method: Proposes CamoNAS, a hierarchical NAS framework with: (1) cell-level operation search and network-level downsampling path search; (2) an RGB frequency dual-stream architecture with learnable wavelet transform to complement spatial features.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art performance on four COD benchmarks: CAMO, COD10K, NC4K, and CHAMELEON.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates the effectiveness of NAS for COD, showing that automated architecture search can outperform hand-designed models in camouflaged object detection tasks.

title: Finite-Lag Operator Geometry of Recurrent Representations
summary: Recurrent representations are trajectories, but representation geometry is often measured from static snapshots. We develop finite-lag operator geometry for recurrent hidden states from observed source-successor pairs $(X_t,X_{t+Δ})$. The primitive is the conditional transport law $Q_Δ(dy\mid x)$, estimated by a dense Gaussian source-smoothing operator. From this directed finite-lag law we derive a source-centered transport tensor $G_Δ$, which decomposes exactly into conditional spread and coherent displacement, and an antisymmetric coordinate circulation $W_Δ^ρ$, which summarizes directed lagged flow. We prove affine covariance with explicit metric dependence of scalar summaries, dense estimator stability on bounded trajectory clouds, and a finite-lag separation result showing that source-centered transport detects deterministic recurrent motion not recorded by infinitesimal carre-du-champ geometry. A linear-Gaussian closed form calibrates the quantities in terms of the update $A_Δ$, source covariance, and innovation covariance. Controlled experiments validate the decomposition, circulation, covariance, and stability predictions. In performance matched repeat-copy networks, the framework reveals architecture dependent differences in total transport scale and coherent displacement trace, while coherent displacement fraction is metric and resolution dependent.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a finite-lag operator geometry for recurrent hidden states using source-successor pairs, deriving transport tensors and circulation measures that decompose conditional transport into spread and coherent displacement, with proven affine covariance and stability.
AI.motivation: Existing representation geometry is measured from static snapshots, but recurrent representations are inherently trajectories. The paper aims to develop a framework that captures directed lagged flow and coherent displacement from observed source-successor pairs, moving beyond static or infinitesimal measures.
AI.method: The method estimates conditional transport laws Q_Δ(dy|x) via dense Gaussian source-smoothing operators, derives a source-centered transport tensor G_Δ decomposing into conditional spread and coherent displacement, and an antisymmetric circulation tensor W_Δ^ρ summarizing directed lagged flow. Affine covariance, stability, and finite-lag separation results are proven, with a linear-Gaussian closed form for calibration.
AI.result: Controlled experiments validate decomposition, circulation, covariance, and stability predictions. In repeat-copy networks, the framework reveals architecture-dependent differences in total transport scale and coherent displacement trace, while coherent displacement fraction depends on metric and resolution.
AI.conclusion: Finite-lag operator geometry provides a principled framework for analyzing recurrent hidden state dynamics, capturing deterministic recurrent motion missed by infinitesimal carre-du-champ geometry, and revealing architecture-specific differences in recurrent network dynamics.

title: JointHOI: Jointly Generating Contact Maps Enhances Hand Object Interaction Generation
summary: Text driven hand object interaction (HOI) generation is gaining attention for immersive applications and robotics, yet producing physically plausible interactions remains challenging. Even when individual motions appear natural, small contact errors can cause conspicuous artifacts such as floating and interpenetration. Prior methods mitigate these issues using explicit contact cues or implicit grasp priors, but typically rely on multi stage pipelines and fail to model temporally evolving contact. We present JointHOI, a single stage diffusion framework that jointly generates 3D hand object motion and dynamic, distance based contact maps from text. By treating contact as an auxiliary inner modality, joint generation enables the model to learn contact motion coupling during training. At inference, contact guided sampling enforces consistency between generated contact maps and motion implied geometry, improving temporal stability and reducing penetration and floating. Experiments on GRAB and ARCTIC demonstrate consistent improvements in text adherence and physical plausibility over prior methods.

AI.tldr: JointHOI is a single-stage diffusion framework that jointly generates 3D hand-object motion and dynamic contact maps from text, treating contact as an auxiliary inner modality to improve physical plausibility by reducing penetration and floating artifacts.
AI.motivation: Existing HOI generation methods produce conspicuous artifacts like floating and interpenetration due to small contact errors, and prior approaches rely on multi-stage pipelines that fail to model temporally evolving contact.
AI.method: A single-stage diffusion framework that jointly generates 3D hand-object motion and dynamic distance-based contact maps, treating contact as an auxiliary inner modality. Contact-guided sampling at inference enforces consistency between generated contact maps and motion-impled geometry.
AI.result: Consistent improvements in text adherence and physical plausibility over prior methods on GRAB and ARCTIC datasets.
AI.conclusion: Jointly modeling contact as an inner modality within a single-stage diffusion framework improves temporal stability and reduces penetration and floating in HOI generation.

title: SkillCoach: Self-Evolving Rubrics for Evaluating and Enhancing Agentic Skill-Use
