AI.conclusion: The proposed method enables accurate, temporally consistent 4D whole-heart mesh reconstruction from sparse cine MRI and supports downstream proof-of-concept electrophysiological simulation.

title: Coding-agents can replicate scientific machine learning papers
summary: Scientific machine learning papers typically make computational claims, e.g., that the relative mean square error is less than 5% or that the 95% predictive credible interval covers the test data. A coding agent can be prompted to replicate those claims from paper materials alone, but the prompt does not by itself reliably preserve progress or check whether generated evidence supports the paper's claims. We introduce Paper-replication, a workflow that makes each selected paper claim a target with recorded evidence, and implement it as a coding-agent skill. The workflow makes the agent record those targets, reconstruct the paper's method, run computational experiments, link generated outputs to provenance and comparisons with the paper's claims, record where matched evidence appears in the replication report, and pass validation checks before completion. We evaluate Paper-replication on twelve independent runs across four scientific machine learning papers. All twelve workspaces pass the completion gate, and all 158 recorded targets are matched with report coverage. Even in this completed workspace state, repeated runs differ in how papers are divided into targets, in numerical fidelity to the source papers, in elapsed replication time, in the number of intermediate executions replaced before final evidence is accepted, and in the rules used to accept evidence. Paper-replication makes completion depend on workspace evidence and validation checks rather than on the agent's final message.

AI.tldr: Paper-replication is a coding-agent workflow that converts computational claims from scientific ML papers into verifiable targets with recorded evidence, ensuring replication validity through provenance tracking, validation checks, and evidence-report matching.
AI.motivation: Standard prompting of coding agents to replicate paper claims does not reliably preserve progress or verify whether generated evidence actually supports the paper's original claims, creating a reproducibility gap in scientific ML research.
AI.method: The workflow: (1) selects paper claims as recorded targets, (2) reconstructs the paper's method, (3) runs computational experiments, (4) links outputs to provenance, (5) compares with the paper's claims, (6) records where matched evidence appears in the replication report, and (7) passes validation checks before completion.
AI.result: Evaluated on 12 runs across 4 scientific ML papers: all workspaces passed the completion gate, all 158 targets matched with report coverage. However, runs varied in target decomposition, numerical fidelity, elapsed time, number of intermediate executions replaced, and evidence acceptance rules.
AI.conclusion: Paper-replication shifts completion criteria from the agent's final message to concrete workspace evidence and validation checks, providing a more reliable framework for automated paper replication.

title: Conditional Co-Ablation: Recovering Self-Repair Backups in Transformer Circuits
summary: Mechanistic interpretability often relies on component-level interventions to discover how a model produces a behavior. This guides attribution, capability knockout, and model pruning downstream to operate by scoring each unit by the effect of ablation in isolation. Such first-order scoring is natural when component importance is additive, but becomes misleading when a transformer self-repairs: after a primary component is removed, a dormant backup can take over, muting the primary's measured effect while the backup itself appears irrelevant on the intact model. We recast this failure as a recovery task, conditional circuit completion, and introduce Conditional Co-Ablation (CoAx), a label-free, output-grounded score that asks how much each remaining unit's ablation effect grows once a primary set has been removed. This conditional growth exposes the second-order interaction that single-unit scores discard. On the GPT-2-small IOI circuit, CoAx raises backup-head recovery from 0.33 to 0.91 ROC-AUC, outperforming all baselines, including self-repair-aware gradient scores (best 0.82); counterfactual patching verifies that the recovered heads causally carry the repair. The same label-free procedure transfers to induction across eight models. Beyond discovery, the recovered backups correct self-repair-masked attribution, identify the components required for capability knockout, and yield repair-aware structured pruning scaling from 124M to 7B. Component importance is therefore not merely an isolated-unit property: in robust circuits, the components that matter can become visible only under the interventions that make them necessary.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Conditional Co-Ablation (CoAx), a method that measures how ablation of one component increases the importance of others, revealing backup components that self-repair mechanisms mask in standard single-unit ablation scoring. CoAx significantly outperforms baselines on GPT-2-small's IOI circuit and transfers across models up to 7B parameters.
AI.motivation: Standard component-level importance scoring (ablation in isolation) fails when models exhibit self-repair: removing a primary component makes a dormant backup take over, hiding the primary's true importance while the backup appears irrelevant in the intact model. This creates misleading attributions for mechanistic interpretability, capability knockout, and pruning.
AI.method: Conditional Co-Ablation (CoAx) computes a label-free, output-grounded score by measuring how much each remaining unit's ablation effect grows after a primary set has been removed, capturing second-order interactions that single-unit scoring discards. This reframes the problem as conditional circuit completion—a recovery task.
AI.result: On GPT-2-small IOI circuit, CoAx achieves 0.91 ROC-AUC for backup-head recovery (vs. 0.33 baseline, 0.82 best gradient-based). Recovered heads are causally verified via counterfactual patching. The method transfers to induction across 8 models and scales from 124M to 7B parameters, improving attribution, capability knockout targeting, and structured pruning.
AI.conclusion: Component importance is not an isolated-unit property; in robust circuits, the components that truly matter become visible only under interventions that make them necessary. Self-repair-aware scoring like CoAx is essential for accurate mechanistic understanding.

title: A$^{2}$utoLPBench: An Auto-Generated, Agent-Friendly LP Benchmark via Inverse-KKT Construction
summary: Most LP-from-text benchmarks are static datasets of word problems written and labeled by hand. Once such a dataset is released, its size is fixed, its difficulty is fixed, and every problem can leak into the training data of future LLMs. We present \textbf{A$^{2}$utoLPBench}, a benchmark for testing LLM-driven agents on linear programming problems written in plain text. We first pick a feasible point and dual, then write down a problem for which that point is optimal and the objective value is known. The answer is known by construction, with no solver call and no human annotator. The evaluation environment bundles a reference solver-critic baseline and a Docker image whose usage instructions are written for an LLM-driven agent to read. With these in place, any agent can run the benchmark and get a calibrated score with one command. Because the benchmark is a generator rather than a fixed dataset, it has properties no fixed dataset can match: an unlimited supply of fresh problems, a difficulty knob set by $(n,m)$, ground-truth answers correct by construction, low LLM-side cost per problem relative to human authoring, repeatable scores across independent batches, and resistance to training-data leakage when fresh post-cutoff seed ranges are used.

AI.tldr: A2utoLPBench is a programmatic benchmark for LLM-driven agents on linear programming word problems, generating unlimited fresh problems with known answers by construction, bypassing human annotation and solver calls.
AI.motivation: Existing LP-from-text benchmarks are static, hand-labeled datasets with fixed size, fixed difficulty, and vulnerability to training-data leakage into LLMs.
AI.method: The benchmark generates problems by first picking a feasible point and dual, then constructing a problem where that point is optimal with a known objective value. It includes a Docker-based evaluation environment with a solver-critic baseline and instructions for LLM agents.
AI.result: The generator yields unlimited fresh problems, adjustable difficulty via (n,m), ground-truth answers correct by construction, low cost per problem, repeatable scores, and resistance to data leakage via fresh seed ranges.
AI.conclusion: The generator-based approach overcomes fundamental limitations of static datasets, offering a scalable, leakage-resistant, and calibrated benchmark for evaluating LLM agents on LP problems.

title: Hybrid quantum-classical neural network for sentiment analysis
summary: Quantum machine learning has recently emerged as a promising paradigm that leverages the expressive power of quantum circuits to address complex learning tasks. In this work, we investigate the applicability of hybrid quantum-classical neural networks to sentiment analysis, a central problem in natural language processing. We focus on a dataset of tweets related to COVID-19, where the textual content is vectorized using TF-IDF and fed into both classical feedforward networks and hybrid architectures incorporating parameterized quantum circuits. Our results show that hybrid models can achieve accuracy comparable to the classical baseline, while exhibiting distinct learning dynamics, especially in terms of validation loss and accuracy, that suggest a richer representational capacity. Moreover, when applying transfer learning to an SMS spam classification task, the hybrid models consistently outperform the classical counterpart, achieving an accuracy increase of 15 percentage points (from 66% to 81%) on the spam class, demonstrating enhanced generalization. These findings highlight the feasibility of employing QML for natural language processing and point toward the potential advantages of hybrid models as quantum hardware continues to advance.

AI.tldr: This paper explores hybrid quantum-classical neural networks for sentiment analysis on COVID-19 tweets, showing comparable accuracy to classical models with richer learning dynamics, and achieves a 15 percentage point improvement (66% to 81%) on SMS spam classification via transfer learning, demonstrating enhanced generalization.
AI.motivation: To investigate the applicability of hybrid quantum-classical neural networks to sentiment analysis, a central problem in NLP, and to demonstrate the feasibility of QML for text classification tasks.
AI.method: TF-IDF vectorization of COVID-19 tweet data; comparison between classical feedforward networks and hybrid architectures incorporating parameterized quantum circuits; transfer learning applied to SMS spam classification.
AI.result: Hybrid models achieve accuracy comparable to classical baselines with distinct learning dynamics; in transfer learning to SMS spam classification, hybrid models outperform classical counterparts by 15 percentage points (from 66% to 81%) on the spam class.
AI.conclusion: Hybrid quantum-classical models are feasible for NLP tasks, offer richer representational capacity and improved generalization, and show promise as quantum hardware advances.

title: Assessing VLM Reliability for Medical Image Quality Evaluation Under Corruption and Bias
summary: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are increasingly applied in medical tasks such as pathology description, report generation, and visual question answering. Medical Image Quality Assessment (MIQA) supports diagnostic accuracy and patient safety by determining whether images meet the standards required for clinical decision-making. Automating MIQA with VLMs may reduce workload, but their behavior under real-world conditions, where images may be degraded or textual context may affect judgments, should be further explored before deployment. We benchmark VLMs on medical image quality using the MediMeta-C dataset zero-shot across seven corruption types and five severity levels. We evaluate sensitivity to degradation patterns, the effect of corruptions on embedding geometry, and whether textual attributes (demographics, expertise, infrastructure, institution) alter scores. Across 16 VLMs and seven modalities, pixelation produced the largest score reductions (mean -20.58%, up to -34.4% for OCT), whereas brightness had limited effect (-0.81%). Embedding displacement was associated with score changes. Same-family models showed correlations of 0.67-0.83; some produced increases up to +31% for corrupted mammography. Textual attributes affected scores: institutional prestige raised them +17.15%, and equipment age lowered them -14.7%. The largest changes were +95.62% (InternVL-8B) and -37.7% (MedGemma). Current VLMs show limitations for medical image quality assessment. Pixelation, a privacy-preserving transformation, reduces performance, indicating a trade-off between patient privacy and reliability. Sensitivity to contextual metadata indicates limited objectivity and marks metadata as a privacy and bias source. Privacy protection and objective quality assessment are related requirements for use.

AI.tldr: VLMs used for Medical Image Quality Assessment show significant limitations: pixelation reduces scores by up to -34.4%, while textual metadata (e.g., institutional prestige +17.15%, equipment age -14.7%) biases judgments, indicating a trade-off between privacy protection and objective quality assessment.
AI.motivation: Medical Image Quality Assessment (MIQA) is critical for clinical decision-making, and automating it with VLMs could reduce workload. However, the behavior of VLMs under real-world degraded conditions and the influence of textual context on their judgments must be explored before safe deployment.
AI.method: Benchmarked 16 VLMs zero-shot on the MediMeta-C dataset across seven corruption types (five severity levels) and seven modalities. Evaluated sensitivity to degradation patterns, embedding geometry changes, and the effect of textual attributes (demographics, expertise, infrastructure, institution) on quality scores.
AI.result: Pixelation caused the largest score reductions (mean -20.58%, up to -34.4% for OCT); brightness had minimal effect (-0.81%). Textual attributes biased scores: institutional prestige raised scores +17.15%, equipment age lowered them -14.7%. Same-family model correlations: 0.67-0.83. Some models showed +31% increases for corrupted mammography.
AI.conclusion: Current VLMs are unreliable for MIQA. Pixelation (a privacy-preserving transformation) degrades performance, creating a trade-off between patient privacy and reliability. Sensitivity to textual metadata indicates limited objectivity, marking metadata as both a privacy and bias source.

title: A rubric-based controlled comparison of frontier language models on expert-authored clinical reasoning tasks
summary: Multiple-choice medical benchmarks are increasingly saturated, and recent rubric-based evaluations such as HealthBench have shown that open-ended clinical performance is far from solved - its "Hard" subset top score remains 32%. We present a small, deliberately difficult evaluation dataset of five clinician-authored clinical scenarios spanning four specialties (anaesthesia, internal/family medicine, emergency medicine, and obstetrics), each accompanied by an atomic, weighted, MECE rubric (25-62 criteria per task; 184 criteria total) authored from a clinician-drafted golden answer. We evaluate three frontier models: GPT 5.4, Claude Opus 4.7, and Gemini 3.1 Pro. Mean rubric pass rates were 0.47 (Claude), 0.39 (GPT), and 0.37 (Gemini). The central finding is an inversion of clinical priority: the highest-weighted (weight-5, critical) criteria passed at only 32.4-41.7%, while low-stakes weight-1 criteria passed at 80-90%. 56 of 108 critical (weight-5) criteria (52%) were satisfied by no model. Three LLM autoraters reproduced expert met/not-met labels on 92.8-94.7% of 552 graded criteria. We position this as a methods-and-preliminary-findings contribution: the five tasks demonstrate a scalable, defensible pipeline ready to develop into a large-scale benchmark.

AI.tldr: A small, deliberately difficult clinical evaluation dataset (5 scenarios, 184 criteria) shows frontier LLMs fail critically: highest-weighted criteria pass at only 32-42% while low-stakes criteria pass at 80-90%, with 52% of critical criteria satisfied by no model.
AI.motivation: Multiple-choice medical benchmarks are saturated, and open-ended clinical performance remains unsolved (HealthBench "Hard" subset top score: 32%). A small, difficult, clinician-authored evaluation is needed to expose persistent gaps.
AI.method: Five clinician-authored clinical scenarios across four specialties with atomic, weighted, MECE rubrics (25-62 criteria per task, 184 total) authored from a clinician-drafted golden answer. Three frontier models (GPT 5.4, Claude Opus 4.7, Gemini 3.1 Pro) evaluated; three LLM autoraters used for reproducibility.
AI.result: Mean rubric pass rates: Claude 0.47, GPT 0.39, Gemini 0.37. Critical weight-5 criteria passed at only 32.4-41.7%, while low-stakes weight-1 criteria passed at 80-90%. 56/108 (52%) critical criteria satisfied by no model. LLM autoraters reproduced expert labels on 92.8-94.7% of 552 graded criteria.
AI.conclusion: The central finding is an inversion of clinical priority: models fail on the most clinically important criteria while passing trivial ones. The five tasks demonstrate a scalable, defensible pipeline for developing a large-scale benchmark.

title: A More Accurate Algorithm Comparison through A/B Testing using Offline Evaluation Methods
summary: A/B testing is the gold standard for selecting the better algorithm in online services. While offline evaluation has attracted attention as a safer alternative due to the high experimental costs and the potential risk of degrading user experience and revenue in A/B testing, it is widely recognized that the estimation accuracy of offline evaluation is substantially lower. As a result, final selection decisions are typically made through A/B testing. Contrary to this conventional view, we reveal a counterintuitive phenomenon in which A/B testing can produce a higher algorithm selection error rate than offline evaluation. This occurs because the sample mean estimator used in A/B testing does not induce positive correlation, which is crucial for reducing critical selection errors, namely underestimating the truly superior algorithm and overestimating the truly inferior one. In contrast, offline evaluation methods unintentionally generate this beneficial correlation by relying on shared offline data when estimating and comparing the performance of multiple algorithms. Building on this insight, we propose an estimator that intentionally induces positive correlation to improve algorithm selection in A/B testing. The key idea is to introduce a hypothetical middle algorithm and to estimate the performance difference between algorithms A, M, and B in a stepwise manner using shared data at each step. This approach enables the application of offline evaluation techniques in each step, thereby inducing positive correlation and reducing critical selection errors. Furthermore, we derive the optimal middle algorithm regarding the resulting variance and analyze its advantages over existing methods through bias-variance analysis. Experiments on real-world data demonstrate that our estimator achieves the same selection error rate as existing approaches while using only one half of the A/B testing data.

AI.tldr: This paper challenges the conventional view that A/B testing is always superior to offline evaluation for algorithm selection. It reveals that A/B testing can have higher selection error rates because its sample mean estimator lacks positive correlation. Offline evaluation unintentionally induces beneficial positive correlation via shared data. The authors propose a new estimator that intentionally induces positive correlation by introducing a hypothetical middle algorithm and using stepwise estimation, achieving the same selection error rate with half the A/B testing data.
AI.motivation: A/B testing, while considered the gold standard, has high experimental costs and risks of degrading user experience/revenue. Offline evaluation is safer but believed to have lower accuracy. The authors aim to challenge this trade-off and improve algorithm selection in A/B testing.
AI.method: The authors introduce a hypothetical middle algorithm M and estimate performance differences between A, M, and B in a stepwise manner using shared data at each step. This induces positive correlation, reducing critical selection errors. They derive the optimal middle algorithm via bias-variance analysis.
AI.result: Experiments on real-world data show the proposed estimator achieves the same selection error rate as existing approaches while using only one half of the A/B testing data.
AI.conclusion: Contrary to conventional wisdom, A/B testing can produce higher selection error rates than offline evaluation due to lack of positive correlation. Intentionally inducing positive correlation via a stepwise estimator with a hypothetical middle algorithm can significantly improve data efficiency in A/B testing.

title: MolSight: A Graph-Aware Vision-Language Model for Unified Chemical Image Understanding
summary: Using molecular large language models (LLMs) as a unified framework for understanding molecular structures and functions is emerging as a new trend in tasks such as molecular design and drug discovery. However, these models struggle to fully capture the visual representation of molecular structures, limiting their potential. While existing molecular vision-language models (VLMs) show promise, they still face challenges in structural alignment and lack the necessary topological modeling for accurate molecular understanding. To address this, we propose MolSight, a graph-aware vision-language model framework designed to enhance the understanding of molecular images by VLMs. MolSight integrates a Molecular Topology Module to inject chemical-bond adjacency information into vision tokens, and a Molecular Grounding Module to align visual features with chemical symbolic semantics. Our experiments demonstrate that MolSight significantly outperforms existing VLMs, molecular LLMs, and specialized tools across multiple chemical visual understanding tasks, achieving a new level of molecular image reasoning.

AI.tldr: MolSight is a graph-aware vision-language model framework that integrates molecular topology and grounding modules to improve molecular image understanding, outperforming existing VLMs, molecular LLMs, and specialized tools across multiple chemical visual understanding tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing molecular LLMs fail to fully capture visual representations of molecular structures, and current molecular VLMs struggle with structural alignment and lack topological modeling, limiting accurate molecular understanding.
AI.method: MolSight integrates a Molecular Topology Module (injects chemical-bond adjacency information into vision tokens) and a Molecular Grounding Module (aligns visual features with chemical symbolic semantics) within a vision-language model framework.
AI.result: MolSight significantly outperforms existing VLMs, molecular LLMs, and specialized tools across multiple chemical visual understanding tasks, achieving a new level of molecular image reasoning.
AI.conclusion: Graph-aware vision-language modeling with explicit topological and grounding modules enhances VLMs' capability to understand molecular structures from images.

title: UA-ChatDev: Uncertainty-Aware Multi-Agent Collaboration for Reliable Software Development
summary: Software development is a complex task that demands cooperation among agents with diverse roles. Large language models (LLMs) have enabled autonomous multi-agent software development frameworks that leverage role-based collaboration to automate requirements analysis, coding, testing, and refinement. However, existing approaches typically assume that intermediate agent outputs are equally reliable, leaving them vulnerable to hallucination propagation, where incorrect decisions generated in early development phases are transferred to downstream agents and negatively impact final software quality. To address this challenge, we propose UA-ChatDev, an uncertainty-aware multi-agent software development framework that integrates uncertainty quantification into agent interactions. It introduces a lightweight uncertainty estimation mechanism based on token-level log probabilities to assess the confidence of agent responses and employs phase-aware threshold calibration to selectively trigger retrieval-based verification when uncertainty exceeds acceptable levels. Extensive experiments on the SRDD benchmark demonstrate that UA-ChatDev consistently outperforms existing single-agent and multi-agent software development frameworks across completeness, executability, consistency, and overall quality metrics. Further ablation studies and communication analyses verify that uncertainty-aware interactions enhance code execution reliability.

AI.tldr: UA-ChatDev is an uncertainty-aware multi-agent framework that quantifies token-level confidence in LLM outputs to detect and mitigate hallucination propagation across development phases, outperforming existing approaches on software quality metrics.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-agent software development frameworks assume all intermediate agent outputs are equally reliable, making them vulnerable to hallucination propagation—incorrect decisions from early phases transferred downstream degrade final software quality.
AI.method: UA-ChatDev integrates uncertainty quantification via token-level log probability estimation, applies phase-aware threshold calibration to detect uncertain responses, and triggers retrieval-based verification when uncertainty exceeds acceptable levels.
AI.result: On the SRDD benchmark, UA-ChatDev outperforms single-agent and multi-agent baselines across completeness, executability, consistency, and overall quality. Ablation and communication analyses confirm that uncertainty-aware interactions improve code execution reliability.
AI.conclusion: Integrating uncertainty quantification into multi-agent software development frameworks effectively mitigates hallucination propagation and improves software quality, demonstrating the value of confidence-aware agent collaboration.

title: Probabilistic Low-Voltage Peak Load Forecasting with Time Series Foundation Models Evaluated on Application-Oriented Metrics
comment: A poster abstract of this publication will be available at the 15th DACH+ Conference on Energy Informatics (2026 in Linz, Austria)
summary: Low-voltage load forecasting is an important component in current and future energy systems with a high degree of electrification and decentralized generation. However, current forecasting methods require significant manual effort, often lack uncertainty estimation and proper peak prediction, and they are often not adequately evaluated in terms of grid requirements. In the present study, we provide an extensive evaluation of short-term net load forecasts of 200 real-world low-voltage feeders with a focus on the rapidly evolving time series foundation models. Our study compares Chronos-Bolt, Chronos-2 and TabPFN-TS to six baseline models and demonstrates superior performance, in particular for Chronos-2. An ablation study, in which weather covariates are omitted, shows that time series foundation models adapt to increased uncertainty, despite the importance of weather information. A novel application-oriented metric links the model's forecasting capabilities in peak prediction to the trade-off in grid asset planning and operation between cost reduction and minimizing the risk of failure.

AI.tldr: This study evaluates short-term net load forecasts for 200 real-world low-voltage feeders, comparing time series foundation models (Chronos-Bolt, Chronos-2, TabPFN-TS) against six baselines. Chronos-2 shows superior performance, and a novel application-oriented metric connects peak prediction accuracy to grid asset planning trade-offs.
AI.motivation: Low-voltage load forecasting is critical for electrified, decentralized energy systems, but current methods require manual effort, lack uncertainty estimation, fail at peak prediction, and are inadequately evaluated for grid requirements.
AI.method: Extensive evaluation of short-term net load forecasts on 200 real-world low-voltage feeders, comparing time series foundation models (Chronos-Bolt, Chronos-2, TabPFN-TS) to six baseline models, with an ablation study omitting weather covariates and a novel application-oriented metric linking peak prediction to grid asset planning trade-offs.
AI.result: Time series foundation models, especially Chronos-2, demonstrate superior forecasting performance. The ablation study shows these models adapt to increased uncertainty even without weather covariates. The novel metric connects peak prediction to cost-failure risk trade-offs.
AI.conclusion: Time series foundation models, particularly Chronos-2, outperform traditional baselines for low-voltage load forecasting. The proposed application-oriented metric provides actionable insights for grid asset planning decisions.

title: Open-Weather Robust 3D Detection via Dual-Critic Diffusion Alignment
summary: Robust 3D object detection under adverse weather remains a critical hurdle for autonomous driving. Despite progress with LiDAR-4D radar fusion, most methods are constrained by a closed-world assumption, implicitly requiring training and test weather to align in both type and severity. This premise fails in practice: the open-ended nature of weather, and even variations within a single type like rain, cause dramatically different LiDAR degradation patterns, leading to significant performance drops in unseen conditions. To address this, we present Dual-Critic Guided Diffusion Alignment (DCDA), a weather-agnostic framework that learns to recover degraded LiDAR features toward a clean manifold. Rather than modeling specific weather types, DCDA employs a 4D radar-conditioned diffusion process to progressively refine features, guided by two complementary critics. (i) A detection-guided critic, anchored by a pre-trained clean-weather model, ensures that the refined features retain object-level discriminability and localization accuracy. (ii) A weather adversarial critic enforces holistic distributional consistency with clean-weather representations. By aligning features through semantic and distributional constraints rather than explicit weather modeling, DCDA generalizes effectively to unseen weather types and severities without requiring paired data or weather labels. We further introduce a structured open-weather benchmark with held-out type-severity combinations and extensive experiments verify DCDA's advantages.

AI.tldr: DCDA is a weather-agnostic framework using dual-critic guided diffusion to align degraded LiDAR features with clean-weather representations via 4D radar conditioning, enabling robust 3D object detection under unseen weather conditions without paired data or weather labels.
AI.motivation: Existing LiDAR-4D radar fusion methods assume training and test weather conditions align (closed-world), but real-world weather is open-ended with varying degradation patterns even within the same type (e.g., rain intensity), causing severe performance drops under unseen conditions.
AI.method: A 4D radar-conditioned diffusion process refines degraded LiDAR features, guided by two critics: (1) a detection-guided critic that preserves object-level discriminability via a pre-trained clean-weather model, and (2) a weather adversarial critic that enforces distributional consistency with clean representations.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on a structured open-weather benchmark with held-out type-severity combinations demonstrate DCDA's generalization advantages over existing methods.
AI.conclusion: DCDA effectively generalizes to unseen weather types and severities through semantic and distributional alignment rather than explicit weather modeling, without requiring paired data or weather labels.

title: Criticality-Based Guard Rail Validation for AI Agent Decisions in Autonomous Telecom Networks
summary: The evolution toward fully autonomous telecommunications networks (Autonomous Network Levels 4-5) requires AI/ML agents to make real-time network decisions without human intervention. However, no standardized runtime mechanism exists to intercept and validate individual inference outputs before they trigger live network state changes, creating risks of erroneous autonomous decisions. This paper proposes the Guard Rail Validation (GRV) framework, a standardizable runtime architecture for intercepting and validating AI-driven decisions before execution. The framework evaluates decisions across multiple weighted dimensions -- including action scope, action type, service criticality, agent autonomy level, reversibility, and temporal behavioural patterns -- to determine a criticality level. Based on this level, graduated validation mechanisms are applied: execute-with-logging, bounds checking, independent agent validation, or multi-agent consensus. The framework additionally provides cross-agent conflict detection with criticality-weighted priority resolution and runtime conformance logging for regulatory compliance (e.g., EU AI Act Article 14). We present the architecture, algorithmic procedures, O-RAN deployment model, and evaluate threat coverage against known AI/ML attacks in telecommunications.

AI.tldr: Proposes the Guard Rail Validation (GRV) framework, a standardized runtime architecture for intercepting and validating AI/ML inference outputs before they trigger live network state changes in autonomous telecommunications networks (Levels 4-5). It evaluates decisions across multiple weighted dimensions, applies graduated validation mechanisms, and provides cross-agent conflict detection and runtime conformance logging.
AI.motivation: No standardized runtime mechanism exists to intercept and validate individual AI/ML inference outputs before they trigger live network state changes in autonomous telecom networks, creating risks of erroneous autonomous decisions.
AI.method: The GRV framework evaluates decisions across weighted dimensions (action scope, action type, service criticality, agent autonomy level, reversibility, temporal patterns) to determine a criticality level, then applies graduated validation: execute-with-logging, bounds checking, independent agent validation, or multi-agent consensus. Includes cross-agent conflict detection with criticality-weighted priority resolution and runtime conformance logging.
AI.result: Presents the architecture, algorithmic procedures, O-RAN deployment model, and evaluates threat coverage against known AI/ML attacks in telecommunications.
AI.conclusion: The GRV framework provides a standardizable runtime safety layer for autonomous telecom networks, enabling safe AI-driven decision-making with graduated validation, conflict resolution, and regulatory compliance support (e.g., EU AI Act Article 14).

title: Do Newer Lightweight CNNs Perform Better Under Resource Constraints? A Controlled Multigenerational Study of Architecture, Initialization, Training Budget, and Efficiency
summary: Newer lightweight convolutional neural networks are often presented as improving predictive performance and deployment efficiency, but such claims require controlled evaluation. This study compares nine lightweight CNN model packages across CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny ImageNet under a shared downstream protocol. We report top-1 accuracy, macro F1, top-5 accuracy, parameter count, FP32 storage, GMACs, batch-size-1 latency on an NVIDIA L4 and AMD Ryzen 5 5500U CPU, peak PyTorch CUDA allocated tensor memory, and point estimate Pareto frontiers. EfficientNetV2-S achieves the highest observed top-1 accuracy on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 at 97.57% and 86.98%, while RepViT-M1.0 leads Tiny ImageNet at 79.87%. EfficientNet-B0 remains within 0.22, 0.85, and 1.79 percentage points of the best result on the three datasets while using approximately 79% fewer parameters and 86% fewer GMACs than EfficientNetV2-S. It also appears on every evaluated accuracy and resource Pareto frontier, making it the most consistently competitive intermediate-budget option. MobileNetV3-Small has the lowest GMAC count, is the fastest model under both CPU thread settings, and records higher observed accuracy than MobileNetV4-Conv-S on all three datasets. Under random initialization, it leads MobileNetV4-Conv-S by 2.55, 1.76, and 0.99 points, with paired test-set intervals excluding zero for the fixed trained models. EfficientNet-B0 remains 3.29, 10.10, and 17.54 points below its pretrained counterpart after 100 epochs of scratch training, despite requiring about five times the recorded training time. SqueezeNet1.1 has the fewest parameters and lowest peak CUDA allocation, but substantially weaker accuracy. Latency rankings differ sharply between the L4 and CPU environments, showing that GMACs alone do not predict measured inference performance. Overall, newer designs provide selective rather than universal gains

AI.tldr: A controlled benchmark of nine lightweight CNN models across three datasets finds that EfficientNetV2-S leads in accuracy on CIFAR-10/100, RepViT-M1.0 leads on Tiny ImageNet, but EfficientNet-B0 is the most consistently Pareto-optimal across accuracy-resource trade-offs; newer models offer selective improvements rather than universal gains.
AI.motivation: Many lightweight CNN papers claim improved predictive performance and deployment efficiency, but these claims are often tested under inconsistent protocols, lacking rigorous controlled comparison across models, datasets, and hardware.
AI.method: Nine lightweight CNN model packages were compared across CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny ImageNet under a shared downstream protocol. Evaluation metrics include top-1 accuracy, macro F1, top-5 accuracy, parameter count, FP32 storage, GMACs, batch-size-1 latency on NVIDIA L4 GPU and AMD Ryzen 5 5500U CPU, peak PyTorch CUDA memory, and point estimate Pareto frontiers.
AI.result: EfficientNetV2-S achieves highest top-1 accuracy on CIFAR-10 (97.57%) and CIFAR-100 (86.98%); RepViT-M1.0 leads Tiny ImageNet (79.87%). EfficientNet-B0 is within 0.22–1.79 points of the best while using ~79% fewer parameters and ~86% fewer GMACs than EfficientNetV2-S, appearing on all Pareto frontiers. MobileNetV3-Small has lowest GMACs, fastest CPU/GPU latency, and outperforms MobileNetV4-Conv-S on all datasets. SqueezeNet1.1 has fewest params and lowest peak memory but weak accuracy. Latency rankings differ sharply between L4 GPU and CPU environments.
AI.conclusion: Newer lightweight CNN designs provide selective rather than universal gains; EfficientNet-B0 remains the most consistently competitive intermediate-budget option across accuracy and resource metrics. GMACs alone do not reliably predict measured inference performance, as hardware-specific latency rankings diverge significantly.

title: Understanding Geometric Representations in Self-Supervised Vision Transformers via Subspace Intervention
summary: We introduce a controlled subspace intervention framework to investigate how self-supervised Vision Transformers (ViTs) encode dense geometric information. While linear probing is widely used to assess geometric representations, it treats features as a black box, failing to disentangle the underlying topology. To address this issue, we decompose the weights of converged linear probes to isolate the low-rank subspaces containing explicit geometric signals using Singular Value Decomposition (SVD). Our perspective yields three key insights: (1) Pre-training objectives determine how features are encoded. DINOv2 aligns spatial features for efficient linear extraction, while Masked Autoencoders (MAE) tend to disperse these signals, requiring a broader spatial context. (2) Explicit geometric representations are highly compressible, suggesting dense predictive heads could potentially be constrained to low-rank subspaces with minimal performance loss. (3) The layer-wise task affinity suggests that geometric precision peaks at intermediate layers before yielding to semantic abstraction in the final layers. By connecting internal encoding mechanics with downstream performance, these findings provide a basis for effective feature selection and lightweight decoder design. The source code is available at https://github.com/Zhou-Weichen/Geosubprobe.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a controlled subspace intervention framework using SVD to analyze how self-supervised Vision Transformers encode dense geometric information, revealing that pre-training objectives affect feature encoding (DINOv2 aligns features, MAE disperses them), geometric representations are highly compressible into low-rank subspaces, and geometric precision peaks at intermediate layers.
AI.motivation: Existing linear probing methods treat features as a black box and fail to disentangle the underlying topology of geometric representations in self-supervised ViTs.
AI.method: Decompose weights of converged linear probes using Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) to isolate low-rank subspaces containing explicit geometric signals in Vision Transformers.
AI.result: (1) DINOv2 aligns spatial features for efficient linear extraction while MAE disperses signals requiring broader spatial context; (2) Explicit geometric representations are highly compressible to low-rank subspaces; (3) Geometric precision peaks at intermediate layers before transitioning to semantic abstraction in final layers.
AI.conclusion: Connecting internal encoding mechanics with downstream performance enables effective feature selection and lightweight decoder design for dense geometric tasks.

title: Purified OPSD: On-Policy Self-Distillation Without Losing How to Think
summary: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) has emerged as a promising paradigm for improving LLM reasoning, where a privileged teacher with access to reference solutions provides token-level supervision on the student's own generated trajectories. However, we find that OPSD consistently fails on long chain-of-thought (long-CoT) reasoning models, yielding at best marginal gains while destabilizing the reflective reasoning capability these models depend on. Through a novel decomposition of the teacher's supervision signal, we identify the root cause: the teacher's supervision is dominated by a reference-induced component that drives rote memorization of reference-specific shortcuts, while the question-conditioned, inference-transferable component is ignored or actively opposed. Based on this diagnosis, we propose a two-step solution. First, we construct a reference-only teacher (the same model conditioned on the reference without the question) to isolate the non-transferable component of the supervision signal; the residual after subtracting this component captures the question-conditioned, inference-transferable correction. Second, we use pointwise mutual information (PMI) as the mechanism to transform this residual into a well-formed PMI target distribution that the student can directly distill from, filtering out the reference-induced shortcut. Experiments on four long-CoT models across two datasets demonstrate consistent improvements over both the base model and standard OPSD, while preserving the models' natural epistemic behavior throughout training.

AI.tldr: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) fails on long-CoT reasoning models because the teacher's supervision is dominated by a reference-induced component driving rote memorization rather than transferable reasoning. The paper proposes a two-step solution using reference-only teacher subtraction and PMI-based distillation, which consistently improves long-CoT models.
AI.motivation: OPSD has shown promise for improving LLM reasoning but consistently fails on long chain-of-thought reasoning models, often destabilizing their reflective reasoning capabilities. The paper aims to diagnose and fix this failure.
AI.method: (1) Decompose teacher supervision to identify reference-induced vs. question-conditioned components; (2) Construct a reference-only teacher to isolate and subtract the non-transferable component; (3) Use pointwise mutual information (PMI) to transform the residual into a well-formed target distribution for student distillation.
AI.result: Experiments on four long-CoT models across two datasets show consistent improvements over both the base model and standard OPSD, while preserving models' natural epistemic behavior.
AI.conclusion: The proposed PMI-based distillation with reference-only teacher subtraction effectively addresses the fundamental failure mode of OPSD on long-CoT models by filtering out reference-induced shortcuts and preserving transferable reasoning.

title: Liquid Latent State Dynamics for Interpretable Turbofan Degradation Modeling
summary: Multivariate time-series models for prognostics are often evaluated by point prediction accuracy, yet their internal states rarely expose a coherent degradation process. We study liquid neural networks as latent dynamics models for aircraft engine health monitoring on the C-MAPSS benchmark. The proposed model encodes a history window into a latent state, evolves that state with a liquid transition model, and decodes future sensor observations. To separate health evolution from operating-condition variation, the latent state is factorized into degradation and condition components. Remaining useful life, monotonic risk, and latent-consistency losses supervise the degradation component, while condition prediction and decorrelation losses discourage operating-condition leakage. Across FD001--FD004, the full disentangled model improves overall sensor forecasting RMSE from 0.2438 for a GRU baseline to 0.2266, with the largest gains on the multi-condition subsets FD002 and FD004. The learned degradation state also forms a clearer temporal degradation axis, reaching an average state-speed Spearman correlation of 0.5960. Direct remaining-useful-life regression remains stronger for the GRU baseline, indicating that the proposed representation is currently more effective as an interpretable world model for degradation dynamics than as a calibrated lifetime regressor. These results suggest that liquid latent dynamics can bridge predictive maintenance forecasting and inspectable health-state modeling.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a liquid neural network model with disentangled latent states (degradation and condition components) for aircraft engine prognostics on C-MAPSS, achieving better sensor forecasting and interpretable degradation dynamics than GRU baselines, though direct RUL regression remains stronger for the baseline.
AI.motivation: Multivariate time-series models for prognostics are often evaluated only on point prediction accuracy, yet their internal states rarely expose a coherent degradation process, motivating the need for interpretable latent dynamics models.
AI.method: The model uses liquid neural networks as latent dynamics: encodes a history window into latent state, evolves with liquid transition model, decodes future sensors. Latent states are factorized into degradation and condition components, supervised by RUL, monotonic risk, latent-consistency, condition prediction, and decorrelation losses.
AI.result: Full disentangled model improves sensor forecasting RMSE from 0.2438 (GRU) to 0.2266, with largest gains on multi-condition FD002/FD004. Degradation state achieves 0.5960 Spearman correlation. Direct RUL regression remains stronger for GRU baseline.
AI.conclusion: Liquid latent dynamics can bridge predictive maintenance forecasting and inspectable health-state modeling, though the representation is currently more effective as an interpretable world model than as a calibrated lifetime regressor.

title: Training-free Controllable Human Motion Generation under Heterogeneous Constraints
summary: Training-free controllable motion generation has attracted growing interest for enabling flexible constraint enforcement without constraint-specific training. However, existing training-free methods require constraints to be continuous objective-based with differentiable losses, while many real-world requirements are criterion-based and provide only discontinuous, sparse, or even black-box feedback. In this paper, we propose Motion-Inference-as-Control (MIC), the first training-free motion generation framework that handles both continuous objective-based and criterion-based motion constraints under a shared mechanism. The key idea is to cast diffusion-based motion generation as a stochastic control problem. This perspective not only provides principled and practically effective step-wise control laws that support criterion-based constraints without requiring differentiability and naturally accommodate objective-based constraints as a special case, but also motivates a control-oriented constraint coordination mechanism that adaptively balances and reconciles motion constraints during generation. Experiments across diverse constraint settings demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework.

AI.tldr: MIC is a training-free motion generation framework that unifies continuous objective-based and discontinuous criterion-based constraints by reformulating diffusion-based motion generation as a stochastic control problem, enabling step-wise control laws and adaptive constraint coordination without requiring differentiability.
AI.motivation: Existing training-free controllable motion generation methods can only handle continuous objective-based constraints with differentiable losses, but many real-world requirements are criterion-based with discontinuous, sparse, or black-box feedback. The authors aim to bridge this gap.
AI.method: The framework casts diffusion-based motion generation as a stochastic control problem, deriving step-wise control laws that support criterion-based constraints without differentiability, and introduces a control-oriented constraint coordination mechanism for adaptive balancing and reconciliation of multiple motion constraints.
AI.result: Experiments across diverse constraint settings demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework.
AI.conclusion: MIC offers a principled and unified approach to training-free controllable motion generation, handling both continuous and discontinuous constraints under a shared mechanism.

title: Copewell: A Multi-Agent Swarm Architecture for Equitable Mental Wellness Support
summary: Mental health disorders affect nearly one billion people globally, yet 75% of individuals in low- and middle-income countries receive no treatment due to workforce shortages, cost barriers, and stigma. Current AI-powered wellness solutions predominantly rely on single-mode conversational interfaces that suffer high abandonment rates and fail to provide measurable, immediate relief calibrated to users' dynamic emotional states. This paper presents Copewell, a novel multi-agent swarm system designed to expand access to mental wellness support through human-centered AI principles. Our architecture introduces three technical innovations: (1) a multi-source assessment framework integrating self-reported, physiological, and contextual data to mitigate algorithmic bias; (2) valence-arousal emotion mapping using Russell's Circumplex Model of Affect to route users to specialized AI agents; and (3) dual-mode intervention delivery combining conversational support with evidence-based sensory wellness protocols. We examine the sociotechnical design considerations underlying Copewell's development, including a privacy-first architecture, embedded ethical oversight through a dedicated Ethics Supervisor agent, and participatory design informed by mental health practitioners. Early practitioner engagement and beta deployment inform design decisions and identify directions for future empirical evaluation. This work contributes to responsible AI discourse by demonstrating how technical architecture can operationalize equity and safety principles from inception.

AI.tldr: Copewell is a multi-agent swarm system that expands access to mental wellness support through three innovations: multi-source assessment (self-reported, physiological, contextual data), valence-arousal emotion mapping using Russell's Circumplex Model, and dual-mode intervention (conversational + sensory wellness protocols), with privacy-first architecture and an Ethics Supervisor agent for responsible AI.
AI.motivation: Nearly one billion people globally suffer from mental health disorders, but 75% in low/middle-income countries receive no treatment due to workforce shortages, cost, and stigma. Existing AI wellness tools use single-mode conversational interfaces with high abandonment rates and fail to provide measurable, immediate relief adapted to dynamic emotional states.
AI.method: The paper presents Copewell's architecture with three technical innovations: (1) multi-source assessment framework (self-reported, physiological, contextual data) to reduce algorithmic bias; (2) valence-arousal emotion mapping via Russell's Circumplex Model for routing users to specialized AI agents; (3) dual-mode intervention delivery combining conversational support with evidence-based sensory wellness protocols. Sociotechnical design includes privacy-first architecture, an Ethics Supervisor agent, and participatory design with practitioners.
AI.result: Early practitioner engagement and beta deployment inform design decisions and identify directions for future empirical evaluation. The paper contributes to responsible AI discourse by demonstrating how technical architecture can operationalize equity and safety principles from inception.
AI.conclusion: Copewell demonstrates a multi-agent swarm approach to mental wellness that integrates multi-source assessment, emotion mapping, and dual-mode interventions within a privacy-first, ethically-governed framework, offering a pathway to scalable, equitable mental health support.

title: Fast and Accurate Anomaly Detection in Time Series
summary: Anomaly detection is a critical and evolving field in Machine Learning, with applications targeting different domains such as cybersecurity, finance, healthcare, manufacturing and IoT (Internet of Things) systems. Traditionally, anomaly detection algorithms have been designed using both supervised and unsupervised learning paradigms. The fundamental challenge in real-world anomaly detection scenarios is related to the inherent class imbalance (anomalies are typically rare) and, for supervised methods, to the scarcity of labelled anomalous data. Indeed, labelling is both expensive and time-consuming. Conversely unsupervised methods do not require labelling, but may suffer from high false positive rates when deployed in safety-critical applications. In this work we introduce a novel unsupervised algorithm for anomaly detection in time series based on the Haar discrete wavelet and a suitably designed $t$-test. We establish the theoretical foundation of the proposed $t$-test and, through extensive experimentation across 343 datasets, demonstrate that our algorithm outperforms state-of-the-art unsupervised and self-supervised benchmarks.

AI.tldr: Introduces a novel unsupervised anomaly detection algorithm for time series using Haar discrete wavelet transform and a custom t-test, outperforming state-of-the-art methods across 343 datasets.
AI.motivation: Anomaly detection faces challenges of class imbalance and scarcity of labeled data. Supervised methods suffer from expensive labeling, while unsupervised methods often have high false positive rates in safety-critical applications. The authors aim to address these limitations with a novel unsupervised approach.
AI.method: Proposes an unsupervised algorithm combining Haar discrete wavelet transform with a specially designed t-test for anomaly detection in time series data. The theoretical foundation of the t-test is established.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across 343 datasets demonstrate that the proposed algorithm outperforms state-of-the-art unsupervised and self-supervised benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: The novel wavelet-based unsupervised approach effectively addresses key challenges in anomaly detection (label scarcity, high false positive rates) and achieves superior performance over existing methods.

title: Mirror Illusion Art
comment: CVPR 2026 Highlight, also got an Efficient CVPR award
summary: Mirror Illusion Art is a novel reflection-conditioned 3D illusion where one object yields two target appearances (front and mirror). The task is formulated as inverse design from two target 2D images (front and mirror) to a printable 3D object with geometry and texture. Prior topology-driven and shadow-based approaches demand substantial manual effort, optimize shape only, and often yield non-smooth or incomplete geometry. To address these challenges, we propose AutoMIA, an automated Mirror Illusion Art design pipeline that jointly optimizes shape and color. To stabilize optimization and suppress artifacts, four mechanisms are introduced: (1) projection-alignment component (PAC) selection to reduce surface noise, (2) position-weighted adaptive (PWA) suppression for background noise, (3) internal voxel preservation (IVP) to prevent internal fractures, and (4) shape-color decoupled (SCD) optimization that balance shape and color optimization. AutoMIA generate diverse smooth Mirror Illusion artworks successfully both in the digital and physical world, with only around 76s design time and 2.6 GB memory on average using a single RTX 3090, advancing inverse graphics and computational design. Our code is available at https://github.com/zxp555/AutoMIA.

AI.tldr: AutoMIA is an automated pipeline for designing Mirror Illusion Art—3D objects that yield two distinct appearances when viewed directly versus in a mirror—by jointly optimizing shape and color, introducing four stabilization mechanisms to suppress artifacts, achieving smooth results in ~76s with 2.6GB memory on a single RTX 3090.
AI.motivation: Prior topology-driven and shadow-based approaches for Mirror Illusion Art require substantial manual effort, optimize shape only, and often produce non-smooth or incomplete geometry. The authors aim to automate the inverse design process from two target 2D images to a printable 3D object with both geometry and texture.
AI.method: AutoMIA jointly optimizes shape and color with four stabilization mechanisms: (1) projection-alignment component (PAC) selection to reduce surface noise, (2) position-weighted adaptive (PWA) suppression for background noise, (3) internal voxel preservation (IVP) to prevent internal fractures, and (4) shape-color decoupled (SCD) optimization to balance shape and color optimization.
AI.result: The method generates diverse smooth Mirror Illusion artworks successfully in both digital and physical domains, with approximately 76s design time and 2.6 GB memory usage on average using a single RTX 3090.
AI.conclusion: AutoMIA advances inverse graphics and computational design by providing an efficient, automated pipeline for reflection-conditioned 3D illusion creation with joint shape-color optimization.

title: AgenticSTS: A Bounded-Memory Testbed for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
summary: Memory for a long-horizon LLM agent is a contract about what each future decision is allowed to see. The simplest contract appends past observations, tool calls, and reflections to every prompt, which makes prior context easy to access but also turns it into a jumbled mixture in which the effect of any single memory component is hard to isolate. We introduce and instrument an alternative bounded contract: every decision is made from a fresh user message assembled by typed retrieval, with no raw cross-decision transcript appended. The prompt thus stays bounded across runs of any length, and any single layer can be ablated in isolation. We instantiate the contract in Slay the Spire 2, a closed-rule stochastic deck-building game whose runs require hundreds of tactical and strategic decisions. A public online benchmark of frontier LLMs on the same game reports zero wins at the lowest difficulty across five configurations, and the developer-reported human win rate at the same difficulty is 16%; the task is hard but not saturated. Within our harness, a fixed-A0 ablation shows the largest observed difference when triggered strategic skills are enabled: the no-store baseline wins 3/10 games and adding the skill layer 6/10. At this sample size the comparison is directional rather than statistically decisive (Fisher exact p\approx0.37); a cross-backbone probe and public accumulating-context baselines are reported as operational comparisons rather than controlled tests of the contract variable itself. We release a reproducible testbed: 298 completed trajectories with condition tags, frozen memory/skill snapshots, prompt records, and analysis scripts -- an agent design and a validated, reusable methodology for studying how explicit memory layers shape long-horizon LLM-agent decisions.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a bounded memory contract for long-horizon LLM agents using typed retrieval instead of appending raw transcripts, tested on Slay the Spire 2 where adding strategic skills improves win rate from 3/10 to 6/10, and releases a reproducible testbed of 298 trajectories.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon LLM agents suffer from unbounded, jumbled context when all past observations, tool calls, and reflections are appended to every prompt. This makes isolating the effect of any single memory component difficult and prompts grow indefinitely across runs.
AI.method: The authors introduce a bounded contract where each decision uses a fresh user message assembled by typed retrieval, with no raw cross-decision transcript appended. They instrument this in Slay the Spire 2, using a fixed-A0 ablation design and a cross-backbone probe for operational comparisons.
AI.result: No-store baseline wins 3/10 games; adding strategic skill layer wins 6/10 (directional, Fisher exact p≈0.37). Public benchmark reports zero wins across five frontier LLM configurations at lowest difficulty, while human win rate is 16%.
AI.conclusion: The bounded contract enables isolation of memory components and reproducible study of how explicit memory layers shape long-horizon LLM-agent decisions. The paper releases a testbed of 298 trajectories with condition tags, frozen snapshots, and analysis scripts.

title: A Memory Efficient Unified Algorithm for Online Learning of Linear Dynamical Systems
summary: Motivated by the challenge of stabilizing a general unknown linear dynamical system (LDS) from observations, we study the natural prerequisite of online prediction. Our goal is to achieve sublinear regret with a memory footprint that adapts to the intrinsic complexity of the dynamics rather than the full hidden -- state dimension. We focus on the practically central regime of systems with low instability complexity -- eigenvalues outside the real stable interval that do not decay rapidly, together with non-semisimple modes-potentially embedded in an otherwise stable real spectrum of much higher dimension; we write $k$ for this count. This regime is the primary setting in which stabilization is plausible: we show that many systems with high instability complexity cannot be stabilized without exponentially large controls. Thus, prediction is meaningful for stabilization precisely when the instability complexity is small. Within this regime, we introduce a unified online algorithm that handles every LDS (including non-diagonalizable systems with complex or exploding modes) with a learnable parameter count of $\widetilde{O}(k)$. Finally, we prove a lower bound showing that $k$ is a valid complexity measure: any filter-based predictor needs at least $k$ filters. Experiments corroborate our theory: on a high-dimensional system, our predictor sharply outperforms prior methods at an equal parameter budget.

AI.tldr: This paper studies online prediction for unknown linear dynamical systems (LDS) with low instability complexity $k$, showing that prediction is meaningful for stabilization primarily when $k$ is small. The authors propose a unified online algorithm with $\widetilde{O}(k)$ learnable parameters and prove a lower bound that any filter-based predictor needs at least $k$ filters.
AI.motivation: To stabilize a general unknown LDS from observations, online prediction is a prerequisite. The authors aim to achieve sublinear regret with a memory footprint that adapts to the intrinsic complexity of the dynamics (instability complexity $k$) rather than the full hidden-state dimension.
AI.method: The paper focuses on the regime of low instability complexity (eigenvalues outside the real stable interval that do not decay rapidly, plus non-semisimple modes). They introduce a unified online algorithm that handles every LDS (including non-diagonalizable systems with complex or exploding modes) with $\widetilde{O}(k)$ learnable parameters, and prove a lower bound that any filter-based predictor requires at least $k$ filters.
AI.result: The algorithm achieves sublinear regret with parameter count adapting to $k$ rather than full state dimension. Experiments show the predictor sharply outperforms prior methods at an equal parameter budget on high-dimensional systems.
AI.conclusion: Prediction is meaningful for stabilization precisely when instability complexity $k$ is small; systems with high instability complexity cannot be stabilized without exponentially large controls. The paper establishes $k$ as a valid complexity measure for filter-based prediction.

title: UnderOneFacade: Worldwide Facade Semantic Segmentation Benchmark Dataset
summary: Globally consistent semantic digital twins require centimeter-accurate and geographically transferable 3D facade segmentation. However, progress in facade parsing is limited by the lack of large-scale, standardized benchmarks for evaluating cross-domain generalization. Existing datasets are geographically narrow, semantically inconsistent, or insufficiently precise. We introduce UnderOneFacade, the largest cross-country and cross-continent 3D facade benchmark to date, comprising centimeter-accurate point clouds with hierarchical, harmonized, and architecturally grounded semantic labels totaling 2.7 billion annotated points. Through a systematic evaluation of representative point-, graph- and transformer-based architectures, we show that current methods struggle to recognize fine-grained architectural elements and degrade significantly across geographic domains, with the best models achieving only up to 33 IoU on the fine-grained LoFG3 benchmark. By combining geometric precision with standardized semantics at unprecedented scale, UnderOneFacade establishes a rigorous benchmark for developing robust and transferable 3D segmentation models. The dataset, evaluation scripts, and pretrained models will be released upon publication.

AI.tldr: UnderOneFacade is the largest cross-continent 3D facade benchmark with 2.7 billion centimeter-accurate annotated points, revealing that current segmentation models (point-, graph-, transformer-based) struggle with fine-grained architectural elements and cross-domain generalization (best models achieve only 33 IoU on fine-grained LoFG3).
AI.motivation: Existing facade parsing datasets are geographically narrow, semantically inconsistent, and lack precision, hindering the development of globally consistent and transferable 3D semantic digital twins.
AI.method: Constructed a large-scale cross-country and cross-continent 3D facade benchmark (UnderOneFacade) with centimeter-accurate point clouds, hierarchical harmonized architectural semantic labels totaling 2.7 billion annotated points. Systematically evaluated point-, graph-, and transformer-based architectures.
AI.result: Current methods degrade significantly across geographic domains; the best models achieve only up to 33 IoU on the fine-grained LoFG3 benchmark, indicating poor recognition of fine-grained architectural elements.
AI.conclusion: UnderOneFacade establishes a rigorous benchmark for developing robust and geographically transferable 3D facade segmentation models, addressing the gap in cross-domain generalization evaluation.

title: A Hippocampus for Linear Attention: An Exact Memory for What the Recurrent State Forgets
summary: Linear-attention and state-space language models compress the prefix into a fixed-size recurrent state, yielding O(1) memory at the cost of a lossy exact memory: when many key--value associations compete, earlier facts are overwritten and needle recall degrades. Inspired by Complementary Learning Systems, we give linear attention a hippocampal complement. HOLA (Hippocampal Linear Attention) keeps the usual delta-rule state as a compressive memory and adds a bounded exact KV cache, forming a semiparametric test-time memory: the state models linearly compressible structure, while the cache stores associations that should not be forced through that state. The cache writes without a learned eviction module, keeping tokens with large beta * ||e||, the prediction residual actually committed to the state; a decoupled RMSNorm-gamma cache read then turns these exact KV pairs into sharp retrieval rather than soft averaging. At 340M parameters trained on 15B SlimPajama tokens, HOLA lowers Wikitext perplexity from 27.32 to 22.92 (-16.1%), below a full-attention Transformer++ (26.88), and improves LAMBADA perplexity from 30.95 to 30.26. It also achieves the best linear in-context retrieval and remains much more robust than GDN or a matched HOLA+recency cache on RULER needle-in-a-haystack recall out to 32k tokens (16x its training length).

AI.tldr: HOLA augments linear-attention language models with a hippocampal-inspired bounded exact KV cache to improve long-context recall and language modeling perplexity.
AI.motivation: Linear-attention and state-space models compress prefixes into fixed-size recurrent states, achieving O(1) memory but suffering from lossy exact memory — earlier key-value associations are overwritten, degrading needle recall performance.
AI.method: HOLA adds a bounded exact KV cache as a hippocampal complement to the delta-rule compressive state. The cache stores tokens with large prediction residuals (beta * ||e||) without a learned eviction module, and uses a decoupled RMSNorm-gamma for sharp retrieval instead of soft averaging.
AI.result: At 340M/15B tokens, HOLA reduces Wikitext perplexity from 27.32 to 22.92 (16.1%↓, below Transformer++ at 26.88), improves LAMBADA from 30.95 to 30.26, achieves best linear in-context retrieval, and maintains robust RULER needle recall at 32k tokens (16x training length).
AI.conclusion: A hippocampal-style bounded exact cache effectively complements compressive linear-attention states, enabling semiparametric test-time memory that preserves recall of hard-to-compress associations without learned eviction, achieving strong long-context performance.

title: Beyond the Performance Illusion: Structure-Aware Stratified Partitioning and Curriculum Distributionally Robust Optimization for Spatially Correlated Domains
summary: Performance evaluation in AI systems commonly assumes that random dataset splits produce independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) subsets. We show that this assumption often breaks down in spatiotemporally correlated domains such as aerial surveillance, precision agriculture, and medical imaging, leading to two systematic failures: data leakage, where correlated samples span training and validation splits and inflate performance estimates, and hidden stratification, where errors on minority subpopulations are obscured by aggregate metrics. To address these issues, we propose a unified evaluation and training framework for spatially correlated data. We introduce Structure-Aware Stratified Partitioning (SASP), which constructs validation splits that reduce spatiotemporal leakage while preserving meaningful class balance, and Curriculum Distributionally Robust Optimization (CDRO), a curriculum-based relaxation of distributionally robust training that stabilizes optimization under these stricter splits. Across multiple benchmarks, this combination yields consistently improved generalization, more reliable confidence calibration, and exposes failure modes that remain hidden under conventional random-split evaluation.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies that random dataset splits fail in spatiotemporally correlated domains (aerial surveillance, agriculture, medical imaging), causing data leakage and hidden stratification. It proposes SASP for leakage-reduced validation splits and CDRO for robust training, improving generalization and calibration over conventional methods.
AI.motivation: Standard i.i.d. assumption in random dataset splits is invalid for spatiotemporally correlated data, leading to inflated performance estimates (data leakage) and obscured errors on minority subpopulations (hidden stratification).
AI.method: Two-component framework: (1) Structure-Aware Stratified Partitioning (SASP) constructs validation splits that minimize spatiotemporal leakage while preserving class balance; (2) Curriculum Distributionally Robust Optimization (CDRO) applies a curriculum-based relaxation of distributionally robust training to stabilize optimization under non-i.i.d. splits.
AI.result: Across multiple benchmarks, the combination yields improved generalization, more reliable confidence calibration, and exposes failure modes hidden under conventional random-split evaluation.
AI.conclusion: Spatiotemporal correlation in AI benchmarks requires structure-aware evaluation and training; SASP+CDRO addresses both data leakage and hidden stratification effectively.

title: Spatio-Temporal and Clinical Conditioning for Fine-Grained Radiology Report Retrieval
summary: Radiology is vital to modern healthcare, but rising imaging demand and persistent workforce shortages strain reporting capacity and clinical workflows. Automated radiology report generation has the potential to support radiologists and help alleviate this burden; however, existing retrieval-based methods remain rigid, lack explicit anatomical grounding, and do not account for longitudinal disease progression or available clinical context. In this work, we introduce STAR3, a multimodal, spatio-temporal, attentive retrieval framework for radiology report generation that aligns region-level anatomical information with clinical indications and longitudinal changes across chest X-ray studies. Our framework employs an object detector to identify anatomically meaningful regions and retrieves semantically relevant report sentences conditioned on both current clinical context and changes observed between prior and current examinations. This design enables anatomically and temporally grounded report generation that better reflects clinical reporting practice. Experiments on the MIMIC-CXR dataset demonstrate that STAR3 outperforms current retrieval-based approaches on retrieval, NLP and clinical metrics, highlighting the value of conditioning retrieval anatomically, temporally and clinically for advancing automated radiology report generation.

AI.tldr: STAR3 is a multimodal retrieval framework for radiology report generation that uses anatomical region detection, clinical context, and longitudinal changes across chest X-rays to produce more clinically grounded reports, outperforming existing retrieval-based methods on MIMIC-CXR.
AI.motivation: Rising imaging demand and workforce shortages strain radiology reporting capacity; existing retrieval-based methods are rigid, lack anatomical grounding, and fail to account for longitudinal disease progression or clinical context.
AI.method: STAR3 uses an object detector to identify anatomically meaningful regions and retrieves semantically relevant report sentences conditioned on both current clinical context and changes observed between prior and current chest X-ray examinations.
AI.result: On the MIMIC-CXR dataset, STAR3 outperforms current retrieval-based approaches on retrieval, NLP, and clinical metrics.
AI.conclusion: Conditioning retrieval anatomically, temporally, and clinically is valuable for advancing automated radiology report generation toward more clinically reflective practice.

title: Grounded autonomous research: a fault-tolerant LLM pipeline from corpus to manuscript in frontier computational physics
comment: 39 pages, 5 figures. Accepted at the ICML 2026 AI for Science Workshop (https://openreview.net/forum?id=R5YXaPgUAx). Includes the pipeline-generated companion physics manuscript as an appendix. Data and scaffolding archive: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21126996
summary: Autonomous-research agents have demonstrated end-to-end LLM automation in machine-learning sandboxes where execution provides calibration. Frontier physical science differs categorically: physical reasoning underlies every methodology choice, toolchains are often underdocumented, and calibration must come from external literature anchors - which unscaffolded agents cite but do not confront, hallucinating plausible, unverifiable results from internal priors. We present a pipeline that runs end-to-end from a corpus of 11,083 recent condensed-matter physics arXiv papers to a publication-grade manuscript with three substantive physics findings (here on altermagnetic piezomagnetism): the agent autonomously conceives a research direction by mapping the corpus, calibrates methodology by reproducing published references, conducts novel first-principles computations, and writes the manuscript - grounded in literature throughout, across 47 fresh-context sessions in six phases sharing only on-disk state, with 2,162 literature-consultation events. Fault tolerance emerges from redundancy: fresh-context isolation, distributed grounding, and adversarial review catch what any single session misses; pre- and post-pilot stages are fully autonomous, and pilot requires bounded human intervention only at reproduction failures - operational knowledge curation, not scientific direction. Two paired failure modes - a pre-architecture baseline and a no-pilot ablation - isolate structurally enforced numerical confrontation at calibration checkpoints as the operative grounding mechanism. The primitives, characterized failure modes, and quantified intervention pattern lay a foundation for autonomous research in high-stakes scientific domains beyond computational physics.
